E. If you recognise the conflict only after the interview has begun, promptly terminate the session, explain that you must withdraw due to a conflict, avoid sharing unnecessary personal details, and arrange appropriate referral pathways.

F. Reallocate the case internally to a colleague by informing your practice manager of a conflict (without disclosing intimate details), and have no further involvement beyond an administrative handover.

question: A principal psychologist in a community clinic supervises a provisional psychologist (age 25, bilingual Hindi-English). A 17-year-old client with recent self-harm and moderate suicide risk is referred by their parents, who prefer sessions conducted largely in Hindi. To manage demand, the principal suggests the supervisee act as an interpreter for the treating clinician and to help produce culturally tailored marketing materials by drawing from de-identified session notes. Which action by the principal best upholds the ethical principle of not exploiting assistants/employees/supervisees while managing clinical risk and confidentiality?
options: A. Arrange a certified health-care interpreter for the sessions (with client/parent consent) and ensure the supervisee is not pressured to interpret outside their role; clarify workload, boundaries, and supervision specific to suicide risk management.
B. Offer the supervisee time-in-lieu for interpreting after hours and ask them to draft marketing content informed by de-identified notes as part of their professional development.
C. Permit the supervisee to provide ad hoc interpretation during therapy only when communication breaks down, and count those minutes toward supervision hours to support competency development.
D. Make interpreting a condition of continuing the placement but pay the supervisee at a casual rate for those hours to avoid exploitation.
E. Ask the supervisee to attend sessions as an observer but step in as a cultural broker when needed and refrain from documenting these contributions to protect confidentiality.

question: A senior clinical psychologist in private practice is responsible for a court-ordered parenting capacity assessment (forensic purpose) with a tight deadline. A newly hired registrar (employee) has appropriate training to administer tests under supervision. The senior learns a colleague in the same practice is dating one of the parents being assessed. The senior is considering how to allocate tasks and manage the deadline. Which actions are ethically appropriate and avoid exploiting the employee/colleague relationship? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Request an extension from the court/solicitor if needed, schedule tasks within paid hours, compensate any optional after-hours work, provide authorship/acknowledgment commensurate with contribution, and disclose and wall off the colleague due to the conflict.
B. Offer the registrar a strong reference and future opportunities in exchange for completing unpaid weekend report-writing, while retaining sole authorship for a unified expert voice.
C. Permit the registrar to administer psychometrics under documented supervision during paid time and credit their contribution (co-authorship or acknowledgment) proportionate to work performed.
D. Have the registrar draft the report while the senior edits and pays overtime, but list only the senior as author because the registrar is not yet endorsed and should not be named.

E. To mitigate the colleague’s conflict, instruct the registrar to testify as the sole witness to testing procedures while the senior signs the report, since the registrar has no personal ties to either parent.

F. Remove the colleague from any involvement in the matter, document the firewall, and invite the registrar to observe court proceedings during paid time with clear learning objectives and the option to decline without penalty.

question: During CBT for a 17-year-old Aboriginal male with major depressive disorder and recent suicidal ideation, a provisional psychologist (under supervision) prepares a single-case manuscript for a practice journal. The provisional conducted most sessions, drafted the manuscript, and analysed session measures. The registered supervisor provided clinical oversight, co-developed the case formulation and safety plan, and made substantial editorial revisions. An Aboriginal health worker facilitated engagement with family and offered cultural guidance in sessions but did not help draft or revise the paper. The service manager, who had no clinical involvement, asks to be listed as an author to recognise the program. Which option best aligns with ethical authorship assignment?
options: A. List the provisional psychologist as first author to reflect primary contribution; include the supervisor as a co-author for substantive supervisory input and critical revisions; acknowledge the health worker and service manager unless they meet standard authorship criteria.

B. Put the supervisor as first author due to legal responsibility for client care and the provisional’s training status; list the provisional second and add the service manager to reflect organisational oversight.

C. Include the Aboriginal health worker as a co-author to recognise cultural expertise and minimise perceptions of cultural insensitivity, even though they did not contribute to drafting or revising the manuscript.
D. Offer co–first authorship to the provisional and supervisor to recognise both the supervisor’s clinical responsibility and the provisional’s writing effort.
E. Add the consulting psychiatrist as an author because risk management was central to the case, even though they did not contribute to the manuscript’s conception, drafting, or revision.

question: A clinical psychologist leads a Family Court child custody assessment involving a Muslim father and two children. The team plans a methods paper about the assessment model using anonymised data. Dr Nguyen designed the battery, integrated findings, and drafted ~70% of the manuscript. Aisha (doctoral student) scored psychometrics, ran reliability checks, and drafted the methods section (~20%). Imam Ali (cultural consultant) advised on culturally appropriate interviewing and provided substantive interpretive feedback and revisions that were incorporated. Mara (social worker) collected collateral interviews and supplied notes but did not participate in analysis or drafting. Liam (research assistant) transcribed recordings and formatted tables. Prof Chen (service director) obtained the contract but did not contribute to conception, analysis, drafting, or revision, and now insists on senior authorship. Which actions best align with ethical authorship assignment in this context?
options: A. Assign first authorship to Dr Nguyen; include Aisha and Imam Ali as co-authors given their substantial intellectual and writing/revision contributions; acknowledge Mara and Liam; do not include Prof Chen based solely on funding or seniority.
B. Add Prof Chen as last author to recognise leadership in securing the contract and to maintain institutional harmony, even though there was no intellectual or drafting contribution.
C. Include Mara as a co-author because data collection is vital and authorship would support career development, despite no involvement in interpretation or manuscript drafts.
D. List Imam Ali only in acknowledgements because he is not a registered psychologist, despite substantive contributions to interpretation and revisions.
E. Offer co–first authorship to Dr Nguyen and Aisha to reflect mentoring and team cohesion, even though their writing contributions were approximately 70% and 20%, respectively.
F. Before submission, discuss and document contribution-based authorship criteria and order with all contributors, and revisit if subsequent revisions change the magnitude of contributions.

question: Maia, a 22-year-old Aboriginal Australian master’s student, completed her thesis analysing de-identified routine outcome monitoring data from adolescents receiving CBT for PTSD at a community clinic. Her clinical supervisor, Dr. Chen, directs the clinic and provided weekly supervision on the cases. They plan to submit a multi-authored paper that presents the same research questions, methods, and primary analyses as Maia’s thesis (with minor edits for journal style). Dr. Chen argues he should be first author because he designed the clinic workflow and obtained the service-wide ethics approval; he proposes listing Maia second. The clinic manager suggests ordering authors alphabetically to avoid perceptions of favouritism given Maia’s Aboriginal identity. Which approach best upholds ethical authorship practice?
options: A. Name Maia as first author because the manuscript is substantially based on her thesis; determine and document co-authorship and order for others according to their specific contributions, and ensure appropriate consent/de-identification before submission.
B. List Dr. Chen first as the senior clinician and custodian of the dataset, with Maia second, since authorship should reflect organisational ownership and service design responsibilities.
C. Use alphabetical author ordering to avoid bias related to Maia’s cultural identity and to appear impartial.
D. Delay submission until Maia is fully registered so that authorship can be reassigned to whomever performs most of the journal rewrite at that time.
E. Designate Dr. Chen and Maia as co–first authors but list Dr. Chen first with an equal-contribution footnote because he oversaw clinical risk and service design.

question: Lina, a 29-year-old international doctoral student, completed a dissertation on the validity of a neuropsychological screener for adults with severe TBI undergoing court-ordered fitness-to-plead evaluations. The team now prepares a multi-authored journal article that keeps the same research questions, measures, and primary analyses as Lina’s thesis, adds 18 new cases collected after her thesis under the same protocol, and includes one additional exploratory ROC analysis proposed by her supervisor, Dr. Patel, a clinical psychologist who is also serving as an expert witness in several related matters. The team includes a hospital speech pathologist and a biostatistician. Dr. Patel proposes listing himself first because he contributed the new cases, added the exploratory analysis, and holds medico-legal accountability; Lina would be second. Lina is now employed at the hospital as a provisional psychologist and is concerned about challenging her supervisor. Client files are de-identified and ethical approvals are in place. Which of the following are ethically appropriate steps or authorship arrangements? Select all that apply.
options: A. Retain Lina as first author because the manuscript remains substantially based on her dissertation’s research questions, dataset framework, and primary analyses; order other co-authors by their actual contributions.
B. Move Dr. Patel to first author because more than one-third of the final dataset and a new analysis were added post-thesis, making seniority and data ownership the deciding factors.

C. Establish and document a transparent authorship agreement that acknowledges the supervisory power imbalance, allows for independent mediation if needed, and revisits order only if the work ceases to be substantially thesis-based.
D. List authors alphabetically to neutralise perceptions of bias given Lina’s international student status and current employment relationship.
E. Remove Lina from the author list to avoid a dual-role conflict now that she is employed by the hospital where the data were collected.

F. Keep Lina as first author if she leads the drafting and the theoretical framing derives from her dissertation, even with the added cases and exploratory analysis; include Dr. Patel and others proportionally as co-authors.

question: A clinical psychologist is planning a public webinar on adolescent self-harm. One illustrative case involves a 15-year-old bisexual student referred by their school for depression and a history of self-harm (no current imminent risk). The parent is enthusiastic and asks the psychologist to thank the young person by first name during the webinar. The young person is ambivalent and has not agreed. Which actions are most consistent with the ethical principle that psychologists obtain consent before identifying people as contributors to published or presented material? Select all that apply.
options: A. Before identifying the client in any way, assess the young person’s decision-making capacity (e.g., Gillick competence) and, if competent, obtain their explicit informed consent (and parental consent if required by law) to be named; if consent is not granted, present the material fully de-identified without any public acknowledgment of their contribution.
B. Proceed with a pseudonym and altered details but verbally thank “the courageous Year 10 student from Southbank” for allowing their story to be shared, relying on the parent’s written consent.
C. Rely on the general intake form that permits use of “de-identified case material for education” and include a brief acknowledgment of the client by first name during the webinar.

D. Consult with a supervisor/ethics lead to evaluate capacity; if the young person is competent and declines being named, do not identify them in the webinar or promotional materials at all, even if the parent wishes otherwise.
E. Seek permission from the school deputy principal to acknowledge the student, since the school initiated the referral and holds a duty of care during school hours.

question: A clinical psychologist completed a court-ordered parenting capacity assessment of a well-known religious leader involved in a custody dispute. The psychologist plans to present on managing high-profile litigants at a national conference and is considering acknowledging the client for his “insightful feedback” and quoting a line from the interview. The court and the other party’s lawyer have indicated there is no legal impediment to presenting the work if confidentiality is protected. Which option best meets the ethical principle regarding consent before identifying contributors? Select ONE.
options: A. Because court reports may enter the public record and the client is a public figure, it is permissible to name him in the presentation without further consent.

B. Obtain explicit informed consent from the client to be identified by name as a contributor (ideally in writing), clarifying the scope and permanence of public identification; if he declines, omit any identifying acknowledgment and ensure any case discussion is truly de-identified.
C. Seek permission from the client’s solicitor to identify the client, as the solicitor can authorise acknowledgments related to court matters.
D. Use the client’s initials and role (e.g., “E.S., a Sydney imam”) and state that he approved the draft without his consent, as initials are a standard de-identification technique.
E. Rely on the court’s approval to disseminate the case as a substitute for the client’s consent to being identified, given the legal context.

question: You are treating Sam, a 17-year-old transgender male with major depressive disorder under a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan. He arrives 25 minutes late due to public transport issues. In session, he discloses escalating suicidal ideation but denies imminent intent or plan. His mother, who struggles financially, asks you to bill today as a full 50-minute session so they can obtain the higher Medicare rebate. Which option best upholds the principle that psychologists are honest in their financial dealings?
options: A. Bill for a full 50-minute session to reduce the family’s financial burden, document the session as extended due to risk, and schedule a free phone check-in later.

B. Charge only for the actual clinical time provided (or as per your disclosed late/cancellation policy), conduct a focused risk assessment and safety plan within that time, and avoid claiming a longer session than delivered.
C. Waive the client’s out-of-pocket fee but still claim a full-length Medicare item, counting any later after-hours phone contact toward the billed duration.
D. Rebook a no-charge 25-minute follow-up and combine today’s contact with the follow-up in your notes as a single 50-minute appointment to bill under one item number.

question: Dr Lee is completing a psychoeducational assessment for Amir, a 9-year-old bilingual Arabic–English student with suspected learning disorder. The school has agreed to fund the assessment and report by a deadline. Amir’s mother asks if the work can be billed as several ‘therapy’ sessions to attract Medicare rebates instead. A tutoring centre that often receives Dr Lee’s assessment referrals offers a $150 ‘thank-you’ bonus for reports that recommend their program. Which actions are consistent with being honest in financial dealings?
options: A. Decline to mislabel assessment as therapy for Medicare billing, provide a clear written quote for the assessment components, and avoid double-charging the school and the family; offer a payment plan if needed.
B. Accept the tutoring centre’s $150 bonus without telling the family or the school because it does not increase the fee charged to them and therefore does not disadvantage the client.

C. Invoice the school only for the actual hours of testing and report writing conducted, and invoice the parent separately for a distinct feedback session if requested, with each invoice accurately describing the service delivered.
D. For the family’s financial benefit, list portions of the assessment as brief therapy sessions focused on coping skills so that Medicare can reimburse some of the time.

E. Propose a staged assessment: complete essential testing now at a lower fee and, if indicated, offer optional additional subtests later; ensure charges match work completed and avoid pre-billing for unrendered services.

question: A 16‑year‑old (Year 11 student) with moderate depression is referred under a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan. Her separated parents share parental responsibility. Her father agrees to pay the gap fee but insists that the psychologist provide him with brief progress updates after each session as a condition of continuing to pay. The adolescent expresses discomfort with this and wants her session content kept private. What is the most ethical course of action that aligns with proper financial arrangements?
options: A. Accept the father’s condition and provide brief progress summaries after each session since he is funding the gap fee and shares parental responsibility.

B. Before commencing, provide a written agreement clarifying fees, who is responsible for payment, cancellation policy, and the limits of confidentiality; explain that payment cannot be contingent on clinical disclosures; offer non-specific updates (e.g., attendance, invoices) only with the adolescent’s consent or when legally/clinically required, and if the father insists, decline or refer.
C. Begin therapy immediately and finalise the financial arrangements with the father at month’s end to avoid delaying care.
D. Require the adolescent to sign a blanket release authorising the father full access to session notes in exchange for payment, documenting the consent.
E. Send invoices with session dates directly to the father without discussing this with the adolescent to avoid awkwardness about who is paying.

question: A solicitor refers a 28‑year‑old Aboriginal man with a history of PTSD for a workers’ compensation psychological impairment assessment. The solicitor proposes a “success bonus” if your report supports the claim and asks you to defer most payment until the matter is won. Which actions are ethically appropriate under the principle of proper financial arrangements? Select all that apply.
options: A. Decline the contingency arrangement and offer a written agreement specifying a fixed fee or standard hourly rate (payable regardless of outcome), scope of service, cancellation policy, and limits of confidentiality; emphasise that opinions will be independent of payer interests.
B. Accept the contingency fee but mitigate by disclosing in the report that your payment is outcome‑dependent.
C. Shift the financial responsibility to the examinee and bill him directly without informing the solicitor, to avoid third‑party influence.
D. Proceed at your standard fee but agree to send a draft report to the solicitor for edits because they are funding the assessment.
E. If the solicitor refuses a non‑contingent agreement, decline the referral and provide the firm with names of other independent providers without disclosing any client information.
F. Convert the referral into treatment to reduce costs and write a supportive treatment letter instead of a formal independent assessment.

question: You are providing therapy to Ms. Linh, a 72-year-old Vietnamese Australian woman with limited English proficiency who has major depressive disorder with psychotic features. She is not at imminent risk but needs a medication review by a psychiatrist. A local multilingual psychiatry group, Harbour Psych, offers to: (1) pay you a $100 “liaison fee” per referral; (2) fast-track your clients if you refer exclusively to them; and (3) host a catered CPD evening for your practice if you join their ‘preferred referrer’ program. Which of the following actions are ethically appropriate under the principle that psychologists do not receive or give any remuneration for referring clients to, or accepting referrals from, other professionals?
options: A. Decline any financial or in-kind benefits linked to referrals, avoid exclusive arrangements, and provide Ms. Linh with a choice of psychiatrists (including Vietnamese-speaking clinicians and/or interpreter-supported services), documenting the clinical rationale for each option.
B. Accept the $100 liaison fee but donate the money to a mental health charity and disclose this to Ms. Linh, as you will not personally profit.

C. Decline the cash but accept the ‘priority access’ and catered CPD offered in exchange for referring only to Harbour Psych; explain to Ms. Linh that these are non-monetary and improve continuity of care.
D. Provide only Harbour Psych’s details because of language match and reduced wait time, and ask them to credit the liaison fee to Ms. Linh’s sessions with you to lower her out-of-pocket costs.

E. Explain you cannot enter any incentive or exclusivity arrangement; if Ms. Linh prefers Harbour Psych, request an urgent appointment without any quid pro quo, while also giving her at least two alternative options (e.g., other Vietnamese-speaking psychiatrists or services with interpreters).
F. Ask Ms. Linh to sign a specific consent acknowledging the incentive arrangement; with her consent documented, proceed with the referral to Harbour Psych under the program.

G. If coordinating the referral is time-consuming, discuss and obtain informed consent to bill Ms. Linh a transparent, time-based coordination fee that is independent of which psychiatrist she chooses.

question: You are conducting a private ADHD and learning assessment for Jordan, a 19-year-old non-binary university student on a student visa with financial stressors. A telepsychiatry company, FocusMed, emails offering a $60 per-client ‘administrative reimbursement’ for each ADHD client you refer for medication review, and proposes reciprocal referrals (they will send their medication-managed clients to you for therapy). They also ask you to list FocusMed as your ‘preferred prescriber’ in reports. There is no imminent risk. Which option aligns with ethical requirements regarding remuneration for referrals?
options: A. Accept the $60 per referral but apply it as a discount to Jordan’s assessment fee; include the arrangement in the consent form for transparency.

B. Decline any per-referral payments and reciprocal referral agreements; provide Jordan with a neutral list of several psychiatrists/GPs (including FocusMed if appropriate) and explicitly state you receive no incentives; do not designate a ‘preferred’ provider.
C. Agree to list FocusMed as preferred only if they fast-track and bulk-bill non-binary clients; as this promotes equity, the arrangement becomes ethically permissible.
D. Accept incoming referrals from FocusMed’s psychiatrists in exchange for sending your clients to them, but cap the volume and monitor for bias to manage conflicts.
E. Decline the $60 payment but accept FocusMed’s offer of free software access for ADHD scales that applies only to clients you refer to them, since it is not cash.

question: A 27-year-old transgender woman you previously treated for major depressive disorder and gender dysphoria has lodged a complaint with Ahpra alleging you misgendered her and failed to respond to a crisis email. The Psychology Board of Australia writes to you requesting the full clinical record for the therapy episode, including intake forms, progress notes, risk assessments, and any psychometric test data. You are concerned about releasing sensitive information about her sexual history and trauma without her consent. What is the MOST ethical and professionally appropriate response?
options: A. Promptly acknowledge the request, notify your professional indemnity insurer, seek legal/peer consultation as needed, and provide the requested records in full and within the specified timeframe, limiting disclosure only if lawfully negotiated with the regulator; avoid contacting the complainant about the complaint.
B. Decline to provide any records until the former client provides explicit written consent, because confidentiality always prevents disclosure to third parties.
C. Provide only a therapist-generated summary of treatment rather than the full file to preserve client confidentiality, unless the client authorises full disclosure.
D. Contact the former client to clarify allegations and see if the complaint can be withdrawn before you respond, to avoid unnecessary disclosure of sensitive material.

question: You completed a court-ordered forensic risk assessment of a 16-year-old Aboriginal boy referred in the context of a custody dispute. Months later, the APS Ethics Committee requests your file and an affidavit because your report has been cited in a complaint against a colleague who later began therapy with the youth. There is no current indication of imminent risk to self or others. Which actions are ethically appropriate and consistent with your duty to cooperate with the investigation? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Respond in writing before the stated deadline confirming your intention to cooperate, and seek advice from your indemnity insurer and/or a lawyer before disclosing records to ensure your response is accurate and appropriately bounded.

B. Provide the requested records directly to the APS Ethics Committee without seeking client consent, limiting disclosure to what is formally requested; include relevant test data if specifically requested by the Committee, noting any proprietary restrictions where applicable.
C. Decline to provide records because the assessment was court-ordered, stating that only the court may access the materials and the professional society lacks authority.
D. Contact the colleague who is the subject of the complaint to compare recollections and ensure your affidavit aligns with their account before sending it to the Committee.

E. Do not alter existing entries in the file; instead, create a dated addendum that transparently corrects minor clerical errors or clarifies interpretations, and disclose both the original record and the addendum.
F. Decline to engage with the APS investigation and propose to mediate directly with the family to resolve the dispute informally and avoid reputational harm to the profession.

question: You are providing therapy to a 17-year-old transgender client with recurrent major depression and a prior suicide attempt. They report that a previous psychologist advised them to halve their SSRI dose without consulting the GP and gave them a printed tapering schedule. The client is experiencing increased low mood and dizziness. The client asks you not to 'dob in' the previous psychologist. There is no current imminent risk, but you consider the advice a significant departure from accepted practice (psychologists in Australia cannot prescribe or direct medication changes). Which actions best meet your ethical obligations under the Code at this point?
options: A. Seek the client’s consent to contact the previous psychologist (or, if more appropriate, their clinical director) to draw attention to the potential breach, cite the relevant Code sections on competence and professional responsibility, and request they cease providing medication advice; document your steps.

B. Encourage the client (and their parent/guardian, given the client’s age) to submit a complaint to the Psychology Board of Australia or the APS Ethics Committee; provide information on how to lodge a report and offer support.

C. Report the conduct yourself to the Psychology Board of Australia or the APS Ethics Committee, providing only necessary information, given the potential risk from a significant departure from professional standards.

D. Present the case with full identifying details, including the colleague’s name, to your peer supervision group to see if others have had similar concerns, and delay any contact or report until you have group consensus.
E. Ask the client to covertly record any future interactions with the previous psychologist to gather stronger evidence before taking any formal action.
F. Refer the client back to their GP for medication issues and take no further steps about the colleague to avoid inter-professional conflict.

question: You are engaged in a forensic context to peer-review a custody evaluation report authored by Dr S, your former supervisor, in a small rural community. The report assigns diagnoses without direct assessment and quotes therapy notes from the child’s mother without documented consent. It also contains stereotyped statements about the mother’s religious practices. A court order restricts disclosure of the report to the court and the instructing solicitor; there is no imminent risk to safety. You suspect ethical breaches and a conflict of interest. Which TWO actions most directly fulfill your obligations under the Code while respecting the legal context?
options: A. Email Dr S directly with your concerns and attach the full report to invite corrections prior to filing your review.

B. Encourage the instructing solicitor (who is directly affected by the report) to consider lodging a complaint with the Psychology Board of Australia or the APS Ethics Committee; offer to provide your review if requested through proper channels.
C. Limit your response to filing a robust critique with the court and take no ethical action, because the court’s oversight supersedes professional codes.
D. Report concerns to a senior psychologist at Dr S’s practice so they can address it internally, even though the report is subject to a court confidentiality order.
E. Lodge your own complaint with the relevant regulatory body, enclosing only necessary information and noting the constraints of the court’s order.
F. Decline the review due to the prior supervisory relationship and take no further action to avoid perceptions of bias.

question: Priya, a clinical psychologist in a community clinic, hears from the mother of a 15-year-old transgender client that another local psychologist, Dr Lee, "refused to use their pronouns" and told the teen it was "just a phase." The teen reportedly presented to the emergency department last week with suicidal ideation. The mother urges Priya to report Dr Lee immediately. Priya has not met the teen, has not seen any records, and the mother declines consent to share documentation. Considering the principle that psychologists do not lodge, or endorse the lodging, of trivial, vexatious or unsubstantiated complaints, what is the MOST ethical next step?
options: A. Immediately lodge a notification with Ahpra/PsyBA detailing the allegations without identifying the client, to protect the public from potential harm.

B. Explain that you cannot lodge or endorse a complaint based solely on hearsay; prioritise the young person's immediate safety, and with appropriate consent and consultation (e.g., supervisor/ethics helpline), seek further information; consider formal reporting only if substantial evidence of serious breach emerges.

C. Encourage the mother to submit a complaint right away to "force a review," even though she will not provide documentation, because alleged discrimination toward a transgender youth is too serious to wait.
D. Email Dr Lee's employer describing the allegations and naming the teenager to prompt internal action, without client consent, given the public interest.

question: Ethan, a clinical psychologist, is providing therapy to a 38-year-old mother involved in Family Court proceedings. The court-appointed independent family assessment was conducted by Ms Nguyen, a colleague. The client is distressed and alleges Ms Nguyen was biased toward the father, who has a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder. She asks Ethan to co-sign a formal ethics complaint against Ms Nguyen and offers to pay for his time. Ethan has not read the assessment and only knows the client's account. In line with the principle against lodging or endorsing trivial, vexatious, or unsubstantiated complaints, which actions are ethically appropriate? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Decline to endorse or co-sign the complaint without firsthand evidence; explain appropriate avenues to challenge the assessment (e.g., via her solicitor, cross-examination, or seeking a properly instructed second opinion); document the discussion.
B. Agree to co-sign the complaint based on the client's report, noting you were not involved in the assessment, to ensure her concerns are taken seriously.

C. Offer, subject to court orders and written consent, to review the report within your competence solely to inform the client's understanding; if you identify clear, evidence-based ethical breaches, advise on proper complaint pathways.

D. Provide a general letter of support for inclusion with the ethics complaint, describing the client's distress and disputing the assessor's impressions, while avoiding clinical details to protect confidentiality.

E. Seek consultation from a supervisor or ethics advisory line regarding role boundaries and potential conflicts; maintain therapeutic focus and avoid advocacy that would create a multiple relationship with forensic implications.

question: You receive a referral for Casey, a 16-year-old transgender student experiencing significant anxiety. Casey asks you not to share session details with their parent, who is conservative and has requested regular updates. There is no imminent risk. Your practice encourages clinicians to pre-book discounted 12-session packages for all new clients. Casey also asks whether medication could help. What actions best align with acting in the client’s best interests and with professional obligations under the Code?
options: A. Begin by explaining confidentiality and its limits to both Casey and the parent; assess Casey’s decision-making capacity to consent to treatment; explore Casey’s preferences (e.g., telehealth/after-hours for privacy); avoid pre-booking any session package until collaboratively agreeing a plan tailored to Casey; discuss evidence-based options and, if needed, arrange referrals.
B. Offer a discounted 12-session package upfront to ensure treatment consistency and reduce cancellations; this aligns with CBT protocols and practice policy.

C. Provide general psychoeducation about anxiety treatments, including that medication may be helpful for some people, and recommend Casey discuss any medication questions with their GP or a psychiatrist; avoid recommending a specific drug or dose yourself.
D. Provide periodic summaries to the parent about progress and themes, even if Casey does not agree, to support parental oversight while avoiding specific details.
E. Seek supervision/peer consultation to ensure competent, affirming practice with trans youth; if outside your competence, discuss and plan a supported referral with Casey.
F. Accept a small gift card the parent offers at intake as a token of thanks, documenting it, to avoid damaging rapport early in treatment.

question: You are appointed by the Family Court to conduct a parenting capacity assessment in a custody dispute. Three years ago, you provided six couples therapy sessions to the father; there has been no contact since. The mother is a recent refugee with limited English; the father suggests a respected community leader act as interpreter. He also offers to pay a higher fee for an expedited report due to an upcoming hearing. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: A. Disclose your prior therapeutic relationship with the father to the court and both parties; seek direction about recusal and, if proceeding, use a certified interpreter for the mother; decline any expedited-fee arrangement; clarify your obligations (primary duty to the court and transparency to all parties) and document your decisions.
B. Proceed without disclosure because the prior therapy was brief and ended years ago; objectivity and thorough documentation will manage any concerns.
C. Accept the father’s expedited fee provided receipts are issued and you apply the same offer to the mother; this is a standard commercial practice and will not affect your findings.
D. Use the community leader as interpreter with consent to build trust and cultural safety, given that formal interpreters can feel intimidating.
E. Immediately withdraw from the matter to avoid any perception of conflict, without informing the court, and ask your administration to reallocate the case.

question: You begin therapy with a 17-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander student referred by their GP after a recent escalation of depressive symptoms. They report passive suicidal thoughts without a plan or intent. The GP commenced an SSRI one week ago. The client's mother is highly concerned and asks you for detailed session notes. The school counsellor has emailed requesting an update. In the first session, the client expresses hesitancy about involving school but is open to some family support. Which actions best align with practising safely, effectively, and in partnership with the client and associated parties, informed by best evidence? Select all that apply.
options: A. Explain confidentiality and its limits; collaboratively negotiate what information (if any) can be shared with the mother and school; obtain and document the client's informed consent preferences; co-develop a culturally appropriate safety plan (including after-hours supports) and, with consent, coordinate with the GP regarding risk and treatment.

B. To build trust, promise the client absolute confidentiality in all circumstances (including risk) and proceed with therapy (e.g., CBT) without contacting the GP to avoid overwhelming the client early on.
C. Provide psychoeducation on antidepressants and advise the client to halve the SSRI dose until therapy takes effect to minimise side effects, while scheduling more frequent sessions.

D. Schedule frequent sessions and immediately arrange a case conference with the GP and school even if the client refuses, because safety considerations always override adolescent consent regardless of current risk level.

E. Use validated measures (e.g., PHQ-9, K10) and culturally safe frameworks; discuss the option of involving an Aboriginal Health Worker or community Elder if the client agrees; document the evidence base and rationale for chosen interventions and monitoring.

F. Clarify to the mother that, given the client's age and decision-making capacity, detailed clinical information cannot be shared without the client's consent; offer to discuss general support strategies and emergency contacts, and revisit consent with the client at the next session.

question: You have been treating Mr Lee for generalised anxiety disorder for 8 months. Mr Lee’s solicitor emails requesting that you conduct a parenting capacity assessment for an ongoing custody dispute and submit an expert report to the Family Court. You have not received any subpoena or court order. What is the most appropriate response to practise safely, effectively, and in partnership with relevant parties while avoiding conflicts of interest?
options: A. Accept the assessment but terminate therapy immediately to avoid a dual role; disclose your prior treatment and obtain consent from both parties; rely on standardised measures to ensure objectivity.

B. Decline to conduct the custody/parenting assessment due to the conflict of interest created by your therapeutic role; with Mr Lee’s informed consent and subject to legal processes, provide a factual treatment summary if requested; recommend referral to an independent forensic psychologist for the evaluation.
C. Agree to assess only the child and the other parent, not Mr Lee, to minimise bias while maintaining involvement.
D. Proceed with the evaluation because the solicitor’s request implies the court’s approval; include a detailed statement of limitations about your prior treatment to mitigate concerns.
E. Decline any involvement, including any release of information, even if later served with a lawful subpoena, to protect the therapeutic relationship.

question: A rural psychologist is asked to assess Jayden, a 16-year-old Aboriginal student, for suspected ADHD to inform school supports. Jayden’s grandmother attends; an Aboriginal Health Worker is available if they wish. Jayden worries about stigma and does not want the full report sent to school. The standard ADHD rating scales the psychologist usually uses have limited validation data for Aboriginal youth. What is the most ethically appropriate next step? Select the single best answer.
options: A. Proceed with the usual rating scales and a DSM-5 interview to expedite support, avoiding involvement of the Aboriginal Health Worker to reduce potential bias.

B. Discuss the purpose and process with Jayden and his grandmother; offer involvement of the Aboriginal Health Worker if they choose; use multiple information sources and culturally reflective approaches (including noting limitations of tools/norms), and agree on what information can be shared with the school via informed consent.
C. Decline the assessment due to limited test validation and refer to a metropolitan clinic 500 km away, without exploring telehealth, interim supports, or coordinating with the GP/school.
D. Provide the results first to the school so they can act quickly, then arrange feedback to Jayden and his grandmother afterward to avoid influencing their responses.
E. Replace standard measures with projective techniques because they are culture-free and avoid language issues.

question: A clinical psychologist is treating Asha, a 32-year-old transgender woman with GAD, referred by her GP who prescribes an SSRI. Asha asks to include her partner in some sessions and wants a letter supporting workplace adjustments after a recent panic episode. The psychologist will be on leave for six weeks soon and has limited experience with transgender clients. There is no imminent risk. Which actions are ethically appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: A. Explore Asha’s goals and preferences, obtain informed consent to involve her partner, and develop a shared, gender-affirming treatment plan; seek supervision or consultation to work within competence.
B. Advise Asha to increase her SSRI dosage with her GP before continuing psychotherapy, and pause therapy until medication changes take effect.
C. Write a detailed letter to the employer including diagnosis, medication regimen, and therapy content to strengthen the case for accommodations.
D. Plan for continuity by discussing the upcoming leave early, offering interim options and a warm handover if desired, and—only with consent—coordinating with the GP.
E. Decline partner involvement to maintain clearer boundaries and instead provide general updates to the partner by email without a formal release.

F. With Asha’s informed and specific consent, prepare a brief workplace letter focused on functional impacts and reasonable adjustments, avoiding unnecessary personal or diagnostic details, and review the letter with her before sending.

question: You are a rural general psychologist treating Arun, a 17-year-old student recently diagnosed with bipolar II by a psychiatrist. He reports passive suicidal ideation but no current plan or intent. He identifies as gay and is concerned about privacy in the small town. You have experience with adolescent depression/anxiety but limited experience with adolescent bipolar. The nearest specialist service is 300 km away; the psychiatrist is open to collaborative care. Which actions best uphold competent, safe practice in this situation?
options: A. Continue with standard CBT for depression, avoid detailed discussion of suicidal ideation to prevent iatrogenic risk, and do not seek consultation to protect confidentiality.

B. Arrange regular consultation/supervision with a child/adolescent clinician experienced in bipolar disorder; with Arun’s consent, liaise with the psychiatrist/GP; co-create and review a documented safety plan and crisis pathway; provide psychoeducation; and revisit referral/telehealth options with Arun.
C. Provide weekly therapy and ask his parents for regular risk updates without informing Arun, as he is a minor and parents should be involved in risk management.

D. Offer a joint telehealth session (with consent) with a city-based specialist to support care planning; discuss benefits/risks of local versus specialist care; monitor mood and risk using validated measures; and maintain detailed records.
E. Ask Arun to sign a no-suicide contract as primary risk management, then continue without further steps given his lack of plan or intent.

F. With Arun’s consent, engage a culturally safe support (e.g., LGBTIQA+ youth service) or cultural liaison if relevant, reflect on and manage any personal biases, and integrate this input into the case formulation and treatment plan.

question: A recruitment agency asks you to conduct a high-stakes pre-employment psychological assessment (including firearm suitability) for a 45-year-old applicant who is also your regular Pilates instructor. You have not completed specialised forensic/fitness-for-duty assessments in several years and have not used current standardised tools recently. The agency offers a significant fee and a short turnaround. What is the most ethically appropriate response?
options: A. Decline the assessment due to the dual relationship and lack of recent competence; disclose these reasons to the referrer, provide the applicant with information about suitable forensic psychologists, and offer to collaborate only within your competence if needed; document your decision-making.

B. Accept the case but update your knowledge by reading recent articles; use an interview and a general personality inventory due to time constraints; disclose the dual relationship in the report to ensure transparency.

C. Accept conditionally: complete a brief CPD module and seek ad hoc supervision while conducting the assessment; inform the applicant of the limits of your competence and their right to a second opinion.
D. Accept the referral but request that the agency assign a different applicant to you to avoid a dual relationship; if they insist you keep the case, reduce your fee to minimise financial influence.
E. Accept the case and ask an experienced forensic colleague to co-sign your report; you will conduct the assessment, and their oversight will address the competence gap and the dual relationship.

question: You are a clinical psychologist in a hospital fertility service. A same-sex couple is referred for mandatory pre-parenthood counselling prior to assisted reproductive treatment. You hold sincere religious beliefs that conflict with supporting same-sex parenting. Which action best upholds the principle of providing access to psychological services free from unlawful discrimination while meeting effective practice elements (respect, non-prejudice, avoiding denial of access due to conscientious objection, and ensuring alternatives)?
options: A. Quietly decline and arrange for the couple to be placed at the end of the clinic waitlist for another clinician, to minimise workplace friction while still technically offering a pathway to care.
B. Accept the referral but keep sessions narrowly focused on procedural information and avoid exploring parenting goals or values that conflict with your beliefs, to prevent any discomfort.

C. Promptly inform your manager of a conscientious objection, and with respectful, nonjudgmental communication ensure a timely transfer to a colleague without additional delay or cost to the clients; provide clear information about alternative options and, if needed, brief bridging support to avoid gaps in access; document your actions.

D. Offer a single screening session and then terminate citing a vague "lack of fit," without disclosing your objection or facilitating alternatives, to avoid potential complaints and protect the therapeutic relationship.

question: You are conducting intake in a community mental health service. A 27-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia is referred for therapy after a recent discharge from hospital. Six months ago, he raised his voice and slammed a door during a distressing appointment at another service; there is currently no indication of imminent risk to self or others. The clinic has duress alarms and access to team-based appointments, but not a dedicated security guard. Which actions are ethically consistent with the principle that access must be free from unlawful discrimination, services should be based on identified needs and effectiveness, and clients should not be denied access if reasonable steps can ensure safety? Select all that apply.
options: A. Conduct a structured risk assessment and collaboratively develop a safety plan (e.g., scheduling at quieter times, team-based appointments, ensuring duress systems are functional), then proceed with intake rather than refusing service solely on the basis of diagnosis or a past incident.
B. Make telehealth the only modality permitted, indefinitely, as a blanket condition of access for this client to protect staff, regardless of clinical appropriateness or client preference.
C. Decline the referral on the basis that his prior behaviour shows he "chose" aggression and would not benefit from psychological therapy, and refer him to non-psychology services instead.

D. Delay the first session by one week to organise proportionate safety measures (e.g., scheduling adjustments, team availability), provide interim phone check-ins, and explain the reason transparently without blaming language.
E. Add a prominent alert to the electronic record stating "dangerous—do not book" to prevent administrative staff from scheduling appointments with any clinician.

F. If your site cannot implement basic safety measures (e.g., no functioning duress alarms), promptly discuss with management and arrange an immediate warm handover to a service that can safely provide care, ensuring the client does not lose their place in the queue and has clear follow-up.

question: You are providing a telehealth therapy session with Keira, a 17-year-old Aboriginal client with a history of major depression and a recent self-harm episode. During the session she says she has a plan, access to means at home, and does not feel safe. Severe flooding has limited road access to her rural community. You are in your clinic; your next client is due in 10 minutes. Which response best reflects ethical emergency intervention (considering your competence, your safety, available options, impact on other clients, and continuing to help until assistance is no longer objectively needed)?
options: A. Keep Keira on the call, conduct a structured suicide risk assessment, ask reception to call 000 with her location while you remain engaged, and—with Keira’s consent—contact her nominated Auntie and the local Aboriginal health service; advise reception to delay your next client; remain on the call until emergency responders or a safe adult are with her.
B. End the call briefly so you can call 000 and her mother yourself, then call Keira back after those calls to avoid alarming her while she is on the line.
C. Offer to drive to Keira’s home after your next session since ambulances may be delayed by floods; reassure her you will arrive as soon as possible.
D. Continue supportive listening but avoid contacting emergency services or family to respect Keira’s confidentiality and cultural preferences; document the plan and schedule a follow-up tomorrow.
E. Establish a verbal “no-harm” contract and finish on time for your next client, encouraging coping strategies and asking Keira to reach out if she feels worse.

question: You are a clinical psychologist leaving a hospital meeting when ED staff request urgent help with a 23-year-old male international student who is agitated, expressing persecutory ideas, and recently discharged with bipolar I disorder. You are off duty and have your 5-year-old child with you. Security is available. You also have a trauma therapy client scheduled in 30 minutes across campus. Which actions are ethically appropriate, given emergency intervention obligations, your safety, your skills, available options, and the need to continue assisting until no longer objectively needed? (Select all that apply.)
options: A. Explain you can assist if your child can be safely supervised elsewhere; request a secure room with a duress alarm and security present; begin brief de-escalation and risk assessment within your competence, and continue until ED psychiatry assumes care or the situation stabilises.
B. Step into the waiting area and conduct a fast assessment with your child seated nearby to avoid delays, limiting questions to minimise escalation.

C. Offer to support via phone/video from a secure office while ED staff maintain visual contact; request urgent review by the on-call psychiatric registrar for medication management, as you cannot prescribe; remain involved until a formal handover occurs.
D. Provide initial de-escalation for a few minutes, then leave to keep your outpatient appointment without confirming who has ongoing responsibility.
E. Insist ED call police to initiate involuntary detention without conducting or arranging a risk assessment due to staffing constraints.

F. Contact a more experienced colleague from the mental health team to take the lead, arrange brief coverage or informed-delay for your outpatient client, and remain available to consult until your colleague arrives.

question: A 16-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander student attends a school-based clinic with a non-Indigenous psychologist. She reports low mood and occasional suicidal thoughts last week but denies current plan or intent; there is no indication of imminent risk. She requests that her Aunty (not her legal guardian) attend the next session but asks that neither parent be told at this stage. The psychologist realises he knows the student’s mother socially from a local sports club. What is the most ethically appropriate next step to support cultural safety and manage the situation?
options: A. Immediately contact the mother to obtain consent for Aunty’s involvement, as the student is a minor, and proceed to schedule the session during Sorry Business if that is the only time available.

B. Explain the limits of confidentiality and your existing social connection with the mother; check the student’s preferences about involving her Aunty or an Aboriginal Health Worker/Cultural Liaison, obtain consent if she agrees, and co-create a safety plan incorporating her cultural supports; if the dual relationship cannot be adequately managed, offer transfer to another clinician.
C. Continue therapy one-to-one using standard CBT and a generic suicide risk protocol, avoiding involvement of cultural or family supports to maintain neutrality.
D. Recommend the student see her GP for antidepressant medication first and pause therapy until pharmacological treatment begins, to reduce risk before involving family.
E. Invite the extended family to the next session without the student’s consent, as kinship decision-making is typically collective in Aboriginal communities.

question: You are conducting a court-ordered parenting capacity assessment for an Aboriginal father whose supervised contact with his child is being reviewed. He requests the assessment be rescheduled because of Sorry Business and asks to have a respected Elder present. The file includes a past diagnosis of schizophrenia, but he reports no current symptoms. The court deadline is tight. What actions best uphold cultural safety and ethical practice in this forensic context?
options: A. Clarify the assessment purpose and the specific limits of confidentiality in a forensic context; seek the father’s informed, written consent to involve the Elder; coordinate with an Aboriginal Liaison/Health Worker to plan a culturally safe process (e.g., yarning style) and proactively notify the court about adjusted timelines due to Sorry Business.

B. Decline the rescheduling request because the court order takes precedence, proceed on the original date without the Elder, and note in the report that cultural considerations could not be accommodated.
C. Rely on historical records to diagnose current schizophrenia to expedite the report, given collateral file information is generally reliable in court matters.

D. Offer to conduct the assessment via telehealth on Country after Sorry Business and use the DSM-5 Cultural Formulation Interview to explore cultural identity, stressors (including racism), and supports; explicitly document how these inform risk and parenting capacity findings.
E. Directly contact the identified Elder to arrange attendance, assuming the father’s request implies consent, to avoid administrative delays.

F. With the father’s consent, arrange a joint session with his caseworker and an Aboriginal Health Worker to clarify roles, ensure he understands the non-therapeutic nature of the assessment, and address barriers such as literacy or language.

question: A non-Indigenous clinical psychologist working in a remote community is asked to assess Lila, a 16-year-old Aboriginal girl referred by her school for anxiety and declining attendance following a recent family death (sorry business). Lila attends with her grandmother (her custodial carer) and asks whether an Aunty and a local Aboriginal Health Worker can be involved. The school has requested a diagnostic letter for “school refusal.” In session, Lila says she sometimes wants to go to the river to be alone “when it all gets too much,” but denies intent or plan to harm herself. Which actions best reflect culturally safe and ethical practice? Select all that apply.
options: A. Issue a brief report diagnosing school refusal and recommending a standard attendance contract, keeping cultural matters out of the report to maintain objectivity.

B. Acknowledge sorry business and explore Lila’s and her grandmother’s understandings of her distress, including the impacts of colonisation; with Lila’s consent, involve a local Aboriginal Health Worker and selected family members; co-design care; and limit any school disclosures to what Lila consents to.
C. Decline any family or community involvement to protect confidentiality and proceed with a standard CBT manual without discussing cultural context to avoid bias.

D. Conduct and document a risk assessment that clarifies intent, means, and the cultural meaning of going to the river; collaboratively develop a safety plan that leverages family and culturally meaningful supports (e.g., safe time on Country) and schedule follow-up with flexibility around cultural obligations.

E. Seek cultural supervision/consultation (e.g., from an Aboriginal clinical leader) to reflect on biases, local protocols, and intergenerational trauma; explain confidentiality and its limits to both Lila and her grandmother; and obtain explicit consent before involving others or sharing with the school.
F. Prioritise symptom reduction by writing to the GP recommending an SSRI, deferring cultural and contextual work until mood stabilises so therapy is more efficient.

question: You are a non-Indigenous clinical psychologist contracted by child protection to complete a parenting capacity assessment for an Aboriginal mother with a history of depression. The department demands a report within 48 hours. The mother requests that her Uncle and an Aboriginal Legal Service advocate be present during interviews. The case manager warns that involving them might be “collusion” and could bias the assessment. What is the best next step? Select one.
options: A. Proceed alone, use standardised tools only, and avoid discussing colonisation or historical child removal to maintain objectivity and meet the deadline.

B. Request a deadline extension to enable a culturally safe process; with informed consent, allow the Uncle and the advocate to be present; seek cultural supervision; use culturally appropriate interview methods (e.g., yarning) and tools; and document how colonisation, community context, and historical child removal inform interpretation while maintaining independence.
C. Decline the case immediately due to cultural complexity and instruct the department to find an Aboriginal assessor, without arranging any interim plan.
D. Permit the Uncle and advocate to attend but keep their involvement off the record so the report appears objective.
E. Obtain collateral information by contacting local Elders and community members without the mother’s consent to gain a holistic view.

question: A non-Indigenous clinical psychologist in regional Queensland is seeing a 19-year-old Aboriginal woman for low mood and intermittent self-harm thoughts without current plan or intent. The client reports frequent experiences of racism at school and in town. The psychologist’s practice follows a brief manualised CBT protocol. The client’s aunt, an Aboriginal Health Worker in the same building, asks the psychologist in the hallway how her niece is going, saying she wants to support her. Which ONE of the following is the MOST ethically appropriate next step to ensure culturally safe practice?
options: A. Continue with the standard manualised CBT protocol without deviation to avoid imposing assumptions; avoid raising colonisation or racism unless the client brings it up, as initiating the topic could be re-traumatising.

B. Seek the client’s consent to invite a support person of her choosing (which may include her aunt) to collaborate on goals; explore how colonisation, racism and cultural identity relate to her wellbeing; offer to integrate culturally relevant healing practices and/or liaise with an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service if she wishes; and decline to disclose information to the aunt without the client’s consent.

C. Provide psychoeducation emphasising that depression is primarily biological and encourage the client to see her GP for medication while sessions focus on individual coping skills; avoid community or historical factors to remain within scope of practice.
D. Give the aunt a brief, non-specific update in the hallway because she is a health worker involved in the client’s care and community partnership supports cultural safety.
E. Offer to transfer the client to an Aboriginal psychologist because cultural safety cannot be ensured by a non-Indigenous clinician.

question: A hospital-based clinical psychologist is asked to conduct a cognitive assessment to inform a guardianship decision for a 45-year-old Aboriginal man with suspected traumatic brain injury. The court deadline is in 10 days. The client requests his cousin and a respected Elder be present and asks whether the assessment could occur in a community-controlled service. Standard tests available have limited validity data for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. The Aboriginal Health Worker is away this week. In a team meeting, a colleague jokes that “our Indigenous clients never show up anyway.” Which of the following actions are ethically required to promote culturally safe practice in this scenario? Select THREE.
options: A. Explain the cultural and psychometric limitations of available tests; co-design an assessment plan with the client that may include flexible scheduling and breaks, participation of the requested support persons, engagement of a cultural broker when available, consideration of alternative or adapted tools, and careful documentation of cultural factors and their impact on interpretation.
B. Proceed with standardised tests immediately to meet the deadline, note the client’s Aboriginality in the report to contextualise lower scores, and avoid community liaison to reduce delays.

C. Obtain informed consent to involve the cousin and Elder, clarify confidentiality and roles, and contact the court to seek an extension if needed, explaining that proceeding without cultural supports risks an invalid and culturally unsafe assessment.
D. Ask a psychiatrist to prescribe a short-term anxiolytic so the client can sit through the assessment without breaks, reducing the need for family involvement and facilitating timely completion.

E. Address the colleague’s stereotyping remark through supervision and appropriate reporting pathways; advocate for anti-racism training that recognises the impacts of colonisation; and promote service policy changes that accommodate structural barriers (e.g., flexible bookings) rather than penalising “no shows.”
F. Decline the assessment entirely because any Western cognitive testing of Aboriginal clients is inherently racist and cannot be made culturally safe.

question: You are a psychologist working with Amina, a 17-year-old student who identifies as lesbian and Muslim. She has moderate depressive symptoms and no current suicidal ideation or intent. Amina asks that you not disclose her sexual orientation to her parents, who have requested regular updates on her progress. Which ONE action best upholds respectful, culturally reflective practice and privacy/confidentiality obligations?
options: A. Invite Amina’s parents to the next session and disclose her sexual orientation to facilitate family support, given the cultural importance of family in many Muslim communities.

B. Explore with Amina what family involvement would feel safe for her; explain limits of confidentiality for minors in your jurisdiction; clarify what, if anything, she consents to share; reflect on your own assumptions about Muslim families and sexuality; and consider culturally informed supervision while de-identifying her.
C. Avoid discussing religion or culture to prevent stereotyping, and focus strictly on symptom reduction with a standard CBT protocol.
D. Email Amina’s parents a general progress summary (no details) because she is a minor, while keeping her sexual orientation private unless risk emerges.

question: You are conducting a court-ordered risk assessment of Tui, a 28-year-old man from a small Pacific Islander community. He has limited English proficiency and asks that his cousin attend to interpret. No imminent risk is identified during the interview. Which actions best align with culturally reflective, respectful practice and privacy/confidentiality obligations? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Use the cousin as interpreter to honour Tui’s preference, provided the cousin signs a confidentiality agreement, because this is the quickest way to complete the court report.

B. Arrange a NAATI-accredited interpreter of Tui’s preferred gender; brief and debrief the interpreter about the forensic purpose and limits of confidentiality; explain to Tui why an independent interpreter is needed, and offer his cousin the option to attend as a support person separately.
C. To meet court timelines, text the probation officer a brief summary of Tui’s cultural barriers and preliminary risk opinion, noting a full report will follow.

D. Reflect on potential stereotypes you may hold about collectivist cultures and violence; seek culturally informed consultation without disclosing identifying details; and document how culture was considered in test selection, interpretation, and recommendations.

E. Provide translated written information about the assessment purpose, who will see the report, and limits of confidentiality; then confirm understanding using a teach-back approach rather than yes/no questions.

question: You receive a referral for Layla, a recently arrived Dari-speaking Afghan woman with PTSD. She has limited English. Her husband insists on interpreting to ‘support’ her and asks to sit in sessions. The only readily available in-person interpreter is a male from the small local Afghan community. Layla appears anxious when her husband speaks for her. Which actions best uphold culturally reflective practice while addressing confidentiality and safety? Select THREE options.
options: A. Decline the husband as interpreter, explain confidentiality and role boundaries, and offer an accredited interpreter while eliciting Layla’s preferences (e.g., interpreter gender and whether the interpreter should be from outside her local community).
B. Accept the husband as interpreter to respect cultural norms and avoid appearing discriminatory, provided he signs a confidentiality agreement.
C. Offer Layla a private pre-session (with an interpreter of her choice) to explain confidentiality, assess for coercion, and clarify who she wants present in future sessions.
D. Proceed with a male accredited interpreter from the local Afghan community without discussing interpreter characteristics to avoid delaying trauma-focused therapy.

E. With Layla’s consent, consult a bilingual cultural liaison worker to co-plan engagement (e.g., use of telehealth to access a non-local female interpreter), and build a safety plan around community connections and privacy.

question: You are a non-Indigenous psychologist asked to conduct a court-ordered parenting capacity assessment for Mr J, an Aboriginal father from a remote community. English is his second language. The agency requests you complete the assessment by videoconference next week using the standard battery and not involve community members. Mr J asks to have his Aunty present for cultural support. What is the most ethically appropriate next step? Select ONE option.
options: A. Decline any request for cultural support to preserve testing standardisation and avoid third-party influence.
B. Proceed by telehealth with the standard English-language battery, noting ‘language limitations’ in the report to satisfy the court timeframe.

C. Seek a variation from the court to allow a culturally safe process: involve a culturally appropriate support person for interviews (not during standardised testing), secure an accredited interpreter aligned with Mr J’s preferences, adapt methods as needed, and explicitly document cultural/linguistic influences and any limitations on inferences.
D. Ask an Aboriginal colleague to write the cultural formulation section without seeing Mr J, to ensure cultural representation while you complete the rest.
E. Decline the case solely because you are non-Indigenous and recommend the agency find an Aboriginal psychologist instead.

question: You are conducting an initial therapy assessment with a 15-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander student who attends with his aunt. He speaks English but uses some Aboriginal English terms. He reports occasional passive thoughts of “being better off dead” without plan or intent. The school referred him after recent conflict with peers. Which action is the MOST appropriate next step to support effective communication and a positive therapeutic relationship?
options: A. Provide a standard consent and confidentiality brochure for the client and aunt to read and sign, and proceed with the session; discuss confidentiality specifics later only if risk escalates.

B. Verbally and plainly explain your role, the nature of your relationship with both the young person and his aunt, the limits of confidentiality (including when you must share information about safety), and how information may be used or shared; check their understanding using teach-back, invite preferences about family or Aboriginal health worker involvement, and adapt language to suit their cultural and communication needs.
C. To protect the young person’s privacy, ask the aunt to leave all discussions, including any safety planning, and state that no information will be shared with her under any circumstances.
D. Use precise clinical terminology (e.g., “suicidal ideation,” “non-specific preparatory behaviours”) throughout the conversation to ensure diagnostic accuracy during the session.
E. Send a clinical summary after the session to the school counsellor and the GP, including sensitive details, to coordinate care given the client is a minor and therefore implied consent applies.

question: You are completing a court-ordered parenting capacity assessment with a recently arrived Syrian refugee mother who has limited English proficiency. The service suggests using her adult son as the interpreter due to scheduling pressure. The client appears anxious and asks whether what she says will be shared with the court. Which actions best align with effective communication and ethical practice in this context? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Proceed using the client’s adult son as interpreter to minimise the client’s distress and reduce costs, assuring the son to translate verbatim.

B. Arrange a NAATI-certified Arabic interpreter who abides by AUSIT’s Code of Ethics; check for dialect and gender preferences, brief and debrief the interpreter about roles and confidentiality, and use plain language with teach-back to confirm the client’s understanding throughout.
C. Given court deadlines, proceed with a bilingual staff member who is not an accredited interpreter and document the limitation in the report.

D. Clearly explain your independent assessor role, the relationship with each party, how the report and information will be used by the court, the limits to confidentiality, and any financial arrangements; provide translated written information where possible and confirm understanding before proceeding.
E. To avoid introducing cultural bias, avoid asking about cultural factors and administer only standard instruments in English with direct translation by the interpreter.

question: Dr Nguyen, a clinical psychologist in a group practice, begins therapy with Alex, a 16-year-old trans male student referred by the school counsellor for anxiety and low mood. Alex appears Gillick-competent, and there is no current risk to self or others. Alex requests that details of sessions not be shared with his parents. After the second session, Alex’s mother emails asking for “all notes and test results” and to be cc’d on appointment reminders. The school counsellor also asks for a written update to support a funding application. The practice has a shared waiting area where conversations can sometimes be overheard. Which actions are ethically appropriate now? Select all that apply.
options: A. Explain the limits of confidentiality to Alex and seek specific, informed consent for any disclosures to his mother and the school; clarify the nature and purpose of any information to be shared and formally document the consent outcomes.

B. Provide Alex’s mother with a brief summary limited to attendance and general coping skills because she is a legal guardian; withhold sensitive details to preserve the therapeutic relationship and proceed without formal documentation.

C. Send the school counsellor an update including diagnostic impressions because they made the referral and the information will assist with school funding; this falls within implied consent for treatment purposes.

D. Review relevant state/territory privacy and health records legislation regarding minors’ consent and access rights; verify Alex’s decision-making capacity; if consent is declined and there is no risk issue, decline third-party disclosures; ensure appointment reminders and reception practices do not reveal sensitive information; brief staff not to discuss clients in shared spaces.

question: Dr Patel is providing CBT via telehealth from a shared consulting room due to a room shortage. The client, a 45-year-old ADF veteran with major depression and alcohol use disorder, states: “I bought a knife today and I’m going to my ex-partner’s house tonight.” He refuses consent for you to contact anyone and will not provide details. The door to the room is occasionally opened by a colleague. After the call, the ex-partner’s sister leaves a voicemail asking for an update. Which ONE action best satisfies privacy/confidentiality obligations while addressing the situation?
options: A. Immediately call police and disclose all therapy notes and diagnostic history to assist their response, then email the ex-partner’s sister to warn her about the client’s statements because the risk is imminent.
B. Terminate the call and text the client that confidentiality prevents you from involving others without consent; advise that you will wait for him to reach out if he changes his mind.

C. Move to the most private space available or end and promptly re-establish the session in a private setting; document the risk assessment and disclose only the minimum necessary information to emergency services to manage the imminent threat; do not share information with family without consent or legal authorisation; afterwards, consider whether any inadvertent overhearing requires action under local privacy/data-breach policy.
D. Continue the session in the shared room but lower your voice; avoid contacting emergency services because the client did not consent; schedule a check-in call for the next day to reassess.
E. Ask a colleague to call the ex-partner’s sister to gather more context so you can better assess risk without directly breaching confidentiality yourself.

question: You are treating a 16-year-old Aboriginal boy referred by his mother for low mood. He reports passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. He has low literacy, prefers plain-language explanations, and asks you not to tell his mother about his suicidal thoughts. His mother phones requesting full access to your progress notes. Which TWO actions best uphold respectful partnership, trust, and effective communication in this situation? Select TWO.
options: A. Explain confidentiality and its limits in age-appropriate plain language; assess the young person's decision-making capacity (mature minor/Gillick competence); collaboratively agree with him what information can be shared with his mother, while also undertaking a safety plan for passive SI; document the discussion and decisions.
B. Provide the mother full access to therapy notes immediately due to her parental responsibility, and avoid discussing this with the young person to preserve the family relationship.
