C. Use simple, culturally sensitive communication aids (e.g., pictorial summaries) and check back for understanding; offer—only with his consent—to involve an Aboriginal health liaison worker or trusted adult to support communication with family.
D. Promise absolute confidentiality to build trust, assuring him you will never share information with anyone, including about self-harm, unless ordered by a court.
E. Write session notes in deliberately coded or vague language so that, if the mother gains access, she will not understand the content, thereby reducing potential harm.

question: A 22-year-old international student is receiving CBT for panic disorder. After an interoceptive exposure task last week, he had a panic attack during a lecture and now fears returning to class. He is prescribed a stimulant for ADHD by his GP. He asks you to adjust his medication dose and requests that you not tell the university counselling service liaison who referred him. There is no imminent risk. Which ONE response best upholds respectful partnership, trust, and effective communication? Select ONE.
options: A. Validate the setback and explain that short-term symptom exacerbation can occur with exposure; review pacing and coping strategies collaboratively; clarify that, as a psychologist in Australia, you cannot prescribe or adjust medication, and—with his informed consent—offer to liaise with his GP about side effects while also agreeing on what, if anything, will be shared with the referrer; document the plan.

B. State that medication is outside your scope and continue the exposure protocol unchanged to avoid reinforcing avoidance; assure him you will not share any information with the referrer under any circumstances.
C. Suggest he halve his stimulant dose until he sees his GP, and pause exposure to minimise distress.
D. Contact the referrer and his GP immediately with full details of the panic attack without seeking his consent, as this is necessary to ensure duty of care.
E. Recommend he use an over-the-counter sedating antihistamine before lectures to blunt panic sensations so exposure can proceed at the same intensity, and monitor response.

question: Riley, a 19-year-old non-binary international student with major depressive disorder, reports passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. Riley asks you to email a brief session summary and wonders about medication options. You realise mid-session that you know Riley’s mother through a local community group. Riley does not want their parents informed. Which actions best uphold the ethical principle regarding high standards of personal conduct and effective relationships?
options: A) Without telling Riley, call their mother to alert her to the risk and arrange additional support, because safety overrides confidentiality in all cases.

B) Explain limits of confidentiality (including when you might need to act), collaboratively assess current risk and develop a safety plan, and obtain Riley’s consent before any collateral contact; provide psychoeducation about treatment options and suggest Riley discuss medication with their GP, offering to liaise with the GP if Riley agrees.
C) Keep the focus strictly on CBT techniques for depression and avoid discussion of gender identity unless Riley raises it repeatedly, to prevent distraction from the treatment plan.

D) Disclose your prior acquaintance with Riley’s mother, explore whether this creates any conflict or discomfort, offer referral options, and proceed only with Riley’s informed agreement; document the discussion and decision.
E) Agree to email a brief session summary using secure communication after discussing privacy risks and what content Riley wants included; obtain consent and limit details accordingly.

F) Offer a small fee reduction if Riley permits you to use de-identified session material in an upcoming professional presentation, as this can benefit the profession while easing their financial burden.

question: You are engaged by an insurer to conduct an independent psychological assessment following a workplace incident. The examinee is someone who lives on your street, and your spouse holds a managerial role at the insurer. During the pre-assessment call, the examinee asks whether they can review your report before it is sent and whether you can prescribe something to help with sleep. There is no imminent risk. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: A) Proceed with the assessment while ensuring your spouse cannot access records, and avoid mentioning your personal connection to prevent making the examinee uncomfortable.

B) Inform the referrer about the dual relationships (neighbour and spouse’s role), disclose the potential conflict to the examinee, and discuss recusal or referral; do not proceed unless the conflict can be managed and the examinee provides informed agreement.
C) Begin the assessment but take extra steps to remain neutral; if the examinee asks about sleep, recommend an over-the-counter antihistamine as a short-term aid.
D) Offer to waive your fee to reduce any appearance of exploitation and allow the examinee to review and edit the report for factual accuracy before submission, to enhance transparency.

E) Explain limits of confidentiality and your reporting obligations to the insurer, clarify that psychologists in Australia cannot prescribe, provide sleep-hygiene advice, and then decide together whether to continue.
F) Ask your spouse discreetly about the organisational context to better understand the referral, but avoid documenting this collateral information to preserve confidentiality.

question: Maya, 15, attends an initial session for panic attacks with her mother, who will pay the fees. Maya requests that the details of her sessions remain private from her mother. There is no imminent risk of harm. The plan is standard CBT with psychoeducation and breathing retraining; no procedures involve physical contact. Which actions best meet informed consent requirements in this situation?
options: A. Evaluate Maya’s maturity and decision-making capacity; explain in age-appropriate terms the nature, benefits, risks, limits of confidentiality, and expected outcomes of CBT; check her understanding; seek Maya’s consent and consider whether parental consent is also required; agree on information-sharing boundaries; document the consent, the period it covers, and when it will be revisited.

B. Rely on the mother’s consent and financial agreement because she is the payer; obtain Maya’s assent only if convenient since attendance implies consent for ongoing therapy unless she withdraws in writing.
C. Provide only a brief verbal overview to avoid overwhelming Maya, commence therapy immediately, and revisit consent only if you later decide to change techniques significantly.
D. Discuss fees only with the mother to obtain financial consent; because no physical contact is involved, there is no need to inform Maya of costs or to document consent beyond a progress note.

E. Obtain general consent from Maya for the planned treatment episode, make clear she can withdraw consent at any time and discuss possible implications; arrange a joint conversation with her mother about confidentiality boundaries; check Maya’s understanding (e.g., teach-back); document and plan to revisit consent after a defined period (e.g., 10 sessions) or sooner if the plan changes.
F. Since there is no imminent risk, defer discussing limits of confidentiality until after rapport is established to avoid discouraging disclosure.

G. If law or organisational policy requires parental or guardian consent for specified elements, seek the mother’s consent for those while still following the informed consent process with Maya as far as reasonably possible to obtain her agreement.

question: Mr. Liang, 72, a Cantonese-speaking man, is referred for a neuropsychological assessment of memory decline. His daughter asks to translate and to consent on his behalf to “save time.” The planned assessment includes an optional student observer and a brief motor exam that involves touching Mr. Liang’s hands. There is no emergency. What is the most appropriate approach to informed consent?
options: A. Accept the daughter’s offer to translate and provide verbal consent to avoid delay; begin testing today and obtain written consent afterwards if needed for the motor exam.

B. Arrange a professional interpreter; screen Mr. Liang’s decision-making capacity; explain in his language the nature, benefits, risks (including the motor exam and student observer), expected outcomes, fees and any referral options; confirm his understanding and allow time for questions and a decision; seek his consent; if capacity is insufficient, obtain consent from the legally authorised substitute decision-maker while still engaging Mr. Liang in the process; obtain written consent for the physical contact; document consent, the period it covers, and plan to revisit if scope or circumstances change.
C. Because neuropsychological testing carries minimal risk, proceed based on implied consent once Mr. Liang sits for testing, ensuring only that the daughter signs a financial consent form.
D. Given possible cognitive impairment, bypass Mr. Liang to prevent distress and rely solely on the daughter’s consent for both the assessment and the teaching component.
E. Complete the full assessment first to establish cognitive capacity, then provide a comprehensive consent discussion before releasing the report.

question: You are seeing a 15-year-old autistic client (ASD Level 1) for low mood and school refusal. Mid-session, he discloses that his stepfather sometimes “hits and shoves” him when angry and asks you not to tell anyone. He denies current suicidal intent and has no visible injuries today. What is the most appropriate next step to ethically manage this disclosure?
options: A. Assure him of full confidentiality and continue therapy without reporting, unless you believe his life is in immediate danger.

B. Explain the limits of confidentiality in developmentally appropriate language, assess immediate safety, and make a mandatory report to child protection as required by law; discuss with him how he can be involved in the reporting process and identify a safe adult to support him.
C. Provide psychoeducation about healthy family dynamics and schedule a joint session with the stepfather to hear both sides before considering any external report.
D. Encourage him to self-report if he chooses, and agree that you will not make any report unless he gives explicit permission.
E. Refer him to his GP for possible medication to stabilise mood and revisit the decision to report once symptoms are better controlled.

question: A 72-year-old immigrant woman with mild neurocognitive disorder and post-stroke expressive aphasia attends psychotherapy for adjustment and low mood. She speaks limited English and intermittently describes her adult son restricting her bank card and medical appointments; you notice fading bruises on her forearm. She is unsure whether she wants outside help and asks you to keep this private. Select all actions that are ethically appropriate.
options: A. Arrange a qualified professional interpreter and use supported communication strategies (written keywords, visual aids, teach-back) to optimise her understanding and participation in decisions.
B. Because she is older and may lack decision-making capacity, obtain consent from her son for all sessions and provide him with session notes to support care coordination.

C. Assess immediate risk and document observed indicators of possible abuse; follow your state/territory elder abuse response pathways and any applicable mandatory reporting obligations (e.g., Aged Care Act settings), keeping her informed and seeking consent to involve an independent advocate where safe.
D. Defer any safety enquiries and resource discussions until her depression has improved, to avoid overwhelming her with complex decisions.
E. Provide accessible information about elder and financial abuse, seniors’ legal/advocacy services, and social supports; offer to facilitate referrals to address barriers to access.
F. Email a summary of your concerns to her GP and her son to expedite interprofessional collaboration, as family involvement is routinely helpful in older adult care.

question: You are providing individual CBT to Alex, a 15-year-old non-binary student referred for low mood and school avoidance. Alex has not disclosed any imminent risk to self or others. Alex’s mother, who is paying for sessions, emails asking for your session notes and a detailed update on what Alex shares in therapy because she is worried Alex is being influenced by peers about gender identity. How should you proceed to align with the principle of being considerate of associated parties and, with appropriate consent or where otherwise permitted, responsive in providing information to them?
options: A. Without consulting Alex or assessing capacity to consent, email the mother a brief summary of each session out of respect for her guardianship and financial responsibility for the therapy.

B. Discuss the request with Alex, assess Alex’s capacity to consent, and—if Alex agrees—arrange a short parent update covering general progress, attendance, safety management, and how the parent can support, without disclosing specific personal content. Offer a joint session to clarify roles and boundaries.
C. Decline to speak with the mother about any aspect of the therapy under any circumstances until Alex turns 18, to avoid any breach of confidentiality.

D. Explain confidentiality limits to both Alex and the mother; document an informed-consent discussion with Alex about what can be shared; with Alex’s consent, provide a high-level update and resources for supporting LGBTQ+ youth, avoiding sensitive disclosures; and record the decision in the file.

E. If Alex withholds consent, offer the mother a general conversation about adolescent mental health and how therapy works, provide publicly available parenting resources, and invite a joint session—without revealing Alex’s personal information.

question: You are conducting an employer-commissioned fitness-for-duty psychological assessment for Jordan, a 42-year-old paramedic recently taken off road due to panic attacks. Jordan has signed consent for you to release a report addressing fitness for duty and work-related recommendations only, and has explicitly declined release of raw test data or full clinical notes. There is no current imminent risk. After testing, (1) the employer’s HR manager requests a copy of your full notes and test responses, and (2) Jordan’s spouse calls asking for detailed results and advice on whether Jordan should start medication to expedite return to work. What is the most appropriate response to align with being considerate and responsive to associated parties while respecting consent?
options: A. Provide the employer with the full test file and clinical notes because they commissioned the assessment and are responsible for workplace safety, then offer the spouse a copy of the report as Jordan’s primary support person.

B. Send the employer a report that answers the referral questions and provides functional recommendations consistent with Jordan’s written consent; decline to release raw notes/data; offer to brief HR on recommendations without personal clinical detail; and, unless Jordan consents, provide the spouse only general caregiver resources and information about panic disorder without disclosing Jordan’s personal results.
C. Decline to communicate with both HR and the spouse to avoid any risk of breaching confidentiality; communicate only with Jordan and keep all results private.

D. Call the spouse and share key triggers identified in testing and your clinical formulation because the spouse is integral to recovery and likely already knows these details; tell HR you can only confirm attendance.

E. Email Jordan’s GP recommending they consider a short course of benzodiazepines to facilitate a quicker return to work, and advise the spouse to discuss obtaining the prescription, since psychologists in Australia cannot prescribe medication.

question: You are an endorsed clinical and forensic psychologist who submitted a court-ordered parenting capacity assessment to the Federal Circuit and Family Court. Two days later, you discover you mis-scored a psychometric instrument, leading to an opinion that the mother showed markedly elevated traits suggestive of risk. The father relied on your report at an interim hearing, and the mother’s time with the child has been restricted. The mother’s solicitor emails alleging your error caused harm and asks what you intend to do and how to lodge a complaint with Ahpra. Under the ethical principle of open disclosure and remedial action when harm occurs, what is the single most appropriate immediate action?
options: A. Do not respond to the mother’s solicitor to avoid prejudicing the litigation; quietly correct your internal file and wait to address it under cross-examination.

B. Issue a formal addendum to the Court immediately acknowledging and correcting the scoring error, with an apology and revised opinion, copying both parties’ legal representatives in accordance with the court order, and outline steps to prevent recurrence.
C. Call the child’s school to explain your misinterpretation and reassure staff about the mother’s risk to mitigate downstream harm to her reputation.
D. Notify your professional indemnity insurer and seek advice about whether any Ahpra/health complaints notification is required; delay sending any written communication until you receive advice.
E. Decline the solicitor’s request for information about complaint pathways until the proceedings conclude, to avoid encouraging a notification.

question: You are providing trauma-focused therapy to a 19-year-old Aboriginal bisexual woman with complex PTSD. After a session in which you introduced trauma-processing exercises earlier than planned, she presented to ED that evening following an overdose. The hospital discharges her the next day and informs you there is no current imminent risk. The client emails alleging the therapy harmed her and asks for details on how to complain to Ahpra. Her mother also calls requesting an update. Which of the following actions are ethically appropriate and consistent with open disclosure and harm minimisation? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Offer an urgent appointment to review what happened, apologise for your role in the adverse outcome, complete a fresh risk and safety assessment, and—if she prefers—facilitate transfer to another clinician or higher-acuity service; with the client’s consent, liaise with her GP and mother; document thoroughly.
B. Pause all contact and send a brief email stating you cannot discuss potential negligence until you have legal advice; do not provide complaint information to avoid prejudicing your position.
C. Complete an internal incident report and contact your insurer or regulatory advice line to clarify whether any regulatory notifications are required; follow your service’s open disclosure policy.

D. Enter a retrospective amendment that replaces your previous progress note so the file emphasises client autonomy and downplays the exposure; defer documenting the client’s complaint until after seeking legal advice.
E. Continue therapy unchanged but add a more detailed consent form; do not involve any third parties to respect confidentiality, and tell the client to return if distress recurs.

F. Provide the client with clear information on how to make a notification to Ahpra and how to lodge a complaint with the relevant state/territory health complaints entity; offer to answer questions about the process.

question: You are providing CBT to a 17-year-old Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander student with major depressive disorder and recent non-suicidal self-injury (no current intent or plan). After a session, the client says a remark you made felt culturally dismissive and states they are considering lodging a complaint with Ahpra, adding that they do not want their parent/guardian informed. What is the most appropriate immediate response?
options: A. Acknowledge their right to raise a concern; provide clear information about Ahpra/Board and other complaints pathways; offer to explore the issue together to see if it can be resolved locally if they wish; discuss confidentiality including their request not to involve the parent, and consider how the concern may affect ongoing care (including offering transfer if trust is compromised).
B. Suggest postponing any formal complaint until their mood improves to reduce impulsivity, and withhold detailed complaint information until a later date to avoid overwhelming them.
C. Inform the parent/guardian because the client is a minor and complaints must involve a parent; provide the parent with session notes to ensure transparency.
D. Explain that all complaints must go through your clinic's internal feedback process first, and provide only the clinic’s form while declining to provide Ahpra/Board details unless they insist.

question: You are conducting a fitness-for-duty psychological assessment for a 38-year-old police officer. Mid-assessment, the officer states they are concerned about potential bias because you previously collaborated with their unit’s leadership on a training project, and says they may complain to the Board. There is no imminent risk. Which responses are consistent with effective practice under the complaints principle? Select all that apply.
options: A. Acknowledge their right to raise a concern; provide information about Ahpra/Board and organisational complaint systems; and invite discussion about whether the issue can be addressed locally, if they wish.
B. Reassure them there is no bias and proceed as planned, noting that lodging an external complaint during a forensic evaluation could be viewed as noncompliance and may harm their employment case.

C. Consider whether the perceived conflict could adversely affect the assessment; if so, pause and offer referral to an independent assessor, documenting the issue and notifying the retaining party according to policy.
D. Proactively call Ahpra to give your account first and inform the client’s supervisor about the intended complaint to ensure transparency.
E. If a complaint is lodged, provide a prompt, open and constructive response to the competent authority when requested, and comply with relevant legislation, policies and procedures.
F. Avoid recording the concern in the assessment file to reduce the risk of medico-legal escalation.

question: A 34-year-old client with recurrent major depressive disorder and hazardous alcohol use has attended your weekly CBT for nine months. Her PHQ-9 has remained 18–20 with minimal functional change despite adequate dose and duration. Attendance has been sporadic, though the alliance is strong. She strongly wishes to continue 'as is.' There is no imminent risk to self or others. You practise in a regional area with limited local services, but evidence-based telehealth options and a nearby dual-diagnosis service exist. Under the ethical principle that psychologists provide services clients are likely to benefit from and, when ending services, minimise negative effects and safeguard continuity, which actions are ethically appropriate? Select TWO.
options: A. Continue indefinite supportive sessions without changing the treatment plan to respect the client's autonomy and avoid perceived abandonment; review again in six months.

B. Discuss the lack of progress transparently, and with the client's informed consent arrange referral to a dual-diagnosis service or a psychologist with substance-use expertise; provide a detailed handover and offer time-limited bridging sessions to support the transition.
C. End therapy at the next session to prevent further cost and time burden, providing crisis numbers and a generic list of community resources.

D. Seek consultation/supervision and propose a time-limited trial of a different evidence-based approach (e.g., behavioural activation with motivational interviewing for alcohol use) with clear outcome measures; if benefit remains limited, implement a collaboratively planned referral and termination with consent and appropriate information transfer.

E. Advise the client to ask her GP about medication options and maintain the current CBT protocol unchanged for another six months to see if the medication makes therapy effective, postponing any referral decisions until then.

question: You are conducting a Family Court–ordered custody evaluation for a 9-year-old child whose parents (who share parental responsibility) are from different cultural backgrounds. You have completed intake and some testing, but not the report. You will relocate interstate in four weeks and must close your practice. There is no imminent risk. According to the ethical principle about concluding services and ensuring continuity, which ONE action best aligns with your obligations?
options: A. Promptly inform both parents, the instructing solicitor(s), and the Court (if appropriate) of your planned closure and timelines; with both parents’ informed consent, coordinate transfer to an independent, suitably qualified forensic practitioner; provide a handover letter and release relevant records/raw data to the successor practitioner as permitted by law and test publisher guidelines; document all notifications.

B. Complete as many reports as possible, but delay informing families until one week before closure to reduce their anxiety; for incomplete cases, provide a generic list of practitioners and ask families to organise transfer after you move.
C. Obtain written consent from the requesting parent only and transfer the child’s materials directly to that parent’s preferred assessor to meet the deadline, given time pressure.

D. Arrange for your spouse, a psychologist in your new practice, to take over the matter and inform the family only once an appointment is secured, to minimise service disruption and decision fatigue.
E. For assessment-only cases, avoid transferring raw test data due to test security and copyright; instead instruct the next psychologist to re-administer all measures to maintain standardisation.

question: You are a male clinical psychologist treating a 16-year-old girl who identifies as bisexual and has a history of childhood sexual abuse and self-harm (no current plan or imminent risk disclosed today). After a difficult session in which she became tearful, she asks, "Can I have a hug?" Which is the most ethically appropriate immediate response? Select ONE option.
options: A. Offer a brief side-hug with the door open, explaining that it is a supportive, non-sexual gesture, and document later if needed.

B. Gently decline physical contact, validate her feelings, explain the boundary and power imbalance in the therapeutic relationship, offer evidence-based grounding/soothing strategies instead (e.g., paced breathing, sensory grounding), collaboratively explore the meaning of the request, and document the discussion.

C. Explain you could incorporate limited, structured physical touch into treatment after supervision; prepare to obtain written consent from the client (and guardian as legally appropriate), justify it ethically and clinically, and document thoroughly.
D. Disclose that you have personally found hugs comforting in hard times to normalise her request, and allow a one-time exception with verbal consent only.
E. Ask a trusted female colleague to enter the room to provide the hug so that the client receives comfort while minimising risks of misinterpretation.

question: Dr Lee, a clinical psychologist in regional NSW, provided 18 sessions of trauma-focused therapy to Jordan (35, male veteran). Therapy ended three months ago after agreed goals were met. Jordan’s then-partner, Mia, occasionally attended joint sessions as an associated party. Dr Lee now matches with Mia on a dating app; Mia and Jordan have recently separated. The same week, Jordan emails asking Dr Lee to write a letter supporting his firearms licence application and offers to pay double fees for the consultation. Which actions are ethically appropriate under the boundary principle? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Refrain from dating Mia unless and until consultation with a senior practitioner confirms that a relationship with an associated party of a former client is not exploitative in this context; likely abstain given the elevated risk, and document the consultation.
B. Proceed to date Mia because Jordan is no longer a client and Mia can consent, while keeping the relationship confidential to protect everyone’s privacy.
C. Accept Jordan’s offer of a higher fee and write a supportive letter if he appears stable, as the treatment relationship provides sufficient information for an opinion.

D. Explain to Jordan that providing an opinion on firearms suitability as his former treating psychologist creates a dual-role conflict; decline to give an opinion and refer him to an independent assessor, offering to share relevant records with Jordan’s written consent.
E. Email Jordan to request his permission to date Mia, because explicit consent from the former client resolves the boundary concerns.

F. If Jordan persists in requesting documentation, provide only a factual treatment summary based strictly on the clinical record, with Jordan’s written consent, clearly stating that you are not offering any opinion on firearms suitability and noting the limits of the information.

question: You are a registered psychologist in a small coastal NSW town providing weekly therapy to Kai, a 16-year-old First Nations student, for depressive symptoms and school refusal. Separately, you are contracted to deliver a general wellbeing program at Kai's school. The principal emails requesting you complete a behaviour and risk assessment for a disciplinary hearing about a vandalism incident involving Kai next week. Your contract does not require you to conduct disciplinary assessments, there is no indication of imminent risk, and an independent assessor via telehealth is available within two weeks. Under the multiple-relationships principle, what is the most ethical course of action?
options: A. Agree to conduct the assessment and use relevant therapy information, as your duty to the school community's safety outweighs concerns about dual roles.
B. Decline the assessment due to the multiple relationship and refer the school to an independent assessor; document your reasoning and inform the school and family of the potential conflict.
C. Proceed only if Kai and the parent/carer provide written consent, as informed consent sufficiently mitigates the conflict of interest.
D. Agree to conduct the assessment because you are already contracted by the school, but keep separate files, document your conflict-of-interest plan, and avoid using therapy notes.
E. Suspend therapy during the disciplinary process, conduct the assessment, and resume therapy afterwards to prevent role confusion.

question: You are a senior psychologist in a public mental health clinic in Victoria. You have been providing CBT to Avery, a 22-year-old transgender woman with major depressive disorder. Due to service demand, the clinic will transfer Avery's ongoing therapy to a provisional psychologist starting tomorrow. Avery disclosed active suicidal ideation with a plan if treatment is delayed. You are the only Board-approved supervisor on site; management asks you to supervise the provisional specifically for Avery's case for up to two weeks until an external supervisor is arranged. This creates a multiple relationship (treating psychologist and supervisor). Under the multiple-relationships principle, which actions are ethically appropriate if you decide to proceed temporarily because of imminent risk and organisational constraints?
options: A. Make contemporaneous notes articulating your reasonable belief that you are ethically/organisationally obliged to accept the temporary dual role, and record the steps you will take to protect all parties' interests.
B. Inform Avery and the provisional psychologist about the potential conflict of interest and its implications, provided doing so will not breach anyone's privacy.
C. Avoid disclosing the dual role to the provisional to minimise bias and preserve their independent clinical judgment; monitor the case closely instead.

D. Establish a time-limited arrangement with scheduled review, actively monitor risk, consult an experienced practitioner if reasonable, and arrange transfer of supervision to an independent supervisor as soon as feasible.
E. Continue in the dual role indefinitely as long as Avery provides written consent and therapy and supervision notes are maintained separately.
F. Decline to accept any supervisory role, directing the team to place Avery on a waitlist until an external supervisor is found, as this avoids any multiple relationship.

question: Liya (32), a recent migrant with limited English, and Tom (45), a senior manager who will pay for sessions, seek couples therapy regarding escalating conflict. Tom emails ahead insisting on starting with joint sessions only, saying “we don’t keep secrets” and that Liya does not need an interpreter because he can translate. At the first appointment, Tom reiterates that separate interviews are unnecessary and requests that anything Liya says be shared with him. In line with ethical obligations for providing the same service to two clients together, which is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Proceed with the conjoint session to avoid delay, obtain joint verbal consent at the start, and allow Tom to interpret for Liya, documenting that time constraints prevented individual consent.

B. Arrange brief individual pre-session meetings with each client—using a certified interpreter for Liya if needed—to assess for coercion or family violence, ensure each client’s voluntary informed consent, clarify confidentiality limits and any couple “no-secrets” policy, and document the rationale for conjoint work and contingencies if individual sessions are required.
C. Ask Tom to sign a single consent form as the contracting party and begin therapy, noting his assurance that Liya agrees; monitor for any coercion concerns in later sessions.
D. Decline all couple work and refer both clients elsewhere immediately because power imbalances always render conjoint therapy unethical.
E. Agree to see them conjointly only if both promise that any information disclosed individually will be shared, and avoid separate contacts to preserve neutrality and reduce misunderstanding.

question: You are contracted by an employer to run a 90‑minute post-incident group session after a traumatic event at a logistics warehouse. Attendance has been advertised by the company, and employees report they feel expected to attend. The group includes a 17‑year‑old apprentice and an employee with a known history of PTSD who appears highly distressed. The employer asks for a list of attendees and a summary of what each person shares. During the session, one participant briefly mentions current thoughts of suicide. Which actions align with ethical obligations when providing the same service to multiple clients together? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Before commencing, explain that participation is voluntary and obtain informed consent from each participant free from undue employer influence; outline confidentiality and its limits; assess whether the group format is safe and effective for each person (offering individual support or an alternative if indicated), and document your rationale for inclusion or alternative arrangements.

B. Proceed because the employer requested the session and attendance implies consent; provide the employer with an attendance list and a brief identified summary of each participant’s disclosures to support their duty of care.

C. For the 17‑year‑old apprentice, assess decision-making capacity (e.g., Gillick competence); obtain their own informed consent if competent, or seek parent/guardian consent if required; additionally consider whether a group format is appropriate for a minor and document the decision and rationale.

D. Establish and communicate clear group confidentiality expectations and limits (e.g., risk of harm), advise that only de‑identified themes will be reported to the employer, and do not share individual disclosures without consent or a legal requirement.
E. Keep the highly distressed employee in the group to maintain cohesion and efficiency; arrange individual support only after the session so as not to disrupt the group process.
F. If a participant expresses current intent to harm themselves, maintain group confidentiality to preserve trust and continue with the session; address the risk privately after the group concludes.

question: You are a clinical psychologist in private practice providing CBT to a 32-year-old Aboriginal man with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. You notice emerging hypomanic symptoms (reduced sleep, increased goal-directed activity). He has a psychiatrist who manages his medications. In a prior case conference the psychiatrist used a stigmatizing phrase about the client's culture, which the client found upsetting. The client is unsure about allowing you to contact the psychiatrist. What is the most ethical next step to promote effective, non-discriminatory collaboration that supports the client’s care?
options: A. Explore the client’s concerns and, with informed consent, contact the psychiatrist to share objective observations and request a joint care plan; raise the prior stigmatizing language privately and respectfully with the psychiatrist, focusing on client welfare and culturally safe practice.
B. Continue therapy and avoid contacting the psychiatrist due to their prior remark; only liaise if the client becomes an imminent risk, as collaboration is secondary to avoiding conflict.

C. Contact the psychiatrist without client consent because sharing clinical details is in the client’s best interests and does not require consent when symptoms may be escalating, even if risk is not imminent.
D. Terminate therapy, citing an inability to collaborate with a discriminatory psychiatrist, and refer the client back to the GP without first discussing options with the client.
E. With the client’s permission, write to the psychiatrist recommending a specific increase in mood stabiliser and outlining a titration schedule to prevent relapse.

question: You are conducting a comprehensive assessment for ADHD for a 15-year-old Muslim student who wears a hijab. The referral came from the school. The parents have consented to the assessment but requested that results be shared only with them and the GP, not with the school. The school counsellor makes a comment that the student’s difficulties are "probably due to strict religious practices" and asks to sit in on testing sessions to "improve buy-in and collaboration." How should you proceed to uphold effective, non-discriminatory collaboration while respecting confidentiality?
options: A. Meet with the counsellor to clarify consent boundaries, explain you cannot share assessment results without parental consent, and invite their observational input about classroom behaviour; set expectations that discussions be culturally respectful and free of bias.

B. Since the school initiated the referral, provide the full assessment results to the counsellor despite the parents’ request, as this is in the student’s educational interests and facilitates collaboration.

C. Seek written consent from the parents to involve the school; in the meantime, offer the school general, de-identified guidance on evidence-based classroom strategies for attention/executive functioning without disclosing the student’s confidential information.
D. Exclude the school entirely to avoid conflict, deliver the report only to the parents and GP, and do not attempt to obtain consent for any school collaboration.

E. Address the counsellor’s comment privately, explain how it risks discriminatory bias and harms the student–school relationship, and propose culturally responsive, strengths-focused collaboration going forward.
F. Allow the counsellor to sit in on testing to strengthen the partnership, provided they agree to keep any information confidential, even though the parents have not consented to school involvement.

question: A 16-year-old transgender student with major depressive disorder reports increased suicidal ideation since a recent medication change by their psychiatrist. They also see a school counsellor. In session, they ask you not to contact the psychiatrist because they "don't listen." There is no current plan or intent for self-harm, a safety plan is in place, and risk is being monitored. What is the most appropriate next step to uphold mutual respect and clear communication with other practitioners while managing confidentiality?
options: A. Explore the client's concerns and explain the benefits of collaborative care; seek informed consent to share relevant observations with the psychiatrist and school counsellor; if consent is withheld and there is no imminent risk, respect the client's decision, document the discussion, revisit it later, and maintain courteous, timely communication within the agreed limits.
B. Email the psychiatrist and school counsellor your full session notes immediately so they are aware of the risk signals, because continuity of care overrides consent when the client is a minor.
C. Manage treatment independently for now and avoid contacting the psychiatrist to preserve rapport with the client, as involving the psychiatrist could undermine the therapeutic alliance.
D. Post an anonymised description of the situation in a closed professional social media group to obtain quick feedback on the psychiatrist's prescribing decisions.
E. Call the client's parent to obtain consent on the client's behalf and instruct the psychiatrist to reconsider the medication given the client's age.

question: Jarrad, a 45-year-old Aboriginal man with chronic pain and PTSD, is referred by his employer's insurer for a psychological assessment to inform return-to-work planning. He has a GP, a physiotherapist co-located in your clinic, an Aboriginal Health Worker (AHW), and an external occupational therapist (OT). You have a marketing cross-referral arrangement with the physiotherapist. The insurer asks to be copied into all team communications. Jarrad consents to you liaising with his care team but is wary about insurer access to clinical details. You previously criticised the OT's blog in a public thread last year. Which actions best uphold mutual respect and clear communication with colleagues while avoiding exploitation of professional relationships?
options: A. Participate in a case conference with the GP, physiotherapist, OT, and AHW; communicate promptly and respectfully, explicitly acknowledging each professional's input and the AHW's cultural expertise; use clear, non-jargon language and confirm shared plans in writing.
B. Decline to include the external OT in the case conference because you prefer to work only with clinicians you know and trust at your site, which streamlines care and avoids mixed messages.

C. Disclose to Jarrad (and, where relevant, to the insurer) your co-location and cross-referral arrangement with the physiotherapist, and avoid recommendations that could be perceived as self-serving or commercially motivated.
D. Post a brief, de-identified tweet about "OTs who overreach in pain cases" to demonstrate your objectivity to the insurer and to crowdsource ideas before the case conference.
E. Copy the insurer into all clinical emails among team members to ensure transparency and timely decisions because the insurer initiated the referral.

F. If you believe your prior public criticism of the OT might affect collaboration, contact the OT privately to acknowledge the past exchange, commit to courteous, evidence-based discussion, and focus communication on Jarrad's needs.

question: You are a clinical psychologist providing CBT to Kye, a 17-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander student with major depressive disorder and recent (now declining) self-harm risk. Kye’s supports include a GP, a school counsellor, and an Aboriginal Health Worker (AHW). Kye’s mother asks for regular updates, and the school counsellor emails asking whether the GP should increase Kye’s SSRI. The team has not explicitly agreed on who coordinates care. What are the MOST ethical and effective next steps?
options: A. Arrange a brief case conference (including Kye, and with Kye’s permission, Kye’s mother and the AHW) to explain each team member’s role, clarify who will coordinate care, and confirm Kye’s consent preferences for information-sharing in a culturally safe way.

B. To avoid mixed messages, routinely email your full session notes to all team members after each session without explicit consent, as shared care implies implied consent for information-sharing within the team.

C. Provide the GP and school counsellor a concise update limited to information Kye has consented to share (including current risk status and therapy focus), note who will coordinate care, and invite the AHW’s input on cultural considerations.
D. Advise the school counsellor that Kye likely needs an increased SSRI dose and indicate the specific medication regimen you will recommend to the GP to expedite care.

E. Clarify that while the GP coordinates medical care, you remain personally accountable for psychological interventions and records, and propose a process for timely cross-discipline updates to support continuity.

question: You supervise a provisional psychologist on an adult inpatient unit. Your client, Amina, a 29-year-old trans woman with borderline personality disorder, has intermittent suicidal ideation. Bed pressure is high. The psychiatrist asks you to document “no current suicide risk” to support discharge today. The social worker asks you to co-sign their discharge plan even though you haven’t reviewed it. What is the BEST course of action consistent with collaborative practice and your personal accountability?
options: A. Decline to alter risk documentation; accurately record your assessment, request a brief team meeting to clarify delineation of roles (psychiatrist for medical decisions, you for psychological care), co-develop a discharge plan specifying each discipline’s tasks and supervision check-ins, and confirm with Amina who will coordinate care post-discharge.
B. Co-sign the social worker’s discharge plan to demonstrate team cohesion, noting that final responsibility lies with the team lead and you can review it retrospectively if needed.
C. Ask your supervisee to enter a “no current risk” note in the shared record to expedite discharge, then use supervision later to reflect on the pressures and learning points.
D. To preserve collegial relationships, avoid raising concerns about discharge pressures; instead, keep detailed private notes while limiting team communication to neutral statements.

E. Acknowledge that the psychiatrist, as medical lead, is accountable for the overall plan; therefore, follow their request regarding risk documentation and consider your own accountability as secondary.

question: You are a psychologist in a community mental health clinic providing CBT groups. A senior clinician posts mocking memes about a provisional psychologist’s ADHD diagnosis in the team’s WhatsApp chat and jokes in a staff meeting that a client who uses a wheelchair is “too hard to schedule.” The client’s intake has been quietly deprioritised. What is the most appropriate immediate course of action?
options: A. Meet privately with the senior clinician to clearly state the behaviour is unacceptable and discriminatory; request it stop; document incidents; check in with and offer support to the provisional psychologist; ensure the client is offered timely access with reasonable adjustments; follow organisational policy to report the conduct; and, if it persists or presents serious/ongoing risk, escalate to the service director and consider notifying Ahpra/the Psychology Board.
B. Send a generic all-staff email reminding everyone of the clinic’s respect policies without naming any person or incident, and avoid direct conversations to preserve working relationships.
C. Defer any action until your next supervision in six weeks to gather more examples and advise the provisional psychologist not to overreact in the meantime.

D. Refer the client who uses a wheelchair to another service “to avoid future conflict,” suggest the provisional psychologist limit communication with the senior clinician to email, and do not report to protect team cohesion.

question: You are conducting a court-ordered parenting capacity assessment. A senior colleague who controls much of the clinic’s referral stream tells you to emphasise one parent’s diagnosis to make them look dangerous, despite your data not supporting elevated risk. They have also told your LGBTQ+ trainee not to attend sessions with a conservative family “so the family isn’t uncomfortable,” and they are posting demeaning, culture-based jokes about the parent on a private Instagram story followed by several staff. What are the most ethically appropriate actions?
options: A. Decline to include unsupported or biased statements; take steps to protect the integrity of the assessment (e.g., request independent peer review or reassign if needed); document and raise a formal concern through organisational channels; support the trainee; and, if there is ongoing and/or serious risk to clients or staff and the behaviour is not addressed, notify Ahpra/the Psychology Board.
B. Quietly correct for bias only in your own report and advise the trainee to remain silent to safeguard the clinic’s reputation and referral sources.

C. If you oversee assessment quality, initiate a formal conduct process addressing discrimination/harassment, provide training and clear expectations, monitor compliance, and protect reporters from retaliation.
D. Post a de-identified description and screenshots in a closed professional Facebook group to seek consensus about what to do before considering any formal report.

E. If you believe the assessment’s integrity is compromised, inform the instructing solicitor/court of limitations and propose remedial steps (e.g., independent second opinion), while documenting and escalating concerns internally and ensuring the trainee has safe supervision and support.

question: You have been treating a 16-year-old Aboriginal student for moderate depression and anxiety around exam stress. They report intermittent passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent, and you have a documented safety plan involving family and the GP. You will be on leave for six weeks. Which actions best align with ethical responsibilities for delegating versus referring/handing over care?
options: A. Before leave, phone a clinician at the local Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service (ACCHS) to confirm availability and their acceptance of the handover; with the client’s consent, provide a detailed handover (risk assessment, safety plan, cultural considerations, progress, and contact details). Responsibility for ongoing service transfers once acceptance is confirmed.
B. Email a generic referral to the ACCHS inbox on your last day and set an auto-reply advising the client to attend there if needed. Your duty ends once the referral email is sent.
C. Delegate weekly risk check-in calls to your practice receptionist who knows the client well, providing a brief script and asking them to alert you if concerns arise.

D. Arrange interim sessions with a provisional psychologist within your practice who has relevant training; ensure board-approved supervision coverage while you are away; document your decision to delegate and remain responsible for overall management and for the delegation decision.
E. Send the GP a note advising they prescribe an SSRI during your leave and label this a referral so that responsibility for the client’s mental health care ends immediately.

F. With the client’s consent, share the current safety plan and key history with both the GP and the accepting service, clearly nominating who will be the primary contact during your leave and how to escalate if risk increases.

question: You are instructed to complete a court-ordered violence risk assessment for a 28-year-old man on remand. You learn your cousin is a senior nurse at the correctional centre where the assessment would occur, and the report is due in two weeks. Which ONE option best reflects ethical management of delegation versus referral/hand-over and conflict of interest?
options: A. Ask an experienced colleague to complete most of the assessment but keep your name as the author after reviewing their draft; this is delegation and maintains continuity while you retain overall responsibility.

B. Refer the entire assessment to an independent forensic psychologist, disclose the potential conflict to the instructing party, obtain consent to transfer, provide a comprehensive handover (including all relevant records and clarifying scope), and confirm acceptance before disengaging.

C. Delegate test administration and scoring to a trained psychology student on placement while you conduct the interview and write the report so the deadline can be met; you will remain responsible for overall management.
D. Send a brief letter to the prison psychology service advising you cannot proceed and close your file; the service is no longer your responsibility once the letter is sent.
E. Proceed with the assessment yourself but include a disclaimer in your report acknowledging the familial connection to mitigate any conflict concerns.

question: A 19-year-old university student who recently came out as gay to a few peers (but not family) seeks weekly telehealth for social anxiety and depression. They live with conservative parents and share a family phone plan; push notifications from apps and SMS preview on the phone’s lock screen. They report occasional passive suicidal ideation but deny plan/intent and agree there is currently no imminent risk. They request to use a popular mental health app for asynchronous check-ins between sessions. Which actions best reflect awareness of potential harm when using technology?
options: A. Agree to use the popular app as-is because it is widely used by students; proceed without additional discussion to avoid pathologising normal technology use.

B. Discuss and obtain informed consent specific to telehealth and the app (including risks of lock-screen notifications, data storage, and who can access the device); assist the client to change privacy settings, agree on safer channels (e.g., in-app messages without previews), develop a crisis plan that accounts for remote care, and document the discussion.
C. Proceed with telehealth and recommend earphones to protect privacy, but avoid documenting technology risks to prevent increasing the client’s anxiety about treatment.
D. Switch to email for check-ins because it is a professional channel; emails sent from a work account are inherently secure enough for sensitive information.

E. Offer an initial in-person session (if feasible) to evaluate risk and environmental privacy, and for ongoing telehealth verify the client’s physical location at each session, check who may overhear, and reassess suitability of the modality over time.

question: You are court-appointed to conduct a parenting capacity evaluation for a 32-year-old mother living rurally with a history of bipolar disorder, currently stable. She requests remote assessment. She proposes: (1) recording interviews and using an AI transcription service that stores data on overseas servers, and (2) completing psychometric questionnaires on a public library computer. What is the most appropriate response?
options: A. Agree to AI transcription because it improves accuracy and efficiency; de-identify the transcript after download to address privacy concerns.
B. Administer the full cognitive battery via screenshare, provided the client promises not to screenshot or look up answers during testing.

C. Explain the risks and limitations of remote assessment and third-party tech (test security/standardisation, confidentiality, cross-border data storage), seek informed consent, verify identity and testing environment, use only secure compliant platforms (preferably Australian-hosted), consult publishers about remote validity, and if adequate conditions cannot be met, arrange in-person options (e.g., local assessor) and inform the court of limitations.
D. Permit questionnaires at the public library if a private booth is available; provide headphones and instruct the client to clear browser history and log out after completion.
E. Proceed remotely with all components but include a prominent disclaimer that findings may be less reliable due to technology constraints.

question: You are the sole psychologist two days per week in a rural public clinic with a long waitlist. You currently see Mr Chen, a 45-year-old engineer with mild performance anxiety, for weekly therapy that has continued for six months with good progress. A new urgent referral arrives for Mia, a 16-year-old Aboriginal student presenting with moderate depression and episodic passive suicidal ideation (no plan or intent). The clinic has access to an Aboriginal Health Worker twice weekly and there are limited places at a nearby headspace and an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service. Which actions best align with the ethical principle of delivering services for optimal benefit to society, including equitable allocation and supporting access? Select all that apply.
options: A. Maintain Mr Chen’s weekly schedule unchanged because he pays privately and provides reliable revenue, and put Mia on the standard waitlist to avoid any perception of preferential treatment.

B. Conduct a same-day risk triage for Mia and prioritise an earlier appointment based on clinical need; with Mr Chen, collaboratively discuss tapering or spacing sessions given his progress, shift to a stepped-care plan, and transparently document the allocation rationale.
C. Offer Mia one crisis session and then direct her solely to generic online self-help; avoid liaison with the Aboriginal Health Worker to conserve clinician time.
D. Cancel all other clients this week to provide daily sessions for Mia until she reports no suicidal thoughts.

E. With Mia’s informed consent, make a warm referral to the local Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service and headspace; involve the Aboriginal Health Worker to plan culturally safe care; schedule brief check-ins until ongoing care is secured.

question: In private practice, you are asked to assess Amir, a 19-year-old international university student with suspected ADHD. His father offers to pay double if you can provide a letter to the university within 48 hours to secure accommodations without a full assessment. Your diary is full for six weeks, including several executive coaching clients. Interpreters are available, but using one will extend appointment time and reduce revenue. Psychologists in Australia cannot prescribe medication. Which ONE response best upholds the principle of appropriate, necessary, transparent and equitable allocation of services while supporting access?
options: A. Accept the higher fee and complete a brief online screening, then write a confirming letter so Amir quickly gains access to supports.

B. Explain that a comprehensive assessment is typically required; offer an initial triage appointment with an accredited interpreter, provide a clearly labelled provisional report (with limitations) recommending the university’s interim supports if urgency is demonstrated, and either schedule the full assessment promptly or refer to other qualified providers who can see him sooner.
C. Offer weekly supportive therapy while postponing the assessment for six weeks because therapy is covered by his insurance and will keep him engaged in the interim.
D. Draft a stimulant titration plan for Amir and send it to his GP to expedite treatment while you arrange testing.
E. Decline the referral due to language barriers and advise returning when his English improves; do not arrange an interpreter because it increases time and cost.

question: A registered psychologist in regional NSW provides trauma-focused therapy to a secondary school teacher following a major bushfire. The school principal invites the psychologist to deliver a staff wellbeing session on coping with trauma. The client worries they could be identified if examples from the local school are discussed. What is the most ethically appropriate approach that best promotes community psychological wellbeing while upholding the client’s interests?
options: A. Accept the invitation and deliver evidence-based psychoeducation on trauma, coping, and recovery without using any case material from current clients; inform the client about the general nature of the session, avoid identifiable details, and signpost local supports.
B. Decline the invitation due to potential dual-role concerns and limit activities strictly to individual treatment of existing clients to avoid any appearance of conflict.
C. Accept the invitation and use de-identified case vignettes drawn from current clients to make the content relatable to staff, as long as no names or dates are used.
D. Accept the invitation and organise compulsory single-session critical incident debriefing for all staff within one week of the bushfire to prevent PTSD.
E. Accept the invitation and request a list from the principal of staff currently receiving therapy so you can tailor the content and provide confidential follow-up.

question: In a primary care clinic in Western Australia, a clinical psychologist assesses a 17-year-old Aboriginal young person with recent onset of hallucinations and marked social withdrawal. There is no imminent risk to self or others. The family asks about medication and early help, and the clinic has noted an increase in youth self-harm presentations locally. Waitlists are long. Which actions best align with the psychologist’s responsibility to promote the psychological wellbeing of the community while using the best available evidence?
options: A. Explain that psychologists in Australia cannot prescribe; arrange an urgent referral to a GP/psychiatrist and an Early Psychosis Program, provide evidence-based psychoeducation to the young person and family, and implement a collaborative safety and support plan while awaiting specialist care.

B. Given waitlists, offer psychoeducation and suggest omega-3 supplementation and computerised CBT as first-line alternatives to psychiatric referral for first-episode psychosis, advising the family that referral can be deferred while trying these options.

C. Partner with the local Aboriginal community-controlled health service to co-design and deliver a culturally safe youth workshop on early warning signs, help-seeking pathways, and available supports, ensuring informed consent and careful handling of privacy.
D. Recommend your own paid mindfulness app to the family and propose the clinic purchase bulk licenses for local schools; disclose your financial interest to manage any potential conflict.

E. Work with clinic leadership to prepare an advocacy brief using de-identified, aggregated data on youth presentations to seek funding for early intervention pathways (e.g., family-inclusive services, cultural liaison), and share it with relevant community stakeholders.
F. Focus solely on individual caseload and defer any community initiatives until workload decreases, as outreach is beyond the psychologist’s core clinical role.

question: You are a non-Indigenous clinical psychologist in a regional town seeing Jye, an 18-year-old Aboriginal man, for therapy following discharge from ED after a suicidal crisis. In session 2 he reports ongoing suicidal thoughts, denies current intent, but mentions he can access a hunting rifle at his uncle’s property. He asks you not to involve his family or anyone from the community. You have limited recent training in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural safety. Which actions are ethically most appropriate to prioritise client safety while respecting cultural considerations?
options: A. Explain the limits of confidentiality; complete a culturally informed suicide risk assessment; collaboratively create a safety plan (including discussing restricting access to firearms); seek Jye’s consent to involve an Aboriginal Health Worker or trusted family member; and if imminent risk emerges, contact crisis services even without consent.
B. Respect his request for confidentiality and focus on building rapport for several sessions before raising safety planning, to avoid cultural insensitivity that could damage engagement.
C. Arrange an urgent joint session with his GP to discuss medication as the primary risk-minimisation strategy and defer comprehensive risk assessment until the medication has had time to work.

D. Seek immediate cultural supervision/consultation and organise a warm referral or shared care with an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service if available, while maintaining continuity and documenting governance and consent processes.
E. Schedule fortnightly sessions to monitor risk to avoid fostering dependency, and email a generic safety plan worksheet for Jye to complete at home.

F. With consent, contact family to remove or secure firearms; if consent is not given but you assess imminent risk, follow local guidelines to contact appropriate services (e.g., crisis team/police) to restrict access to lethal means.

question: A court orders you to complete a violence risk assessment of Mr. K, a recently arrived refugee with limited English, within two days. The only immediately available interpreter is his adult cousin. You last used the specified risk instrument several years ago and have not completed recent training updates. During intake, Mr. K makes ambiguous statements about getting even with his ex-partner. What is the most appropriate action to uphold client safety and ethical practice?
options: A. Proceed with the assessment using the client’s cousin as an interpreter after having them sign a confidentiality agreement, and note the limitation in the report.

B. Request an adjournment to secure a NAATI-certified interpreter and, if needed, a cultural consultant; update your competence with the instrument or consult a suitably trained supervisor/colleague; and document any immediate risk management steps if threats are disclosed.
C. Conduct the interview in English and have Mr. K write responses in his first language, then translate them with an online tool to score the risk instrument.
D. Decline the assessment due to cultural complexity and refer the court back to the panel without providing any interim risk triage or guidance.
E. Use telehealth with a friend as interpreter to reduce stress, and avoid asking about recent threats to prevent escalation; focus on historical risk factors only.

question: You are a registered clinical psychologist in a rural private practice providing therapy to a 16-year-old Aboriginal boy referred by his school counsellor for low mood and bullying. He reports intermittent suicidal ideation without plan or means, and recently disclosed intrusive violent fantasies about a specific peer who has bullied him. He denies intent, plan, or access to weapons. His mother requests that you keep everything confidential from the school and police. Your practice currently has no formal incident monitoring or risk register. Which actions best align with effective risk management obligations?
options: A) Co-develop a culturally safe safety plan with the client (and caregiver as appropriate), seek consent to involve an Aboriginal health worker or liaison for support, establish a simple practice-level risk log and debrief protocol, schedule proactive follow-up, and document your decision-making and governance obligations.
B) Maintain detailed progress notes but postpone creating any risk management procedures until a professional college releases a standard template; taking extra steps now may confuse the family.
C) Immediately notify local police about the violent fantasies to avoid potential liability and do not discuss this with the client first, as confidentiality does not apply to any mention of harm.

D) Conduct and document a structured risk assessment focused on intent, plan, means, and specificity; if content escalates to a reasonably believed serious threat, act under the Privacy Act serious threat exception to notify the school principal and parent/guardian to reduce risk, after explaining limits of confidentiality and cultural considerations to the client.
E) Stay strictly ‘value-neutral’ by avoiding conversation about the client’s cultural identity or experiences of racism, and focus solely on CBT techniques to prevent bias in risk discussions.

F) Seek timely peer supervision and participate in any available regional quality assurance/risk-review processes; review and update the safety plan after any incident or near miss, and log near misses to monitor potential harm.

question: You are the team lead in a multicultural community mental health service. A psychologist on your team consults about a 24-year-old man with schizophrenia who is on a Community Treatment Order (CTO) under psychiatric care. Today he described increasingly detailed surveillance of his ex-partner (who is from a culturally and linguistically diverse background), but still denies a specific plan or means. It is late Friday afternoon. Your service has a risk escalation policy and an incident reporting system. Which single option BEST aligns with your risk management obligations?
options: A) Follow the service’s governance and risk-escalation policy immediately: support the clinician to complete and document a structured violence risk assessment today; if a serious threat is reasonably believed, act under the Privacy Act serious threat exception to notify appropriate parties (e.g., police and/or through approved channels to the potential victim), lodge a critical-incident alert, arrange increased monitoring/contact, and provide supervision and debrief for the clinician.
B) Encourage the clinician to preserve therapeutic rapport and confidentiality and plan to review the risk next week; reporting is not appropriate unless there is absolute certainty of imminent harm.
C) Because the client is on a CTO, defer responsibility to the treating psychiatrist and take no further steps within your team.
D) Send a general reminder to staff to be vigilant without naming the client to avoid breaching confidentiality, and do not file any formal report to prevent unnecessary alarm.
E) Telephone the ex-partner directly and provide detailed clinical information immediately, bypassing the service policy to save time in warning them.

question: You are an early‑career clinical psychologist in an outpatient service working with Kai, a 17‑year‑old transgender Aboriginal student with major depressive disorder who reports recent self‑harm urges. You are recovering from a post‑viral illness and have noticed memory lapses and slowed processing that led you to miss parts of a previous session’s safety planning. You are worried this could compromise care. Which actions best align with effective practice to minimise risk to the client and meet your ethical obligations?
options: A. Acknowledge the potential impairment and urgently seek supervision; complete a structured suicide risk assessment and safety plan at the next contact; if impairment persists, arrange a supported transfer or co‑management with a more experienced clinician.
B. Shorten sessions and rely on Kai’s reassurance that they will be okay until next week; avoid involving caregivers due to confidentiality because Kai is 17.
C. Notify your practice manager and adjust workload consistent with workplace health and safety policies; obtain a medical review and take short leave if indicated; document all steps and rationale.
D. Contact your professional indemnity insurer’s ethics line to clarify obligations and obtain guidance on handover and documentation while you recover.
E. Continue sessions as usual to avoid disrupting rapport; use discreet sticky notes with prompts to compensate for memory issues without informing anyone.
F. With informed consent and clear explanation of duty‑of‑care limits to confidentiality, involve a supportive caregiver in safety planning and increase monitoring (e.g., check‑ins, crisis contacts).

question: You supervise a registered psychologist colleague in a small rural service. They return from bereavement leave and you notice alcohol on their breath and slurred speech as they begin a trauma‑focused session with a 28‑year‑old client who has disclosed escalating suicidal ideation. You are concerned the colleague’s performance could place the client at risk. What is the most appropriate immediate course of action?
options: A. Prioritise client safety by respectfully ending your colleague’s session and arranging an immediate suicide risk assessment by a competent practitioner; notify your manager, document your concerns, initiate a mandatory notification to AHPRA for practising while intoxicated, and support your colleague to access help and safe transport.
B. Allow the colleague to complete the session to preserve rapport; afterwards, privately encourage them to take leave and seek support, but avoid formal reporting to maintain trust.
C. Sit in to provide oversight this once, schedule intensive supervision over the next week, and consider notifying the regulator only if problems continue.
D. Call the client’s GP to request a medication review to reduce risk while advising your colleague to hydrate and take a short break before their next client.

question: A 19-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander man presents with PTSD symptoms following a racially motivated assault. He reports no current intent or plan for self-harm, but intermittent intrusive memories and sleep disturbance. You are an experienced clinical psychologist in a regional service with solid CBT training from a decade ago, but limited recent CPD in culturally responsive trauma care. The service has just introduced a digital CBT program you have not yet used. Which actions align with the ethical principle of maintaining current, culturally reflective competence through self-reflection, ongoing development, and service-improvement participation? Select all that apply.
options: A. Arrange cultural supervision/consultation with the service’s Aboriginal Health Worker or an external Indigenous psychologist; complete targeted CPD in culturally responsive, trauma-informed care; adapt assessment and CBT interventions using validated, culturally appropriate measures; and document reflective learning goals.
B. Proceed immediately with your standard CBT protocol as manualised in your original training to avoid delaying care, and plan to review cultural training after the case concludes.

C. Use your performance appraisal to co-create a development plan addressing cultural responsiveness and digital mental health; propose a service improvement to include validated screening tools and referral pathways for Indigenous clients; and evaluate outcomes.

D. Encourage the client to ask their GP about medication options for PTSD while you continue your usual CBT approach without seeking cultural consultation, prioritising symptom reduction over updating your skills in the short term.

E. If timely cultural supervision is unavailable, negotiate a shared-care or supported transfer to a clinician with demonstrated competence in Indigenous mental health while you commence relevant CPD, ensuring a warm handover and continuity of care.

question: You are asked to conduct a court-ordered psychological assessment to inform parenting capacity in a custody dispute involving a recently arrived Arabic-speaking mother with limited English. The court wants an opinion on cognitive and psychosocial functioning within three weeks. You have not completed formal training in interpreter-mediated assessment and have not yet upskilled in the newest digital administration standards for the relevant instruments. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Proceed with administration of the cognitive test in English, using the client’s adult cousin as an interpreter to meet the deadline, and document limitations in your report.

B. Request an extension from the court to obtain appropriate consultation/training and secure an accredited interpreter; if competence cannot be achieved in time, decline and refer to a suitably qualified colleague, providing a clear rationale and assisting with transfer.

C. Use an older English-language version of the cognitive test you are comfortable with to avoid complexities of interpreter-mediated testing, and state that language differences limit the conclusions.
D. Administer tests in English while using an online translation app to ensure literal translation of items, and include extensive caveats about validity in the report.
E. Add multiple validity indicators and symptom inventories to compensate for language barriers and proceed, noting that these additional measures offset the risks.

question: You are a registered psychologist in regional NSW providing therapy. A 26-year-old new mother (8 weeks postpartum) presents with severe intrusive harm obsessions and compulsive checking consistent with OCD. She denies intent but is highly distressed and sleep-deprived. Local services are limited and waitlists are long. You have general CBT experience but last completed formal CPD on OCD more than five years ago and have not trained in ERP specific to perinatal populations. Which course of action best meets your obligations to keep your practice within your current competence and to maintain ongoing CPD under the Board’s registration standard?
options: A. Accept the client and provide supportive, general CBT while you enrol in an ERP training to be completed in several months; inform her you are not trained in ERP and proceed without additional supervision given service scarcity.

B. Accept provisionally only after a structured risk assessment; arrange immediate consultation/supervision with an ERP- and perinatal-competent clinician; complete targeted CPD on ERP for perinatal OCD before initiating ERP; document a learning plan as per the Board’s CPD standard, and coordinate a timely referral if you cannot become competent soon enough.
C. Decline and place the client on an indefinite waitlist, explaining that CPD can be pursued later if similar cases continue to present.
D. Begin ERP immediately based on your general CBT background and past exposure to two OCD cases; monitor outcomes and treat CPD as discretionary unless there is deterioration.

E. Provide psychoeducation and safety planning, liaise with her GP about medical options, enrol in a perinatal OCD CPD course next month, and start ERP now while using self-reflection notes to consolidate learning after the course.

question: You are asked to start telehealth therapy with a 17-year-old refugee who has PTSD symptoms after recent trauma exposure.
