question: During a multidisciplinary case conference for a 17-year-old non-binary adolescent with recurrent major depressive disorder and recent self-harm, the senior consultant repeatedly uses the wrong pronouns and remarks that “social media trends” are confusing the patient. A non-binary registrar appears distressed but remains silent. The patient will rejoin shortly for feedback. As the supervising psychiatrist in the clinic, which actions best uphold the Code’s requirement to promote an environment of mutual respect, free of discrimination and bullying? Select all that apply.
options: A) In the moment, respectfully correct the pronouns and refocus on clinical needs; afterwards, privately discuss expectations for inclusive, respectful language with the consultant, linking to service policy.
B) Say nothing during the meeting to preserve hierarchy, but later correct the pronouns only in the written note.
C) Offer the registrar immediate debrief and support; inform them of psychological safety resources and reporting avenues, and invite their input into team norms.
D) Send a department-wide email naming the consultant and demanding disciplinary action, without first attempting local resolution or following procedural fairness.
E) Quietly remove the registrar from this clinic to prevent further harm, without addressing the consultant’s behaviour to avoid conflict.
F) If the behaviour persists or is severe, escalate through formal channels (e.g., clinical director, HR) with objective examples, seeking training for the team.

question: On an inpatient detoxification unit, after a case review of a 45-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder and recent suicidal ideation, a junior nurse tells you the visiting locum psychiatrist made sexually suggestive comments to her in the staff room. She asks you not to tell anyone because she fears retaliation. As the treating consultant on the unit, what is the most ethically appropriate next step to uphold a workplace free of sexual harassment while respecting her autonomy? Select ONE best answer.
options: A) Respect her wish entirely and take no action, but advise her to avoid being alone with the locum.

B) Explore her wishes and immediate safety; inform her of support and reporting options; seek her consent to notify appropriate hospital channels; if there is immediate risk or evidence of a pattern, consider reporting per policy even without consent.
C) Confront the locum in a public corridor and threaten formal complaint unless he apologises.
D) Quietly alter the roster to ensure she never works with the locum, without reporting the issue to avoid escalation.
E) Document the allegation in the patient’s medical record to ensure there is a timestamped account.

question: A 32-year-old woman, 4 weeks postpartum, is being treated for bipolar II disorder with hypomanic symptoms in the perinatal psychiatry clinic. A digital health company that makes a mood-tracking app has offered your service an unrestricted grant if 20 patients use the app and allow de-identified data to be shared with the company. You previously received a one-off honorarium from the company for a webinar 8 months ago. The app’s privacy policy permits sharing aggregated data with third-party partners. The patient is interested in digital tools to help track sleep and mood. In keeping with the ethical principle of dealing with the health care industry in an open and transparent way, being aware of potential bias, and working to minimise it, what is the single best next step? Select one best answer.
options: A. Recommend the app now since only de-identified data are shared, and disclose your prior honorarium later via the clinic website rather than to the patient to avoid influencing her decision.

B. Decline the grant offer, disclose your prior honorarium and potential bias directly to the patient, discuss balanced evidence and non-industry alternatives (including apps with stronger privacy protections), review institutional requirements for any data sharing, and document the consent discussion if she still wishes to use the app.

C. Accept the grant for general clinic education materials but recuse yourself from advising this patient by asking your registrar to introduce the app instead, without disclosing the grant to the patient to avoid confusion.

D. Seek approval from the hospital privacy officer to proceed and, once obtained, recommend the app without detailing your prior honorarium to the patient to prevent undermining the therapeutic relationship.
E. Recommend a different company’s app immediately to avoid the specific conflict, and omit any mention of the offer you received since you chose not to act on it.

question: You are the treating psychiatrist for a 67-year-old Māori man with chronic schizophrenia who is relapsing on his current oral antipsychotic. A newer, more expensive long-acting injectable (LAI) has emerging evidence and may be appropriate. You have been invited by the LAI’s manufacturer to sit on an advisory board with an honorarium and conference travel. You also serve on your hospital’s psychopharmacology formulary committee. Which of the following actions are ethically appropriate under the principle of transparent interactions with the health care industry and minimising bias? Select all that apply.
options: A. Before discussing the new LAI, disclose to the patient (and whanau/family if involved) your advisory invitation and any financial relationship, present balanced evidence from independent sources alongside alternatives, and document the discussion.
B. Recommend the new LAI without disclosure to avoid creating mistrust, ensuring your decision is purely clinical and independent.
C. Accept the honorarium but donate it to charity and forgo any disclosure because the donation removes any material conflict.
D. Declare your conflict to your employer and the formulary committee and recuse yourself from committee deliberations about LAIs.
E. Invite the company’s medical science liaison to attend the patient’s review to teach injection technique, relying on the patient’s verbal consent because it is an educational purpose.
F. Seek an independent second opinion or multidisciplinary case conference regarding the medication choice if you perceive potential bias in your judgement.

question: You work in a publicly funded community trauma clinic with a fixed number of weekly psychotherapy slots. An internal review shows that older migrant women with limited English are rarely allocated therapy because interpreters are not routinely funded. Today, the allocation committee must decide between Ms K, a 62-year-old refugee woman with severe PTSD, significant functional impairment, and limited English (no current suicidal intent), and Mr T, a 26-year-old university student with panic disorder and no imminent risk whose family are known hospital donors. You are both Ms K’s assessing psychiatrist and a member of the allocation committee. Which actions best promote fair allocation of resources and contribute to service improvement?
options: A. Develop and apply transparent triage criteria (e.g., symptom severity, functional impairment, risk, anticipated benefit, and barriers to access), advocate for interpreter funding for Ms K and similar patients, and commit to auditing allocation outcomes by language/ethnicity to monitor equity.
B. Prioritise Mr T this week to maintain positive donor relations and seek extra funding later so Ms K can be seen when more resources become available.

C. Decline to offer Ms K a slot due to complexity and interpreter needs, refer her to her GP for medication only, and place her on an indefinite waitlist, noting that limited English may reduce therapy efficacy.

D. Raise the inequity pattern with service leadership, propose a group-based trauma intervention with interpreter support to extend reach, and submit de-identified allocation data to the quality committee to drive system change.
E. Allocate slots strictly on a first-come, first-served basis and avoid collecting demographic data like ethnicity or language to minimise the risk of discriminatory decision-making.

question: You are the on-call psychiatrist in a rural hospital during a severe bed shortage. Two public inpatient beds remain. Patient 1 is a 45-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder and recurrent major depression, expressing passive suicidal ideation, living alone. Patient 2 is a 17-year-old Aboriginal girl with first-episode psychosis, active command auditory hallucinations to self-harm, and police requesting admission; her family and the Aboriginal Health Worker are present. You also hold a separate private contract with a nearby for-profit detox facility that could accept Patient 1. What is the single best action that aligns with fair resource allocation and contributes to improving services?
options: A. Recuse yourself from the allocation decision because of the private detox contract and defer the decision to the next formal committee meeting in several days to avoid any perception of bias, keeping both patients under ED observation in the interim.
B. Allocate the beds to those who can pay a private co-payment to reduce strain on the public system, then submit a business case for more public beds next quarter.

C. Allocate an inpatient bed to the adolescent with psychosis given higher imminent risk and cultural safety considerations; for the man with alcohol use disorder and depression, urgently activate community-based detox/withdrawal supports and enhanced monitoring; disclose your private contract and present neutral referral options (including non-contracted services) to avoid conflict of interest, and document service gaps to inform local service planning.
D. Flip a coin between the two patients to minimise unconscious bias and ensure a procedurally neutral allocation.
E. Admit the man with alcohol use disorder to demonstrate parity for substance use conditions; manage the adolescent in ED observation overnight with a plan for community follow-up the next day.

question: You chair the triage meeting for a publicly funded community mental health service that has funding for only five long-acting antipsychotic (LAI) outreach slots this quarter. The criteria were co-designed with consumer and carer representatives, approved by the district, and publicly posted: priority is given to (1) imminent risk of harm, (2) recent ED or inpatient utilization due to non-adherence, (3) lack of alternative supports, and (4) expected benefit. Today’s applicants include: (a) a 23-year-old Māori man with first-episode psychosis, homelessness, and two recent ED presentations after stopping oral medication; (b) a 52-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia, stable on tablets with good family support; and (c) a local councillor with bipolar disorder who emails to request priority access, adding that they can “champion future funding” if assisted promptly. Which ONE action best aligns with the ethical duty to promote the patient’s welfare while ensuring just distribution of resources and abiding by open, ethical expectations?
options: A. Apply the published triage criteria consistently, document the rationale, allocate a slot to those meeting highest need (e.g., the young man with recent ED presentations and homelessness), communicate the decision transparently to all applicants (including the councillor), and notify management of the attempted influence.
B. Prioritise the councillor this round to build goodwill with decision makers, noting the potential downstream benefits for many future patients.
C. Split clinician time across more patients than funded by offering brief check-ins to all three while postponing full LAI support for the highest-risk patient until the next quarter.
D. Suspend the posted criteria for this round and adopt a developmental/ROI approach (youth first) without consulting funders, given the potential long-term gains.
E. Invite the councillor to a same-day triage meeting to discuss a special exception in return for convening a meeting with funders next week, documenting the discussion to ensure transparency.

question: You lead a public outpatient service with one DBT skills group (8 places per intake) and a formal, published eligibility policy agreed with funders: prioritise those with recent self-harm or high relapse risk, limited access to alternatives, and capacity to engage; active methamphetamine dependence is excluded pending stabilisation with integrated AOD care. The current candidates are: (1) a 29-year-old single mother with borderline personality disorder (BPD), two recent ED presentations for self-harm, and limited social supports; (2) a 23-year-old university student with BPD traits, no recent self-harm, good family support, and private insurance; and (3) a 40-year-old man with BPD and active methamphetamine use declining AOD treatment. You also run a separate private DBT group after hours. Which TWO actions best align with the duty to promote individual patient welfare while ensuring fair resource distribution and adherence to open and ethical service expectations?
options: A. Allocate a public DBT place to the single mother based on published criteria; for the student, provide interim evidence-based supports and information about external options (including generic pathways to private providers) without steering to your own practice; for the man with methamphetamine use, coordinate integrated AOD care and reconsider DBT once stabilized; document decisions and rationale.
B. Offer the student a discounted, immediate place in your own private DBT group to ease pressure on the public waitlist, disclosing your role to manage any perceived conflict.

C. Propose to the service manager a time-limited increase in public DBT capacity by rebalancing underused clinic time, seek funder approval, publish the temporary change in eligibility/throughput, and then adhere to the updated expectations.

D. Reserve a public DBT slot for the man with active methamphetamine dependence to counteract stigma and structural inequity, even though this contravenes the current published criteria, because equity goals supersede process in urgent cases.

E. Accept a local philanthropist’s donation to add two DBT places this intake with the condition that one specific person (the donor’s friend) receives a place, documenting the expansion to demonstrate benefit.

question: You are court-appointed to conduct an urgent pre-bail psychiatric assessment of a 22-year-old Aboriginal man with first-episode psychosis and methamphetamine use. He denies current suicidal intent; acute risk to others is low. He has no GP, lives 300 km from the remand centre, and there is no local inpatient bed. He and his aunt consent to you sharing clinical information for treatment purposes. In your forensic role you must remain impartial to the legal questions, but the Code of Ethics requires advocacy to ensure the best attainable care. Which actions best meet the advocacy obligation while maintaining role boundaries?
options: A. Provide an impartial diagnosis and risk formulation in your report, explicitly recommend diversion to a culturally safe early psychosis program, and—using the patient's consent—telephone the Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation and correctional health to flag urgent assessment pathways; document these advocacy steps.
B. Confine your report strictly to diagnosis and risk, avoiding any treatment recommendations or contact with services to prevent any perception of bias.

C. Decline the assessment due to potential dual-role conflict with your on-call clinical duties, even if doing so causes a multi-day delay during which the patient remains in custody without treatment.

D. Arrange a brief case discussion with the duty solicitor and the Aboriginal health worker (with the patient's consent) to coordinate post-hearing linkage, clearly separating this care coordination from the opinion you provide to the court.
E. State that, because of stimulant use, the patient is unsuitable for community treatment and should be remanded to prison to detox before reconsidering care.

F. With consent, alert the emergency department and telepsychiatry service that if the court remands him to hospital, he should receive urgent review and initiation of antipsychotic treatment if indicated; note in the report that these arrangements are for clinical care and do not influence your legal conclusions.

question: A 17-year-old lesbian patient with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted medically unstable after syncope. The local adolescent eating-disorder unit declines transfer because she resides just outside their catchment, and the insurer signals it will not fund an out-of-area admission. She remains at high, imminent medical risk. Her parents are Jehovah's Witnesses; the patient and parents consent to sharing clinical information for care coordination. Which action best fulfils the psychiatrist's ethical duty to advocate for the best attainable care?
options: A. Respect the catchment policy and insurer decision; continue current ward management, file a standard appeal through administrative staff, and await response while monitoring risk.

B. Convene a rapid multidisciplinary meeting; contact the out-of-catchment specialist unit's intake and medical director for a senior-to-senior clinical appeal; escalate within the hospital to the clinical director and bed manager; document imminent risk; involve the social worker, peer worker, and LGBTQIA+ liaison; and, if required for safety, initiate an emergency transfer pathway while keeping the patient and family informed and involved.
C. Ask the family to sign a private agreement to self-fund the out-of-area admission to avoid delays, and proceed without further escalation to maintain the service's relationship with the insurer.
D. Discharge with a plan for private dietetics and telehealth psychiatric follow-up, emphasizing outpatient autonomy while the insurer appeal proceeds.
E. Decline further involvement due to complexity and request the GP manage referral pathways, to avoid conflicts with hospital policy.

question: A 17-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young man is brought to the emergency department after intoxication at a party. He reports low mood, recent Sorry Business in his community, and feeling disconnected from Country since moving for school. He currently denies intent or plan, is medically stable, and an Aboriginal Liaison Officer (ALO) can attend in 45 minutes. The ED is pressuring for a timely discharge. His Aunty is in the waiting room. Which ONE of the following is the most ethically appropriate immediate next step?
options: A. Perform a standard risk assessment, document his Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status, discharge with a mainstream outpatient referral, and avoid involving the ALO to respect his autonomy and ED patient flow.

B. With the young man’s consent, involve the ALO and offer to include his Aunty/Elder, explore cultural determinants (e.g., recent Sorry Business, connection to Country, community supports), and integrate culturally safe strategies into the formulation and safety plan even if this prolongs the ED stay.
C. Focus on substance misuse as the primary driver; advise abstinence and postpone any cultural engagement until he demonstrates sustained sobriety to avoid mixed messaging.
D. Provide culturally neutral psychoeducation and a crisis number; explain that treating everyone identically avoids discrimination, so no cultural adaptations are necessary.
E. Document that cultural practices are exacerbating distress and advise minimising participation in Sorry Business and community events until symptoms remit.

question: A 28-year-old Māori woman presents with moderate postpartum depression. She requests that her whānau attend the next session and asks if it would be acceptable to begin with a karakia. Her partner asks whether a kaumātua can be involved. There is no imminent risk. Your service has access to a Māori Health Unit for cultural consultation. Which of the following actions best uphold the ethical principle of acknowledging Māori as tangata whenua and respecting diverse knowledge, culture, history, and traditions? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Explain confidentiality and obtain informed consent from the patient about what can be shared; then arrange for whānau involvement and invite karakia at the start of the session as per her wishes.
B. Decline whānau presence to reduce undue influence and preserve clinical objectivity; reconsider whānau involvement only after initiating pharmacotherapy.
C. With the patient’s agreement, request a cultural consultation from the Māori Health Unit or kaumātua to guide culturally safe care and align treatment with kaupapa Māori options where appropriate.
D. Proceed with a standard DSM-5 assessment only; defer any cultural formulation because it risks stereotyping and should be reserved for treatment-refractory cases.
E. Offer flexible arrangements (e.g., telehealth for distant whānau or scheduling to accommodate a marae-based meeting) if preferred and clinically safe.
F. Ask the partner to summarise the patient’s cultural background and decision-making preferences to save time and avoid overwhelming the patient.

question: You are the on-call psychiatrist in a metropolitan ED assessing a 19-year-old Aboriginal man with a first episode of psychosis, auditory hallucinations commanding self-harm, and poor insight. He is homeless and lacks reliable supports. Hospital management has recently instituted a performance target limiting acute psychiatric admissions to 72 hours to reduce bed-days. The nurse unit manager reminds you of the KPI and suggests early discharge with community follow-up. What is the most ethically appropriate course of action consistent with the principle that psychiatrists' primary responsibility is to patients, including advocacy when services fall below acceptable standards?
options: A. Comply with the 72-hour KPI by planning discharge with an increased antipsychotic dose, a safety plan, and next-day community follow-up, documenting that service constraints necessitated this approach.

B. Escalate to the clinical director to override the KPI and provide guideline-concordant care; if refused, arrange transfer to an alternative unit capable of safe ongoing treatment, file a contemporaneous incident report, and notify clinical governance—prioritising the patient's safety and rights.

C. Discharge to crisis accommodation with close case-management follow-up within five days to avoid prolonged admission, noting that the patient’s housing instability can be addressed by community services.
D. Convene a case conference with family and an Aboriginal health liaison to ensure culturally safe planning, but maintain the fixed discharge timeline to comply with employer directives.
E. Raise the systemic concern by sending a de-identified email to hospital executives and await their response before determining disposition to avoid conflict with management.
F. Limit contact with family to respect autonomy, continue brief ED observation until the KPI discharge time, and avoid escalating concerns that might damage working relationships.

question: You are contracted by a government police service to perform a fitness-for-duty assessment of a 35-year-old woman police officer following a critical incident. The employer asks you to avoid diagnosing PTSD because of liability concerns and to deliver a rapid clearance to return to armed duties. The officer reports nightmares and hypervigilance but denies current intent to harm herself or others. What actions best align with the principle that psychiatrists' primary responsibility is to the person assessed, requiring advocacy for appropriate standards of care and, if necessary, dissociation from substandard services?
options: A. Accept the employer’s instruction to avoid a PTSD label to protect the officer’s career and focus your report on resilience and training recommendations.

B. Before proceeding, clarify in writing your duty of care to the officer and the limits of confidentiality, insist on independence in clinical judgment, conduct a comprehensive assessment, and refuse to continue if the employer requires predetermined conclusions.
C. Provide two tailored reports: a reassuring version for the employer and a separate, frank report for the officer kept outside official channels to mitigate the conflict.
D. Issue a preliminary opinion on fitness for duty based on a brief screening to meet contractual timelines, noting that a fuller assessment will follow.

E. If pressure to shape conclusions persists, formally decline the referral, advise the officer about options for independent care, and suggest the employer engage an assessor who can work without constraints; document the reasons.
F. Proceed with the assessment but add a disclaimer that the employer influenced the process, thereby preserving transparency.
G. Share the report only with the employer as the paying party and avoid discussing findings with the officer to maintain role clarity.

question: Dr K, a consultant psychiatrist with a PTSD specialty, is invited to a national breakfast show to discuss a new neurostimulation device that a manufacturer claims can “cure PTSD” in returned defence force veterans within two weeks. Dr K received an honorarium for a single lecture from the company 18 months ago and is currently site PI on an investigator-initiated trial funded by a public grant; the company supplies devices at no cost. The producer wants a “strong take” and on-air mention of the brand. Which approach best upholds the ethical principle that psychiatrists should be prepared to disseminate scientific knowledge and consensus professional views?
options: A. Participate after clearly disclosing the past honorarium and the device-supply arrangement both to the producer and on-air; avoid brand names; summarise consensus guidance (e.g., that evidence is promising but preliminary, indications/contraindications, alternatives), distinguish personal opinion from consensus, provide reputable resources, and decline promotional statements.
B. Decline all participation because any prior industry contact is an irredeemable conflict, and recommend a veteran spokesperson to share lived experience instead of a professional perspective.
C. Participate but disclose the conflicts only to the producer; on-air, provide a balanced view yet include the brand name to meet the show’s request so the information reaches more viewers.
D. Participate and provide a strong endorsement based on several successful cases from your clinic to counteract “anti-innovation bias,” as veterans urgently need hope.
E. Send a registrar with no conflicts and instruct them to use the manufacturer’s slide deck verbatim to ensure technical accuracy and avoid misstatements.

question: Following a cluster of self-harm among Aboriginal teenagers in a remote community, a rural hospital psychiatrist is asked to join a livestreamed town-hall. The mayor wants “frank discussion” about exact methods used and asks the psychiatrist to name families to raise awareness. How can the psychiatrist best uphold the duty to disseminate scientific knowledge and consensus professional views while navigating confidentiality, contagion risk, and cultural safety?
options: A. Agree to participate only with conditions: use evidence-based, consensus-aligned messaging (e.g., national safe-communication guidelines), avoid graphic method details or sensational framing, use accessible language, and include crisis and support pathways.
B. Decline to speak publicly about self-harm altogether due to contagion risk, explaining that any public discussion is unethical.
C. Share de-identified clinical anecdotes about individual teens to convey seriousness; in a small community, de-identification should be sufficient to protect confidentiality.
D. Co-design key messages with local Aboriginal health workers/elders to ensure culturally safe communication, reflect consensus views, and tailor resources to the community context.
E. Promise to answer individual diagnostic and treatment questions from viewers during the livestream to maximise engagement and practical impact.
F. Recommend, on-air, a councillor-owned wilderness “boot camp” as an evidence-backed solution to reduce self-harm, to show local support and unity.

G. Provide clear disclaimers distinguishing general information from personal medical advice, identify uncertainties, cite consensus positions, and direct people to appropriate local and national supports.

question: A consultant psychiatrist in a public early psychosis service is invited to a live radio segment about adolescent cannabis use and psychosis after a local case involving a 16-year-old Māori student. The psychiatrist also sits on the board of a community group advocating for tighter cannabis controls. Which approach best aligns with the code of ethics principle on public communication? Select the single best option.
options: A. Introduce yourself by hospital title and RANZCP fellowship, then state, "We in psychiatry know cannabis causes psychosis in vulnerable teens," without any further clarification to avoid confusing the audience.

B. Accept the interview and begin by stating you are speaking in a personal capacity, not on behalf of your employer or any professional body, disclose your community-group role, and note that your stance on cannabis control differs from some commonly held views in psychiatry before discussing the evidence.
C. Ask the hospital communications team to pre-approve your remarks and present them as the hospital’s official position to ensure consistency, omitting any personal disclaimer.
D. Decline the interview because psychiatrists should avoid public advocacy to prevent reputational risk to the profession.

question: A psychiatrist who conducts court-ordered forensic assessments is asked to appear on a national TV program to discuss violence risk assessment and involuntary treatment following a high-profile violent offence by a 28-year-old man intoxicated with methamphetamine. The psychiatrist plans to critique commonly used actuarial tools and propose a different approach. Which actions comply with the ethical principle on public communication? Select all that apply (3 correct).
options: A. Open the interview by clearly stating you are speaking in a personal capacity and that your comments do not represent the court, your employer, or any professional college.
B. Introduce yourself as a court-appointed psychiatrist and state you will not discuss the specific case, without clarifying whether your comments represent the court or the profession.

C. Allow the program to identify you solely by your hospital role (e.g., "Consultant Psychiatrist, Central Hospital") and discuss general principles without any disclaimer, as transparency about employment suffices.

D. When presenting a minority position on risk assessment tools, explicitly acknowledge that many psychiatrists hold a different view and briefly state the mainstream position before outlining your own.
E. Request the on-screen caption to read "Views are personal" and avoid using hospital or agency logos to reduce the impression that you speak for your employer.

question: During a televised sports panel on mental health in elite athletes, you are the consulting psychiatrist to a professional football club. Live on air, a journalist asks you to "set the record straight" about rumours that the team's star forward is receiving treatment from you for stimulant use disorder and depression following a recent suspension. The player is currently stable, has not authorised any disclosure, and there is no immediate risk to self or others. What is the most appropriate immediate response?
options: A. Acknowledge that patient confidentiality limits details, but confirm you are providing care to the player and emphasise recovery.
B. Decline to confirm whether anyone is your patient and pivot to general, non–case-specific information about substance use, stigma, and available resources.
C. Clarify that while you cannot name the individual, you can confirm that "the case being discussed" involves stimulant misuse and comorbid depression to counter misinformation.
D. Indicate you will discuss the matter with the player's coach and media manager after the show and, if they consent, provide limited details to protect the team's reputation.
E. Share a composite vignette closely resembling the player's situation, stating it is anonymised, to educate the public on treatment options.

question: An involuntary inpatient recently died by suicide shortly after discharge in a small rural town. The family has publicly named their relative and described their bipolar diagnosis on social media, and rumours about hospital failures are spreading. The mayor and local radio invite you, the on‑call psychiatrist, to discuss the event to "reassure the community." There is concern about suicide contagion but no immediate public safety threat. Which actions are ethically appropriate when engaging with the public or media? Select all that apply.
options: A. Participate only if you can focus on general suicide-prevention principles and available services, avoid confirming care or identity, and adhere to media-reporting guidelines (e.g., wording, helpline signposting).
B. Because the family has already publicised details, confirm that the person was your patient and briefly outline key aspects of the recent care to correct misinformation.
C. Decline any media involvement because public messaging risks contagion; do not liaise further, even to provide de-identified education.
D. Coordinate with the hospital communications team and, if participating, agree on key messages that avoid patient-specific disclosures and signpost supports for the community.
E. Share high-level findings from the preliminary internal review without naming the person, to reassure the community that systems are safe.
F. Seek written consent from the next-of-kin to discuss diagnosis and treatment publicly, and if obtained, provide a factual summary to promote transparency.

question: You are a RANZCP Fellow appointed as an OSCE examiner for the College assessments. On arrival you notice that one of the candidates scheduled at your station is your current registrar, whom you directly supervise on the acute inpatient unit. The station involves assessing imminent risk to self in a 19-year-old non-binary patient presenting after a suicide attempt. The convenor is onsite. What is the most ethical action consistent with conscientiously performing the reasonable duties of your College office?
options: A. Proceed to examine your supervisee but declare the relationship on the scoring sheet and aim to "mark conservatively" to minimise perceived bias.
B. Inform the exam convenor immediately, request reassignment for that candidate due to a conflict of interest, and continue to examine other candidates as rostered.
C. Withdraw from the entire day’s examining to avoid any perception issues, without offering to assist with alternative duties.
D. Ask the candidate directly whether they are comfortable with you examining them, and proceed if they consent.
E. Arrange an informal swap with another examiner for that single candidate without notifying the convenor, so the session isn’t disrupted.

question: You have been elected as the College Branch representative and spokesperson on a state taskforce responding to a recent inpatient suicide of a 17-year-old Torres Strait Islander young person. Duties include attending fortnightly meetings, contributing to a written report on risk assessment and inpatient systems, and handling some media inquiries. You realise you provided brief therapy two years ago to the deceased patient’s sibling, who may be affected by public commentary. The taskforce deadlines clash with two of your private clinic sessions. Which actions best reflect conscientious performance of the reasonable duties of your College office? Select all that apply.
options: A. Decline all media engagements and miss several meetings due to discomfort and clinic pressures, allowing administrative staff to issue a standard "no comment" without informing College leadership.

B. Disclose the prior therapeutic contact with the sibling to the taskforce chair and the College, recuse from case-specific deliberations while contributing to systems-level recommendations, and request agenda management to avoid breaching any patient confidentiality.
C. In a webinar for clinicians, share de-identified clinical details from the sentinel event to educate the sector, without explicit family consent, as long as no names or dates are used.

D. Seek media training from the College and coordinate with a co-spokesperson to share duties; prepare key messages focusing on system improvement and evidence-based risk management, avoiding discussion of case details.
E. Delegate the drafting of the College’s report to an advanced trainee due to workload and plan to sign off without detailed review, trusting their competence.

F. If critical meetings or deliverables conflict with clinic times, negotiate rescheduling or organise temporary locum cover where feasible, documenting efforts and communicating proactively with the College to meet agreed timelines.

question: Dr K, a consultant psychiatrist in an early intervention service, is attending a bi-national in-person College committee meeting to revise a position statement on off-label ketamine for treatment-resistant depression, including patients with comorbid methamphetamine use. The agenda is running over time and the travel/venue costs for members have been substantial. Dr K holds a minority view based on a new RCT and a case series from their service (which includes Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients) urging stronger cautions. Dr K has previously received a modest honorarium from a company marketing intranasal esketamine. Which actions best align with the principle that the College is entitled to members’ best arguments and that the financial cost of bi-national meetings should be respected?
options: A. Declare the conflict of interest at the outset, present a succinct, evidence-based rationale for the minority position, and offer to circulate a one-page summary to avoid prolonged in-room debate.
B. Withhold the dissenting view to keep to time and minimise costs, and send the chair a private email later if time permits.
C. Advocate for a second in-person meeting to fully explore the minority view so it is heard in depth, even if this incurs additional travel costs.
D. Defer to the most senior member’s opinion to streamline the meeting, as seniority likely reflects consensus.
E. Propose that detailed points be finalised by a small, time-limited virtual subcommittee, provided you submit your best arguments in writing beforehand.

question: Dr S, a psychiatrist on a bi-national College working group drafting guidance on confidentiality in adolescent gender dysphoria assessments, is preparing for an in-person summit. The topic involves balancing confidentiality with safety in teenagers with depression and intermittent suicidal ideation. Dr S is also the clinical director of a unit that might be affected by the guidance and is a close friend of a parent whose child is currently being assessed at that unit. Given the considerable cost of the summit to members, what is the single best course of action that aligns with the College’s entitlement to the best arguments from members while respecting the cost to membership?
options: A. Attend quietly without declaring the personal connection, and contribute only if directly asked to avoid derailing the agenda.

B. Disclose the personal connection at the outset; submit a concise, evidence-based written brief in advance; and ask the chair whether to abstain from voting while still allowing the analysis to inform discussion.
C. Decline to participate entirely and request postponement of the agenda item to a later in-person meeting when a replacement can attend, even if this increases travel costs.
D. Participate fully and advocate primarily for the position that benefits the friend’s child, using their case as an exemplar; disclose the connection only if challenged.

question: Dr K, appointed by the Rural and Remote Branch to a College working group on guidance for long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics in early psychosis, attends a meeting where consumer representatives and youth psychiatrists raise concerns about autonomy and consent in 17–19-year-olds. Dr K’s Branch has circulated a directive to push for early LAI use due to workforce constraints in rural areas. Dr K also treats a 19-year-old Aboriginal man stable on oral medication and considers citing his case in detail to illustrate potential harms of a blanket LAI-first approach. According to the College principle on balancing representation and collegiality, which action is most appropriate?
options: A. State the Rural and Remote Branch’s known position, fully engage with opposing arguments, and then vote according to her own considered judgement, even if it differs from the Branch directive.
B. Abstain from the discussion and vote to avoid the appearance of conflict between her Branch’s directive and her personal view.
C. Vote in strict accordance with the Branch directive out of respect for the constituency that appointed her.
D. Share detailed clinical information about her 19-year-old patient to better represent rural practice realities.
E. Avoid stating the Branch’s view to preserve collegiality and only present her personal perspective.

question: Dr M, appointed by the Addiction Psychiatry Faculty to a College committee drafting a position statement on assessment and management of substance use in pregnancy, participates in deliberations. The Faculty’s published stance supports routine urine drug screening in late pregnancy when there is suspected hazardous use to reduce neonatal risk. Dr M also works part-time at a private inpatient detoxification service that could receive referrals if screening thresholds are broadened. Perinatal mental health colleagues and consumer representatives present new evidence about harms of coercive testing and barriers to care. Which actions are ethically appropriate under the principle that members must balance representation with collegiality and independent judgement? Select all that apply.
options: A. Disclose the employment relationship with the private detoxification provider before or at the start of deliberations.
B. Clearly state the Addiction Faculty’s known position, listen to and contribute to the debate, and vote according to her best judgement, even if it diverges from the Faculty’s preference.
C. Refrain from engaging in discussion to avoid perceived bias and submit a written vote in alignment with the Faculty’s published position.
D. Emphasize the Faculty’s stance during meetings without entertaining counterarguments to avoid undermining the constituency she represents.
E. Integrate the evidence and consumer perspectives presented and propose amendments that may depart from the Faculty’s position if this better serves patient care and ethical practice.

question: Dr Singh, a consultant psychiatrist on an acute inpatient unit, has been elected by the hospital’s psychiatry staff to represent them on the regional restrictive practices committee following a critical incident review. The committee is considering changes to trial leave policies after a recent in-hospital suicide of a 19-year-old patient from a minority cultural background whom Dr Singh had treated. Which ONE approach best fulfils Dr Singh’s ethical duty as an appointed representative to report back and consult those he represents, while maintaining professional standards?
options: A. Draft a position statement based on his clinical expertise and submit it directly to the committee to avoid delays, informing colleagues after the recommendations are finalised.

B. Organise a structured consultation (e.g., a brief anonymous survey and an open department meeting) that includes consultants, registrars, nursing leads, allied health, and the rural outreach team; provide de-identified, high-level summaries of committee discussions for input before key votes; and report back outcomes after each committee meeting.

C. Present detailed, anonymised case narratives from his own patients (including the recent incident) to influence the committee debate, and seek colleagues’ feedback only once the new policy is implemented to prevent confusion.

D. Seek targeted views only from senior consultants most experienced with leave policies, as they are the primary stakeholders he represents, and then provide a summary to juniors once the committee has reached consensus.
E. Request permission from the committee chair to defer all communication with his department until the committee’s final report is issued, to ensure a single, consistent message.

question: Dr Tan is the RANZCP Branch representative on a national guideline committee considering updates on long-acting injectable antipsychotics for people with co-occurring substance use disorders, including specific guidance for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. She provides clinical services in a small regional community and also has a declared paid advisory role with a company that manufactures one of the proposed agents. What combination of actions best meets her ethical obligation to report and consult with those she represents so their views inform the committee’s work, while managing confidentiality and conflicts appropriately? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Disclose the industry relationship to both the committee and the Branch; establish a culturally safe consultation process with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clinicians and liaison groups through Branch networks; circulate a high-level summary of committee deliberations and invite feedback from Branch members before major votes.
B. Because of the conflict of interest, refrain from any consultation or reporting to Branch members to avoid the appearance of bias, and limit contributions to personal expertise only.

C. Host a Branch webinar that includes consumer and carer representatives alongside psychiatrists; present de-identified vignettes to frame the issues; summarise and thematically analyse feedback and bring it to the committee.
D. Rely on informal conversations with two senior hospital colleagues whose views likely approximate the Branch position, to minimise the burden on members.

E. Provide periodic, high-level updates to the Branch mailing list that exclude confidential committee details; use a brief opt-in survey targeted to rural and addiction psychiatrists to capture specific perspectives; aggregate and report this feedback to the committee.

F. Use a closed social media group for psychiatrists to collect rapid opinions, encouraging discussion of de-identified cases, and screenshot the comments to present directly to the committee as evidence of member views.

question: Dr Patel, a consultant psychiatrist and member of the hospital’s Morbidity and Mortality committee, participates in a review of a seclusion incident involving a 16-year-old Māori trans boy with autism spectrum disorder and major depressive disorder, admitted after a serious suicide attempt. The committee discusses clinical errors, family dynamics, and new disclosures about possible ongoing harm to siblings. After the meeting, she considers the following actions. Which actions are ethically permissible under the College’s code? Select all that apply.
options: A. Present a de-identified summary of the committee discussion to her external peer supervision group to explore systems issues, because no names would be used and it would improve practice.
B. Ask the committee chair to formally notify the clinical director, so the treating consultant is informed through governance channels about unresolved observation policy risks.

C. Decline to answer questions from the boy’s aunt (a fellow member of her temple) about “what really happened on the ward,” explaining that committee proceedings and individual cases are confidential.
D. Email the school counsellor a copy of the committee minutes, given the counsellor’s ongoing involvement and the guardian’s general consent to share mental health information with the school.

E. Seek advice from the committee chair and the hospital’s child protection liaison and, if indicated, make a minimal necessary mandatory report about newly disclosed ongoing sibling harm via the proper institutional pathway, documenting the rationale.

question: Dr Chen, FRANZCP, sits on a College accreditation committee assessing a rural psychiatry training post. One agenda item concerns remediation planning for an IMG registrar he currently supervises in psychotherapy, and another pertains to accreditation of a ward overseen by a consultant with whom Dr Chen shares a private practice partnership. What is the most appropriate immediate step under the College’s conflict-of-interest requirements?
options: A. Declare both the supervisory relationship and the business partnership as potential material conflicts as soon as he becomes aware, and withdraw from the discussion and decision on those items unless the non-conflicted members resolve that he should remain (for a limited, defined purpose).
B. Remain silent about the conflicts during the meeting to avoid disrupting the agenda, submit a written disclosure afterward for the minutes, and participate fully given his expertise.
C. Disclose the conflicts and contribute to the full discussion but abstain only from the final vote to balance transparency with the committee’s need for his specialist input.
D. Resign from the accreditation committee entirely to avoid any appearance of conflict for this and all future agendas.
E. Disclose the conflicts and remain present for the entire discussion so long as the chair agrees, while refraining from voting on the final decision.

question: Dr. K serves on a RANZCP branch working group developing opioid agonist treatment guidance for public mental health services. The majority votes to require 12 weeks of supervised dosing before take-home doses, citing recent overdoses. Dr. K dissents, concerned this will disproportionately disadvantage Aboriginal clients living remotely who are stable in treatment. The working group’s report is due to the College Board for endorsement next week. A hospital ward team asks Dr. K today how to proceed for a 28-year-old Aboriginal woman with opioid use disorder who has been adherent and requests limited take-home doses to care for her child. Which immediate action best aligns with the ethical principle on committee conduct?
options: A. Present the majority resolution as the committee’s position to the ward team, and ensure your minority concerns are included in the formal report submitted to the College Board.
B. Advise the team to continue the previous practice for this patient group until the College Board rules, noting you personally found the new requirement harmful.
C. Decline to comment on the committee’s decision because you dissented, to avoid misrepresenting your personal view.
D. Send a separate letter to the College Board opposing the policy and simultaneously circulate a petition among prescribers urging them to ignore the committee decision.
E. Withhold your signature from the committee report to signal your disagreement and leave the chair to defend the decision.

question: A psychiatrist sits on a RANZCP Section committee revising guidance on involving families/carers when treating adolescents with early psychosis. The majority supports a recommendation that, when there is a credible risk of self-harm, clinicians may share limited information with parents even if the adolescent (who is a 17-year-old LGBTQ+ student) withholds consent, to support safety planning. The member dissents, concerned about autonomy and potential harm if parental relationships are strained. The committee must report to the College Board. Which actions are ethically appropriate?
options: A. Draft an annex that accurately summarises the minority view (including evidence and limits of disagreement) for inclusion with the committee’s report to the College Board.

B. When teaching local registrars, present the recommendation as the committee’s position and avoid suggesting non-adherence; if asked, acknowledge you dissented and clearly identify it as a minority view, not College guidance.
C. Decline to present or implement the guideline locally because doing so would compromise your personal ethical stance.
D. Publish a commentary in a professional newsletter criticising the committee process and urging services to delay adoption until the Board revisits the issue.
E. Propose that the committee include an implementation evaluation and schedule a formal review within 12 months, and volunteer to help collect outcome data on LGBTQ+ youth.

F. When briefing a consumer group, state that although the committee endorsed early disclosure under risk, you recommend clinicians use discretion to avoid informing families in youth cases to respect autonomy.

question: You are the appointed chair of the hospital's Perinatal Mental Health Pathway Committee. The committee is considering a proposal to expand home-visiting services for women with postpartum psychosis, including culturally responsive supports for recently arrived refugee families. You are aware that a close colleague with whom you co-author papers leads one of the private providers tendering for the contract. Meetings have been drifting off agenda, and Finance has signalled tight limits this quarter. In line with the Code principle above, what is the most appropriate action for you to take at the next meeting? (Select ONE)
options: A. To foster inclusivity, open the floor to extended personal reflections and defer agenda items as needed, accepting that budgeting and timelines can be revisited in later sessions.
B. Step aside as chair for the remainder of the term to avoid any conflict, and allow meetings to proceed without you, even if you cannot attend more than half of them due to clinical commitments.

C. Declare your conflict of interest and hand the chair to a deputy for that agenda item; keep the meeting to a focused agenda with clear timekeeping; and request a budget impact statement before any vote on the proposal.
D. Approve a pilot with discretionary funds immediately to expedite care, with the intention of seeking retrospective financial approval at the next quarterly review.

question: You chair the Seclusion Reduction Working Group after a sentinel event involving an Aboriginal teenager with autism and concurrent cannabis use on the adolescent unit. There is staff distress and a strong push to purchase a costly sensory de-escalation suite; Finance warns there is no additional funding. There is also a request to discuss the specific case in detail, which includes confidential clinical information. In line with the Code principle above, which chair actions are appropriate? (Select ALL that apply)
options: A. Circulate a targeted agenda in advance, ensure any case review is de-identified for learning points, and use timekeeping to keep the group on planned decision items.
B. Commit to personally attending at least 80% of meetings this year; if unavoidably absent, arrange a deputy chair to facilitate the meeting and maintain progress in line with the group's mandate.
C. Approve the purchase of the de-escalation suite now because of clinical urgency, and seek retrospective ratification regardless of current budget limits.
D. To promote psychological safety, allow unlimited discussion of staff distress even if the agenda is not completed and key decisions are deferred indefinitely.
E. Guide the group to prioritise interventions with measurable impact that can be delivered within the existing budget, and set clear timelines for action and review.

question: Dr Singh, a consultant psychiatrist, has been appointed for the usual two-year term to the district Mental Health Clinical Governance Subcommittee (overseeing seclusion/restraint and ECT). In the first six months, Dr Singh has missed 4 of 6 meetings due to on‑call demands and caring responsibilities for an elderly parent. The next agenda includes a review of ECT outcomes for a 17-year-old Aboriginal patient with complex PTSD and substance-use disorder whom Dr Singh currently treats. The committee permits secure videoconferencing and has a process to grant formal leave. Which of the following actions are consistent with the ethical expectation that members attend a majority of meetings in any year of office unless formally granted leave? Select TWO.
options: A. Continue in the role, attend only when agenda items do not relate to their own patients to avoid conflicts, and catch up by reading minutes and emailing comments for the rest of the meetings.
B. Nominate their advanced trainee to attend and vote on their behalf for the remainder of the year, with those appearances counting toward Dr Singh’s attendance.
C. Inform the Chair and seek formally recorded leave of absence for the months when caring responsibilities peak; if the pattern persists, offer to step down or not seek reappointment.

D. Whenever feasible, attend by secure videoconference to achieve majority attendance, and during meetings attended, declare a conflict on the agenda item involving their current patient and recuse for that item while remaining for the rest of the meeting.
E. Ask that the patient’s case be moved to the end of the meeting so they can leave early, which counts as attendance, thereby avoiding the need to disclose any conflict.

question: Dr Lopez, a psychiatrist elected to a two-year term on the Hospital Suicide Risk Review Committee, anticipates intensive research commitments for the next six months and is also providing a court-ordered forensic report in a high-profile homicide case. An upcoming meeting will review a recent inpatient suicide of a person whom Dr Lopez currently treats as an outpatient. They are concerned about workload, confidentiality, and conflict of interest. Which ONE plan best aligns with the attendance expectation for office-holders and appropriately manages conflicts/confidentiality?
options: A. Attend only meetings where their subspecialty is on the agenda and compensate by attending more meetings in year two to offset absences in year one.

B. Request formal leave of absence for the months when research workload is heaviest; when available, attend by secure videoconference to help achieve majority attendance; declare a conflict regarding their patient and recuse for that agenda item only while remaining for the rest of the meeting.
C. Ask a senior registrar to attend in their place with a verbal briefing to ensure continuity, without seeking the committee’s formal approval.
D. Skip the meeting that includes their patient to avoid a conflict, without advising the Chair, but attend all other meetings this year to achieve majority attendance.
E. Resign immediately from the committee solely to avoid media attention related to the high-profile case, despite being able to attend most meetings.

question: Dr K, a 42-year-old forensic psychiatrist, is elected for a 2-year term to a hospital research ethics committee that meets monthly. Over the past 7 months (more than a quarter of the term), Dr K has missed 5 consecutive meetings. No formal apologies or leave of absence were submitted to the chair or secretariat, although a colleague received brief post hoc emails from Dr K saying they were tied up with an urgent court-ordered assessment and a patient with escalating homicidal ideation. As chair, what is the most appropriate next step under the College’s Code of Ethics and governance policies?
options: A. Notify Dr K in writing that, because they have missed a consecutive majority of meetings over more than a quarter of the term without appropriate apology or leave, the matter will be referred under the relevant College policies; offer to discuss support and how to formalise future leave without seeking confidential clinical details.
B. Defer any action because clinical emergencies justified the absences, and treat the emails to a colleague as sufficient apology for governance purposes.
C. Ask Dr K to provide de-identified case summaries and copies of court orders so you can decide whether the absences were clinically justified before deciding on referral.
D. Count meetings for which Dr K later read the minutes and emailed comments as attendance, thereby avoiding a referral.
E. Terminate Dr K’s committee membership immediately without notice, to preserve committee function and avoid further nonattendance.

question: Dr S, a 55-year-old psychiatrist on a Branch trainee selection panel (3-year term; monthly meetings), has missed 6 consecutive meetings over 9 months (more than a quarter of the term). No formal apologies or leave of absence were lodged. A panel colleague has SMS messages from Dr S mentioning on-call duties for an acutely suicidal Aboriginal adolescent and evening religious observance during Ramadan conflicting with meeting times. As chair, which actions are ethically appropriate and consistent with the College attendance principle?
options: A. Confirm the attendance/apology record with the secretariat, then advise Dr S in writing that the threshold has been met and, absent appropriate apologies or approved leave, the matter will be referred in line with College policies; invite correction of any record-keeping errors before referral.
B. Because the absences relate to high-risk clinical care and religious observance, exercise discretion to ignore the attendance rule for the remainder of the term to support cultural safety.

C. Offer reasonable accommodations (e.g., virtual attendance, adjusted scheduling) and invite Dr S to request a formal leave of absence prospectively; nonetheless proceed with referral now if the threshold has been met without appropriate apologies or leave.
D. Accept the informal SMS messages to a colleague as appropriate apologies and update the formal record to avoid referral, even though the designated process was not followed.
E. Request detailed clinical information about the adolescent to judge whether the emergency warrants retroactive acceptance of apologies.

F. If College policy permits, consider a time-limited retrospective leave of absence where justified by significant health or caregiving circumstances (e.g., documented illness), documenting the decision; if granted, pause or withdraw referral accordingly.

question: Dr. K is the elected Clinical Director of a metropolitan adolescent inpatient unit serving a culturally diverse catchment, including gender-diverse youth. A recent cluster of suicide attempts has increased service acuity. Dr. K plans to accompany her partner overseas for 14 months. Her partner sits on the hospital’s philanthropic foundation board, which prefers minimal leadership disruption. Dr. K is considering how to manage her role during her absence to ensure continuity of care and safety. Which actions are ethically appropriate under the principle that if seeking leave for a year or more, the Member should resign so the position can be filled by proper election or appointment?
options: A. Submit a formal resignation before commencing leave, offer structured handover to an incoming appointee, and make herself available as an unpaid advisor only if invited by the incoming appointed/elected director, without any decision-making authority.
B. Retain the title of Clinical Director while on 0.2 FTE remote work for the 14 months, delegating day-to-day duties to an acting director to preserve continuity during the suicide cluster.
C. Delay resignation until the end of the financial year (four months into her leave) to align with budget cycles, continue signing service directives remotely during that period, and then resign.

D. Resign before leave, disclose the potential conflict arising from her partner’s position on the foundation board, and recuse herself from the selection process for her successor while supporting transition planning.
E. Keep an honorary "Director Emeritus" title with veto power over major clinical decisions for the duration of the leave, arguing this preserves safety without adding salary costs.

question: Dr. S is an appointed psychiatrist on a statutory Mental Health Review Tribunal that reviews involuntary treatment orders for a culturally and linguistically diverse population. He is newly diagnosed with bipolar I disorder, and his treating team recommends at least 12 months leave to stabilise his health. A high-risk review of a long-standing case is scheduled soon, and Dr. S is concerned about continuity and his reputation. Which SINGLE option best aligns with the ethical principle that a Member who needs a year or more of leave should resign so the position can be filled by proper process?
options: A. Tender a resignation effective before the leave begins, assist with handover of ongoing matters, and limit disclosure of personal health details to what is necessary for the Tribunal to manage the vacancy and continuity.
B. Request a formal 12-month unpaid leave while retaining the appointment, recusing himself from all hearings during the absence but keeping his seat for return.
C. Stay on the panel solely for the upcoming high-risk case to maintain continuity, then commence leave while retaining the appointment for the remainder of the year.
D. Nominate his advanced trainee to act in his seat during his leave, with a written agreement that the seat reverts to him upon return.
E. Resign in name only but continue to attend closed preparatory meetings as a non-voting observer to maintain familiarity with cases until he returns.

question: During a hospital Suicide Mortality Review Committee meeting chaired by Dr S, a senior psychiatrist member, Dr L, repeatedly interrupts and derails deliberations, accuses a 26-year-old Māori registrar of incompetence, refuses to consider the evidence base, circulates emails with identifiable patient details to unrelated staff, and filibusters to block adoption of systemic recommendations. This pattern has recurred across the last three meetings and appears intentional. Dr S is also the registrar’s clinical supervisor. According to the code and good governance, what is the most appropriate next step for Dr S?
options: A. As chair, make a formal referral of Dr L’s conduct to the Clinical Governance Board to which the committee reports, documenting the repeated, intentional obstruction and the confidentiality concerns; to manage your supervisory conflict, initiate the referral and then delegate further liaison to the deputy chair while you preserve the committee’s functioning.
B. Pause the meeting and warn Dr L that future interruptions will result in removal; defer any referral until after the audit cycle is complete so as not to prejudice outcomes.
C. Unilaterally remove Dr L from the committee roster and appoint a temporary replacement under your authority, managing the issue internally without escalation.

D. Escalate only the confidentiality breach to Privacy/Information Governance and handle the disruptive behavior within the committee through a civility agreement, avoiding formal referral to reduce interpersonal conflict.
E. Put the question of referral to a vote of committee members to ensure procedural fairness and avoid any perception of bias given your supervisory role.

question: You chair a university Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC) for mental health research. While reviewing a multi-site esketamine trial for treatment-resistant depression including participants with recent suicidal ideation, member Dr Q—who is also an undeclared co-investigator at a private clinic offering ketamine—repeatedly filibusters, introduces irrelevant objections, leaks draft documents to an industry sponsor, and circulates mass emails that intimidate other members, delaying risk review. Despite prior informal caution, the pattern continues and appears designed to obstruct deliberations. Which actions are consistent with the code and appropriate governance? Select all that apply.
options: A. As chair, document the behavior and refer Dr Q’s conduct to the Research Governance Board to which the HREC is accountable, ensuring separation between the committee’s deliberations on the protocol and adjudication of conduct.
B. If permitted by bylaws, place Dr Q on temporary leave from the committee to protect deliberations, and simultaneously refer the conduct to the responsible Board for formal consideration.
C. Because the member cites religious objections, avoid referral to prevent perceived discrimination; instead, arrange facilitated mediation and revisit in six months if disruption recurs.
D. Resolve the matter internally by majority vote to censure Dr Q and proceed with business; only refer if a formal complaint is lodged by another member.
E. Given potential participant safety impacts from delay, issue a formal warning letter and bypass referral to avoid further delay.
F. Refer Dr Q’s conduct to the responsible Board and notify the institution’s conflict-of-interest office regarding the undeclared dual role.

question: Dr Chen is the Clinical Director of an acute adolescent inpatient unit that serves a large proportion of Indigenous young people. A College accreditation team led by the Branch Chair (an elected office holder) arrives for a scheduled training site visit following a period of increased seclusion rates and a recent coronial inquest. The team requests trainee supervision logs, de-identified critical incident summaries, and access to interview junior staff. Dr Chen has previously disagreed publicly with the Chair’s views on culturally safe practices and is concerned about reputational harm. Which response best aligns with the College Code of Ethics principle that office holders are entitled to respect, assistance, advice, and cooperation in the discharge of their duties?
options: A. Arrange a timely meeting with the team; provide trainee supervision records and de-identified incident data; facilitate interviews with staff without coaching; declare the prior public disagreement; and transparently outline current remedial actions to reduce seclusion while safeguarding patient and staff confidentiality.

B. Repeatedly reschedule interviews and delay provision of documents, citing the ongoing coronial inquest and the need to protect staff from stress, intending to defer scrutiny until media attention subsides.

C. Offer a curated written summary of positive service activities and request that the team avoid interviewing junior staff to prevent intimidation, assuring the team that the summary accurately reflects practice.

D. Provide full patient-identifiable incident files directly to the accreditation team on the assumption that the College process is part of clinical governance and therefore overrides usual consent requirements.

E. Insist that the Branch Chair be replaced due to past disagreements before engaging, and in the meantime instruct staff to present a consistent message and remove materials that might be misinterpreted by visitors.

question: Dr Singh supervises a registrar, Jordan, who has ADHD and a recent relapse of stimulant misuse. They are also family friends. After an ED triage error involving a violent patient, the College’s Fitness to Practise investigator (a College office holder) requests a confidential statement about Jordan’s performance and supports in place. How should Dr Singh respond to best uphold the principle that College office holders are entitled to respect, assistance, advice, and cooperation, while maintaining other ethical duties?
options: A. Respond promptly with an objective statement focused on observed clinical performance, documented supervision, and remediation steps; disclose the dual relationship; and avoid sharing specific health details without consent unless directly necessary for patient or staff safety.
B. Decline to participate on the basis that such processes stigmatize neurodivergence, advising the investigator to contact hospital HR instead, and stating you will not comment further.
C. Provide a supportive reference that omits the triage incident to avoid jeopardizing Jordan’s career, with the intention to address issues informally within the team.

D. Request to be recused due to the personal relationship; identify an alternative supervisor to provide the primary statement; and continue to assist by facilitating access to rosters and supervision records.
E. Send the investigator copies of Jordan’s private psychiatric therapy notes and diagnostic reports without consent to ensure the investigator has complete information about health issues.

F. Seek the investigator’s advice on framing reasonable adjustments and a remediation plan, providing a de-identified outline of proposed supports and escalation pathways, while committing to supply any further information needed within privacy constraints.

question: You are the clinical lead of a public opioid treatment program serving a culturally diverse cohort with high rates of polysubstance use and unstable housing. A College office-holder (the CPD Committee Chair) has issued a policy statement recommending tighter thresholds for take‑home doses. You disagree with aspects of the statement based on your service’s outcomes data and concern for overdose risk on missed doses. In supervision, registrars ask how to respond. Which is the most ethically appropriate immediate action?
options: A. Acknowledge the office-holder’s entitlement to a presumption of good faith; provide evidence-based teaching to trainees; submit structured feedback through College channels (e.g., policy consultation or correspondence) without disparaging the office-holder, and continue to follow best-practice care while meeting any mandatory standards.
B. Advise registrars to disregard all guidance from that College committee until there is a change in leadership, and to rely exclusively on local protocols.
C. Share excerpts of internal College committee emails with a patient advocacy list to mobilise opposition to the policy.
D. Decline to participate in an upcoming College audit led by the office-holder solely because you disagree with their stance, to avoid ‘endorsing’ it.
E. Implement the policy without question because it originates from a College office-holder, suspending your independent clinical judgement.
F. Lodge an immediate misconduct complaint alleging bad faith by the office-holder, even though you have no evidence beyond policy disagreement.

question: You are part of a forensic assessment team for a 22‑year‑old refugee man facing sentencing after a violent offence. A public statement from a College Vice‑President endorses structured risk assessments has drawn sharp debate on a private online forum you moderate for psychiatrists. You disagree with the statement’s emphasis but recognise its relevance to your report. Which actions are ethically appropriate? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. As forum moderator, remove ad hominem posts impugning the Vice‑President’s motives, remind members to presume good faith while encouraging evidence‑based critique, and steer discussion to method and data.
B. In your court report, question the Vice‑President’s integrity and suggest their statement is agenda‑driven, as justification for preferring your approach.
C. If you believe the statement may have unintended harms, seek a meeting or submit feedback via College governance channels, declaring any conflicts or roles that could affect your perspective.
D. Share a redacted thread from a confidential working group to illustrate political pressures on the office‑holder, so colleagues can ‘understand the context’.

E. In teaching and case conferences, discuss limitations of various risk tools, making clear that reasonable experts—including College leaders—may disagree; avoid undermining trust in the College when speaking with patients or the public by keeping comments focused on evidence and process.
F. Encourage colleagues to boycott College education events led by the Vice‑President until the statement is withdrawn, even though you have no evidence of misconduct.

question: Dr S is a consultant psychiatrist in a community perinatal service working with a 23-year-old Aboriginal woman on methadone maintenance who is early in pregnancy. Dr S learns that the College President’s office intends to issue a draft position statement recommending routine mandatory notification to child-protection services for all pregnant people on opioid agonist treatment. Believing this will deter antenatal engagement and is not evidence-based, Dr S is in serious disagreement with those presently in office. Which actions BEST align with the ethical principle about addressing serious disagreement with College officers? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Prepare a formal, referenced critique of the draft (including relevant perinatal and confidentiality literature), and submit it to the College Policy and Advocacy Committee, copying the President, with a request for the item to be placed on the consultation agenda.
B. Publish an open letter on social media using a de-identified vignette of the 23-year-old patient to illustrate likely harms, tagging major media outlets to increase pressure on the College.
C. If internal consultation does not address the concerns, coordinate with fellow Members to requisition an extraordinary general meeting in accordance with College procedures.
D. Provide an interview to a journalist and share the embargoed draft statement to demonstrate urgency and spur public debate before the College finalises it.

E. Write to the local Branch Chair and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Mental Health Committee requesting a formal stakeholder review, disclosing your service role and any potential conflicts of interest.
F. Encourage trainees and colleagues to boycott College CPD activities until the proposed statement is withdrawn.

question: Dr M is a senior forensic psychiatrist on an inpatient unit. The College Board has indicated it will endorse a policy recommending routine transmission of a brief risk summary to employers upon discharge of patients in safety-sensitive occupations (e.g., pilots, surgeons). Dr M, who is married to a current Board member, believes this overreaches and risks deterring help-seeking. A 45-year-old surgeon with bipolar I disorder in remission has expressed strong privacy concerns. Dr M is in serious disagreement with those presently in office. What is the SINGLE BEST next step that aligns with the ethical principle for addressing such disagreements?
options: A. Prepare a written submission, with supporting evidence and ethical analysis, to the Ethics and Professional Standards Committee and Board Secretariat requesting a formal review meeting, and disclose the spousal relationship as a potential conflict of interest.
B. Ask the spouse to raise his concerns informally at the Board and share relevant Board papers so he can better formulate counterarguments.
C. Email the Health Minister and professional regulators denouncing the impending policy and copy national media to ensure the issue receives immediate public attention.
