D. Draft a blog post using de-identified clinical vignettes from his unit to illustrate potential harms, publishing without explicit patient consent because the vignettes are anonymised.
E. Immediately requisition an extraordinary general meeting to halt the policy process before attempting internal submissions.

question: You are a consultant psychiatrist and College Fellow supervising a forensic assessment clinic. The Branch Chair (a College office-holder) is your colleague and has allegedly pressured examiners to pass a friend in a recent clinical examination and asked registrars to modify case summaries used for exam calibration. You possess strong evidence, including emails and voice messages. Several registrars (including an international medical graduate on a visa) have expressed fear of retaliation if a complaint becomes public. There is no imminent risk to patient safety, but trainees’ fairness and exam integrity are at stake. According to the College’s Code of Ethics regarding concerns about an office-holder not acting in good faith or with due care, which ONE action is most appropriate as your next step?
options: A. Lodge a formal, confidential complaint with the College’s responsible body (e.g., Board or designated governance/ethics committee), submit the evidence for an independent review, and refrain from broader dissemination pending due process.
B. Raise the allegations from the floor at the next Annual General Meeting so that members can immediately vote on confidence in the office-holder.
C. Notify only your hospital’s medical administration and defer any approach to the College to avoid conflicts given your supervisory relationship.
D. Attempt a quiet, informal resolution with the office-holder first, keeping the evidence private unless the behaviour recurs.
E. Seek informal advice from a trusted senior colleague outside the College and delay any formal notification to avoid adversely affecting trainee morale during the current exam cycle.

question: You are the clinical lead of an addiction service treating people with severe alcohol and methamphetamine use disorders. A trainee from a minoritized ethnic background reports that the College Censor-in-Chief (a College office-holder) who also chairs a regional hospital credentialing committee appears to be manipulating training post accreditation to favour facilities linked to a family member. You receive sworn statements and documentation suggesting conflicts of interest and potential adverse impacts on patient care due to threatened de-accreditation of your public clinic. You have strong evidence. What actions are most consistent with the College’s Code of Ethics regarding office-holders and governance?
options: A. Submit a documented complaint to the College Board or the appropriate governance/ethics committee with the evidence, request an independent investigation, and maintain confidentiality on a need-to-know basis.
B. Because there may be patient risk, immediately requisition an extraordinary general meeting to seek removal of the office-holder, bypassing any Board or committee processes.

C. If you sit on a relevant College committee, declare your conflict of interest and ask an uninvolved colleague to lodge the complaint so the matter can be referred to the responsible body without perceived bias.

D. In parallel with a formal College complaint, notify the hospital’s credentialing committee and relevant health authority about specific service risks, limiting disclosures to what is necessary to protect patients and staff.
E. Post an anonymised summary on the members’ listserv to gather more accounts before deciding whether to inform the College formally.

F. If the responsible body is unable or unwilling to act after a reasonable opportunity, consider supporting a requisition for an extraordinary general meeting strictly as a last resort under College rules.

question: Dr Chen, a community psychiatrist, inherits a 29-year-old Pasifika man with generalized anxiety disorder and opioid use disorder from a private telepsychiatry clinic run by a local colleague. The patient has been on long-term high-dose alprazolam alongside oxycodone. Dr Chen strongly disagrees with this treatment approach and suspects it contributed to dependence. A journalist covering “overprescribing” contacts Dr Chen for comment. Dr Chen’s service also competes with the colleague’s clinic for referrals. Which actions best uphold the ethical principle about handling disagreements on diagnosis or treatment? Select THREE.
options: A. Publish a LinkedIn post summarising concerns with de-identified details and linking to guidelines, avoiding the colleague’s name, to inform the public and referrers
B. Propose a de-identified case discussion at the hospital psychopharmacology meeting, presenting relevant data and literature on benzodiazepine tapering in comorbid substance use
C. Write to the private clinic’s medical director/request a collegial peer review of prescribing practices, offering objective data and guidelines to support change
D. Submit an anonymous op-ed to the local newspaper calling for an investigation into “pill-mill practices” among some psychiatrists
E. If credible evidence of unsafe practice exists, lodge a confidential concern with the appropriate regulatory or credentialing body, providing objective documentation

question: A child and adolescent psychiatrist treats a 16-year-old transgender student with major depression and recent suicidal ideation. A prominent senior psychiatrist has just criticised gender-affirming care on national radio, naming clinicians. A parents’ advocacy group invites the treating psychiatrist to join a live broadcast debate next week to counter those views. Which single action best aligns with the ethical principle regarding disagreements about theory, diagnosis, or treatment?
options: A. Decline the media debate and instead propose a closed professional CME session through the local college branch, and/or submit an evidence-based correspondence to a peer-reviewed journal addressing the topic without personalising criticism
B. Accept the debate but commit to discussing only general principles and cite research, avoiding mention of specific clinicians or cases
C. Post an evidence-based thread on a professional social media account that does not name the senior psychiatrist but robustly rebuts their arguments
D. Provide the advocacy group with anonymised clinical vignettes and a statement for their press release describing harm caused by the senior psychiatrist’s comments
E. Write to the senior psychiatrist’s hospital demanding disciplinary action and copy journalists to ensure transparency

question: Dr. N, a child and adolescent psychiatrist, treats a 16-year-old high school student with depression and anxiety. A local school district is proposing mandatory mental health screening with automatic reporting of positive screens to parents. Dr. N has previously done paid consultancy for a company that develops school screening tools. Concerned about potential unintended harms for vulnerable students, Dr. N wishes to engage in the public debate. Which actions are consistent with the ethical principle that public policy disagreements are a matter of public interest and should be argued with cogent evidence, expressed respectfully, and without self-promotion or denigration? Select all that apply.
options: A. Draft an op-ed for a major newspaper that summarises peer-reviewed evidence on benefits, risks, and implementation safeguards, discloses the prior consultancy, avoids identifiable clinical anecdotes, and uses respectful language towards proponents.

B. Post a viral thread on social media labelling supporters of the policy as “dangerous ideologues,” include a link to Dr. N’s private clinic for “evidence-based care,” and encourage readers to leave negative reviews of named school board members.

C. Share a de-identified vignette from a current patient without consent, altering some demographic details, to illustrate potential harms, ensuring readers understand it is a real case from Dr. N’s practice.

D. Speak at a school board meeting to present a balanced summary of systematic reviews and implementation guidance, acknowledge uncertainties, avoid patient-specific details, and invite constructive dialogue.

E. Organise colleagues to sign an open letter that calls policy proponents “ethically negligent,” includes booking links and marketing slogans for signatories’ private clinics, and cites select case anecdotes in lieu of data.

F. Request a meeting with the local MP to provide a brief that references robust evidence and ethical considerations, disclose the prior consultancy, avoid discussing identifiable patients, and propose respectful, practical amendments.

question: Dr. K is a consultant psychiatrist on a public inpatient unit caring for people with psychosis, including several with recent suicidal and violent risk. A televised debate is being held on proposed budget cuts to community mental health services. Dr. K has recently co-founded a private telepsychiatry start-up. Which approach best aligns with the principle that public policy disagreements may be discussed in public, provided views are evidence-based, respectful, and free of self-promotion or denigration?
options: A. Accept the debate invitation, open with a detailed vignette from a current inpatient (with minimal changes to protect identity), then conclude by encouraging viewers to try the new telepsychiatry platform as a solution to service gaps.
B. Decline to speak publicly and instead circulate views only on a closed professional listserv, urging colleagues to keep the discussion within the profession to avoid confusing the public.

C. Accept the debate invitation, prepare a succinct evidence summary from peer-reviewed studies and official data, disclose the start-up affiliation at the outset, avoid discussing identifiable cases, and use respectful language toward opponents.

D. Accept the debate invitation and state that the Minister is “reckless and ignorant,” relying primarily on informal comments from current inpatients (without identifying them as patients) to illustrate the harms.

E. Accept the debate invitation and bring a currently involuntarily detained patient who agrees on the ward to share their story live using first name only, to humanise the issue and highlight mismanagement by the unit’s leadership.

question: You are the consultant psychiatrist for an Older Persons Mental Health (OPMH) team in regional Aotearoa New Zealand. Hemi, a 74-year-old Māori man living in a residential aged care facility, has major depressive disorder and mild neurocognitive disorder. He primarily speaks te reo Māori. His GP requests shared care for persistent depressive symptoms. Your service manager is considering merging OPMH into an 'ageless' adult community team due to staffing pressures. A local public health researcher asks whether to exclude residents with cognitive impairment and those with English as a second language from an upcoming regional mental health survey to streamline consent. Which actions best align with RANZCP recommendations?
options: A. Endorse merging OPMH into the adult community mental health team for efficiency, and transfer Hemi’s care to the adult team with the proviso that OPMH will be re-engaged only if risk escalates.
B. Advocate to retain and strengthen a dedicated OPMH stream and request involvement of a Māori health worker/kaumātua and interpreter to ensure culturally safe, accessible care for Hemi.
C. Decline the GP’s shared-care request, explaining that specialist services should focus only on the most severe presentations to build primary care capacity.
D. Offer shared care with the GP, including a collaborative management plan, case-based education, and ready access to specialist review for relapse or complexity.
E. Advise the researcher to exclude residents with cognitive impairment and those with English as a second language to reduce consent complexity and sampling bias.
F. Recommend that the district establish benchmarks for access and quality in older persons’ mental health, including in residential facilities, to guide service planning and accountability.

question: In an urban Australian ED, you review Mary, a 78-year-old transgender woman (she/her) who speaks Vietnamese as her first language. She has PTSD, alcohol use disorder, and expresses active suicidal ideation without a current plan. The after-hours triage suggests referral to the generic adult crisis team because the OPMH service operates 9–5. Her GP requests guidance for follow-up. Which single next step is the most ethically appropriate and aligned with RANZCP recommendations?
options: A. Refer Mary to the adult crisis team for assessment and ongoing follow-up, noting that after-hours services are ageless, and document that OPMH can review her if concerns persist next week.

B. Liaise with the on-call older persons psychiatry/geriatric liaison via the ED, request a professional interpreter, ensure linkage to LGBTIQ+-affirming supports, and arrange handover for next-business-day OPMH follow-up with a shared-care plan for her GP.
C. Discharge Mary with a safety plan and written resources for LGBTIQ+ support services, asking her GP to monitor and re-refer if alcohol use worsens.
D. Admit Mary to an adult inpatient unit for detoxification under the adult team, with a plan to consider OPMH referral after discharge if over-65 beds are unavailable tonight.
E. Book Mary into the next available OPMH outpatient clinic in six weeks and advise the GP to increase monitoring in the interim.

question:
In a regional town of 30,000 without on-site old age psychiatry or geriatric medicine, an 82-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease dementia in a residential aged care facility becomes acutely agitated and physically aggressive after a fall. He is febrile and has dysuria. The adult mental health team is asked to advise. The old age psychiatrist and geriatrician are available only via telehealth. The facility has previously used Dementia Support Australia (DSA) for behaviour coaching. What is the most ethically appropriate next step according to the service-relationship principles?
Relevant ethical concerns in this scenario include demographics (age), comorbidity (neurocognitive disorder), imminent risk to others (aggression), and service availability.
options: A. Arrange urgent medical assessment by geriatric medicine for possible delirium (including ED transfer if needed), concurrently organise a telehealth review by old age psychiatry for behavioural and psychological symptoms, and maintain adult mental health team accountability until the accepting service formally takes over; involve DSA as a complementary resource within the integrated care plan.
B. Recommend the facility contact DSA immediately to manage the behaviour and defer specialist assessment until DSA has provided strategies, given limited local resources.

C. Transfer the patient directly to the metropolitan old age psychiatry ward without consulting geriatric medicine, as severe behavioural disturbance in dementia should be handled solely by psychiatry.

D. Convene a joint telehealth case conference with the GP, RACF staff and DSA, but transfer clinical accountability to the RACF after the meeting to avoid duplication until either specialist service is ready to accept.
E. Decline specialist involvement because the population is under 50,000, advising the GP to optimise psychotropics and re-refer if problems persist.

question:
In a city of 120,000 where old age psychiatry and geriatric medicine are co-located, a 74-year-old transgender woman living alone presents with new memory complaints and fluctuating attention after commencing oxycodone for a hip fracture. She has a history of major depression and alcohol use disorder in remission. Her GP explicitly refers her to both the memory clinic and old age psychiatry. The clinic manager proposes to triage only to psychiatry to ‘avoid duplication’. The old age psychiatrist is on an outreach day but can provide telehealth. Which actions are ethically appropriate under the service-relationship principles? Select ALL that apply.
Relevant ethical concerns include demographics (gender identity), comorbidity (possible delirium vs early dementia, depression, substance use history), and referral pathway integrity.
options: A. Honour the GP’s explicit request by arranging joint assessment by geriatric medicine and old age psychiatry; if delirium is suspected, ensure acute/geriatric physicians lead medical management while cross-referral and clinical reviews remain freely available, with clear clinical accountability during any transfer.
B. Triaging solely to old age psychiatry is preferable because of the mental health history; geriatric input can be considered later only if psychiatry requires it.
C. Because the services are co-located, face-to-face assessment must be used; telehealth should be avoided to maintain continuity of care.

D. Ensure the memory clinic has accessible input from both an old age psychiatrist and a geriatrician; if rosters prevent in-person input, schedule telehealth participation to maintain joint involvement.
E. Keep the division of responsibility informal to enable flexibility; publishing criteria risks constraining clinical judgment.
F. Document and disseminate clear, mutually accepted criteria for division of responsibility and catchment/referral pathways so that unilateral triage overrides do not recur.

question: An on-site psychiatrist at an offshore immigration detention centre assesses Mr T, a 28-year-old Kurdish asylum seeker who reports having been tortured prior to arrival. He presents with nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance consistent with trauma-related disorder, has recent scars consistent with assault, and acknowledges passive suicidal ideation without plan. The private security contractor requests a report rating Mr T’s “resilience to stress during prolonged separation” to guide placement in an isolation regime and asks you to omit reference to the alleged torture “to avoid political complications.” Your fee is contingent on providing the report this week. Mr T’s spouse and 5-year-old child, living in the community, are distressed and seeking guidance. Which actions are the most ethically appropriate? Select TWO.
options: A. Decline to provide any opinion that would facilitate or legitimise segregation practices amounting to inhuman treatment; explicitly document torture-related sequelae and the impact on the family; advocate for humane alternatives; offer trauma-informed care and, with consent, support/education for the spouse.

B. Provide a neutral functional assessment limited to current mental state and tolerance of isolation, deliberately avoiding mention of torture to remain objective and maintain a constructive relationship with the contractor.
C. Provide the requested resilience rating to meet operational needs but add recommendations for frequent welfare checks and access to diversional activities while in separation to minimise harm.

D. Submit a sanitised report to the contractor omitting torture history while keeping a detailed clinical record of torture sequelae; this balances confidentiality with service expectations and allows ongoing therapy.

E. Refuse the request and notify appropriate clinical governance, human rights, or professional bodies about concerns of potential inhuman treatment; ensure the patient is not abandoned by arranging alternative pathways for care and continuing therapeutic support.

question: A university-affiliated psychiatrist is designing a longitudinal study on the psychological effects of torture among a recently arrived ethnic minority refugee community and their families. The study will measure PTSD symptoms, family functioning, and service outcomes. Funding includes a grant from a national security agency that requires access to de-identified data to “enhance interview strategies in high-stress environments.” The psychiatrist also provides clinical care to some potential participants at a refugee health clinic. The draft protocol plans to obtain consent via caseworkers to reduce participant burden, does not budget for interpreters, and provides no guaranteed referral pathways for treatment. Which SINGLE approach best aligns with the ethical principle described?
options: A. Proceed with the current protocol but add a distress management plan and ensure all shared data are de-identified to protect participants while meeting funder requirements.
B. Limit recruitment to family members (not survivors) to lower risk and retain the security agency’s data-access clause to preserve funding, while adding post-assessment check-ins by caseworkers.

C. Redesign the study to be trauma-informed: ensure voluntary consent is obtained directly with independent interpreters, provide clear clinical referral pathways and safety protocols, engage community representatives, and implement binding data-use agreements that prohibit any use that could facilitate torture or inhuman treatment; if the funder refuses these conditions, decline the grant.

D. Shift to a retrospective de-identified chart review approved by the ethics committee to avoid re-traumatisation, and allow the security agency to access the de-identified dataset for secondary analyses.
E. Resolve dual-role concerns by delegating study leadership to a colleague with no clinical role in the clinic, keeping the existing protocol and funder data-access requirements unchanged.

question: You are the acting clinical director of an inner-city hospital’s emergency department (ED) psychiatry service. Presentations have surged among recently arrived refugees with trauma-related disorders and among people intoxicated with methamphetamine. Interpreters are inconsistently available after hours, and staff report escalating distress and occasional agitation in the ED. The hospital CEO asks you to propose a plan to improve flow within existing budget constraints. Which single option best aligns with the RANZCP recommendations for mental health systems while addressing this context?
options: A. Prioritise triage strictly by immediate medical risk and potential legal liability, refer non–English-speaking patients to community settlement services for assessment within two weeks when interpreters are unavailable, and concentrate on rapid discharge to reduce access block.

B. Co-design a rapid assessment and care pathway with local refugee health services, bicultural workers, and people with lived experience; ensure accredited interpreters are routinely available (including after-hours) and provide supported decision-making aids; train ED staff in trauma-informed and culturally safe de-escalation; establish integrated follow-up with community services; and stratify and monitor wait times/outcomes by demographic groups for continuous quality improvement.

C. Develop a separate ‘substance use fast-track’ that excludes methamphetamine-intoxicated patients from psychiatric assessment unless they declare imminent suicidality, and rely primarily on security-based containment to maintain throughput.

D. Implement telepsychiatry assessments for non–English-speaking patients using an offsite psychiatrist, with standard English-language consent forms and no local cultural liaison to streamline approvals.

E. Introduce a strictly evidence-based triage algorithm that prioritises acute psychosis over trauma-related presentations and defer workforce training and community partnerships until performance metrics improve.

question: You are leading a redesign of a community bipolar disorder clinic in a regional area. Data suggest long waits and low attendance among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander youth and LGBTQIA+ clients. Families report that supported decision-making is inconsistently practiced when patients’ capacity fluctuates, and the service currently collects minimal quality-improvement data. Which actions best align with the RANZCP’s system-level recommendations? Select all that apply.
options: A. Establish a paid consumer and carer lived-experience advisory panel to co-design service changes and participate in ongoing evaluation, including defining measures of person-centred outcomes and experience.

B. Implement supported decision-making practices: advance statements, decision-making aids, and staff education on capacity assessment and local legal frameworks; document preferences and revisit them when capacity fluctuates.

C. Embed cultural safety by partnering with local Elders and LGBTQIA+ organisations to co-facilitate staff training; create cultural liaison roles and integrate culturally responsive pathways with primary care and youth services.

D. Enforce a strict ‘no appointment, no service’ policy to deter missed appointments, redirect frequent non-attenders to online self-help modules, and discourage family involvement to avoid confidentiality concerns.

E. Begin coordinated, de-identified collection of access, process, and outcome data stratified by demographics and diagnosis; set up regular quality-improvement cycles and publicly report aggregate findings.
F. Pause research activities and student placements until the waitlist is cleared to reduce operational complexity, even if this delays planned service evaluations and staff development.
G. Recruit additional peer workers and plan workforce expansion, but defer all training until new staff arrive to avoid duplication and lost productivity.

question: You are assessing a 22-year-old gay male university student presenting to your outpatient clinic with major depressive symptoms and intermittent methamphetamine use. He has no known medical comorbidities and is not currently under the care of a sexual health service. He appears ashamed when discussing substance use and has not volunteered information about sexual practices. What is the most appropriate next step that aligns with RANZCP recommendations regarding HIV and mental health care?
options: A. Prioritise mood symptoms and defer any sexual or drug risk screening to a later appointment to avoid stigma and preserve rapport.

B. Incorporate a routine, nonjudgmental sexual and substance use history into this initial psychiatric assessment; discuss HIV risk, offer HIV testing if indicated with informed consent, provide brief prevention education, and (with consent) facilitate referral to local HIV/sexual health services.
C. Limit risk screening to substance use only; sexual history is outside the core remit of psychiatric assessment and should be handled solely by primary care.
D. Discuss HIV only if he discloses an HIV-positive partner or explicitly requests testing to avoid overstepping clinical boundaries.
E. Provide HIV prevention brochures in the waiting room and rely on self-referral to sexual health services rather than raising the topic directly in session to respect autonomy.

question: On an acute inpatient psychiatric unit, a 38-year-old pregnant woman from Nigeria is admitted involuntarily with acute psychosis. Her husband requests that staff avoid discussion of sexual matters due to cultural sensitivities. The unit has no formal links with local HIV services. She intermittently injects methamphetamine per collateral history. You are considering unit-level and patient-level actions. Which actions best align with RANZCP recommendations? Select THREE.
options: A. Arrange in-service training for unit staff on HIV awareness and risk reduction, local epidemiology, and the interactions between antiretroviral medications and commonly used psychotropics (including pregnancy considerations).

B. Establish a formal referral pathway or memorandum of understanding with the local HIV/sexual health service to facilitate co-management, consultation on medication interactions, and on-site prevention education.
C. Postpone any discussion of sexual practices or drug use until her psychosis fully resolves or unless her husband consents, to respect cultural sensitivities.

D. Conduct a routine, nonjudgmental sexual and substance use risk assessment during her psychiatric assessment; provide brief HIV prevention education; and, if risk is identified, offer HIV testing when she has capacity to give informed consent (reassessing capacity regularly).
E. Implement a policy of compulsory HIV testing for all new female inpatients due to potential fetal risk.

F. Restrict HIV prevention resources and screening offers to patients in presumed high-prevalence groups (e.g., only to African-born women and men who have sex with men) to minimise unnecessary concern among other patients.

question: A 16-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander boy presents after an overdose. He is under a temporary care order; there is no current evidence of imminent harm if supported in a kinship setting. A child protection worker pressures you to write a letter recommending permanent removal from his family, citing his mother’s alcohol dependence. The young person expresses a wish to reconnect with extended family and Country and shares that his grandmother was removed as part of the Stolen Generations. Which actions best align with the RANZCP’s commitment to prevent the practices of the Stolen Generations from recurring?
options: A. Provide the requested letter recommending permanent removal to prioritise stability, and avoid discussing the Stolen Generations to prevent re-traumatisation during the acute phase.

B. With the young person’s and guardian’s consent, involve the Aboriginal liaison/health unit and local Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service to co-develop a culturally safe care plan that acknowledges intergenerational trauma.

C. In correspondence to child protection, explicitly recommend exploration of Aboriginal-led family support and kinship placement options before any removal, and document concerns about policies that may disproportionately remove Aboriginal children.
D. Focus solely on pharmacological treatment for depression in the ED and defer cultural, historical and family context to later outpatient reviews, as the ED is not conducive to these discussions.
E. Offer referral (with consent and risk considerations) to AIATSIS Family History and Link-Up services to support his stated wish to reconnect with family and culture.

question: You lead a metropolitan community mental health team. A departmental directive proposes that when Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander clients with severe mental illness and substance use miss appointments, the service should automatically request police "welfare checks" and share attendance information with child protection to "prevent neglect." There is no immediate risk and no specific legal requirement to share identifiable information. What is the most ethical response consistent with the RANZCP’s commitments?
options: A. Implement the directive as written to prioritise safety, then monitor outcomes and adjust later if harms emerge.

B. Seek urgent review through clinical governance and consult local Aboriginal leadership (e.g., Aboriginal Community Controlled Organisations and the hospital Aboriginal health unit) to challenge the policy, advocate for Aboriginal-led, culturally safe outreach alternatives, and ensure no identifiable information is shared without consent or a clear legal mandate.
C. Apply the policy only to clients with a documented history of violence to limit potential harms while honouring safety concerns.
D. Proceed with the directive but pair it with mandatory cultural awareness training for staff to mitigate unintended impacts.
E. Refuse to engage with the directive entirely, stating that policy matters are outside the clinical role.

question: You are asked by the Children’s Court to assess a 9-year-old Torres Strait Islander boy with suspected ADHD and trauma-related symptoms. Child protection seeks an opinion on placement; a maternal grandmother is willing to be a kinship carer. You also consult privately for a non-Indigenous residential care provider that may receive the child if kinship placement is not recommended. The family expresses mistrust of services due to past removals. Which ONE action best aligns with the RANZCP recommendations in this context?
options: A. Proceed with the assessment but deliberately ignore cultural identity, kinship, and past removal policies to prevent bias, relying solely on standardised symptom scales and risk instruments.
B. Accept the brief and recommend a mainstream residential care placement because it offers greater structure, noting that community input can be fragmented and slow.

C. Disclose your conflict of interest to the court and involved parties and offer to withdraw if preferred; if proceeding, explicitly address the impact of Stolen Generations policies, prioritise safe kinship placement where feasible, involve an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community-controlled service for family-led planning, and offer a culturally respectful apology for the profession’s past failures.
D. Provide a neutral report stating that while culture is important for identity, historical policies are not directly relevant to current placement decisions and may unduly influence outcomes.
E. Avoid any apology or acknowledgement of past harms during meetings with family, as apologies are political and outside the clinical remit in forensic contexts.

question: A 24-year-old international student from India presents to a university mental health clinic with moderate depression and social anxiety. He reports occasional binge drinking and betting on online sports most nights. He denies current suicidality but worries that discussing gambling could affect his visa and future employment. Your service has long wait times and no dedicated gambling clinician. Which ONE of the following next steps best aligns with the RANZCP/RACP recommendations on gambling-related harm?
options: A. Defer any assessment of gambling until his depressive symptoms improve, to avoid overwhelming him and to prioritise mood treatment.

B. Explain confidentiality and its limits to reduce stigma-related concerns; complete a brief validated screen for harmful gambling (e.g., Lie/Bet or PGSI), provide brief psychoeducation and self-help options, and offer referral to accessible, culturally appropriate gambling services (including peer/helpline supports) with an early follow-up plan.
C. Provide a generic financial counselling pamphlet and avoid documenting gambling-related concerns to minimise the risk of stigma or discrimination affecting his visa.

D. Focus first on alcohol use with motivational interviewing and postpone addressing gambling until rapport is stronger, as gambling is primarily a behavioural issue rather than a mental health concern.
E. Recommend self-exclusion tools for online betting and advise return if significant impairment develops, without further assessment at this time.

question: Dr K, a clinical director of a public youth mental health service in a low-income suburb with a high density of electronic gaming machines (EGMs), is drafting a 12-month strategy to address gambling-related harm among young men with psychosis and substance use. She is also offered an honorarium by a national sports betting company to deliver clinician webinars on “responsible gambling.” Which of the following actions are MOST consistent with the RANZCP/RACP recommendations? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Integrate routine screening for harmful gambling into assessments for clients with comorbid mental health and substance use disorders, and provide staff training and resources for early identification and intervention.
B. Accept the betting company’s honorarium to fund clinician education and use their materials as-is, disclosing the relationship later if concerns arise.
C. Partner with local Māori and Pasifika community groups and individuals with lived experience to co-design early-intervention programs for priority populations and their whānau.

D. Advocate within the health service and to relevant government agencies for regulatory measures that restrict maximum bets, jackpots, and EGM numbers in venues, and support cessation of gambling advertising on television and online.
E. Defer investment in gambling-related research until more definitive evidence emerges, focusing resources only on confirmed cases of gambling disorder.
F. Keep the strategy within mental health only and avoid multidisciplinary involvement (e.g., physicians, allied health), as a narrower focus improves fidelity.

question: You are a consultant psychiatrist providing care in a regional immigration transit centre. A 16-year-old unaccompanied Hazara boy has been detained for three months and is under your care with PTSD and moderate major depression, with intermittent self-harm ideation but no current plan. An immigration case officer emails requesting your full clinical notes to inform an expedited status determination. To date, interpreting has sometimes been done by his 12-year-old sibling due to resource constraints. Which actions are ethically appropriate under RANZCP principles?
options: A. Provide the full clinical record to the immigration case officer upon written request because timely decisions may benefit the young person by shortening detention.
B. Without consent, send a de-identified risk summary to the case officer because the presence of self-harm ideation overrides confidentiality outside the treating team.

C. Seek the young person’s assent and guardian consent, explain confidentiality and its limits, provide only the minimum necessary clinical opinion focusing on current risks and care needs, and advocate in writing for transfer to a community setting given the harms of detention to child development.
D. Continue therapy but avoid using a professional interpreter to minimize costs and protect privacy; use the younger sibling as interpreter since they are trusted family.

E. Share clear, age-appropriate written and verbal information about assessment, treatment, and supports in the family’s preferred language, using a trained interpreter; coordinate care with the multidisciplinary team (e.g., GP, trauma counsellor, social work).
F. Decline to provide any advocacy regarding the child’s setting because that could be seen as political and compromise professional neutrality.

G. Maintain clinical records securely and release only with informed consent or if legally required and ethically justified; seek advice from the service’s privacy officer before any disclosure to immigration authorities.

question: A 32-year-old Tamil man presents at intake to a mainland immigration facility on the day of arrival. He reports recent methamphetamine use, prominent insomnia, and persecutory ideas, with no current suicidal or homicidal intent. The facility contractor asks you to (1) defer any mental health screening for six weeks due to volume constraints, and (2) store your clinical notes in a shared system accessible to immigration compliance staff to facilitate visa decisions. What is the MOST ethical immediate course of action?
options: A. Accept the workflow and schedule mental health screening at six weeks post-arrival, prioritising only those with overt psychosis for earlier assessment.

B. Implement mental and physical health screening at intake using an accredited interpreter; provide written and verbal information in his preferred language; negotiate safeguards that preserve clinical independence and confidentiality (notes kept in a health record not accessible to compliance without consent or proper legal/ethical basis); and embed care within the multidisciplinary team.
C. Perform brief screening now but store a duplicate of your notes in the immigration-shared drive with a general disclaimer about confidentiality; defer interpreter use to avoid undermining rapport.
D. Decline any involvement until national detention policies are reformed, citing the RANZCP position that detention should not occur.
E. Proceed with screening but avoid any advocacy about the man’s living setting; limit recommendations to symptom management to maintain neutrality.

question: During an after-hours emergency department assessment of a 24-year-old Aboriginal man with methamphetamine intoxication and escalating agitation, the senior consultant publicly makes demeaning remarks about the registrar's accent and international training, questioning their ability to assess risk. You are the second on-call psychiatrist and witness this. Security is present and the immediate risk is being stabilised. Which actions best uphold the Code principle of promoting psychological safety and eliminating bullying and harassment?
options: A. Briefly redirect focus to the patient's immediate safety; after the assessment, privately name the behaviour as unacceptable, check the registrar's wellbeing, and support them to file a factual report under the bullying/harassment policy, offering to co-sign and escalate to the Director of Training.
B. Defer any discussion to the next journal club and raise the incident as a case vignette without informing the registrar to prevent further distress.
C. Send a department-wide email that evening naming both the consultant and registrar to 'model transparency' and deter future incidents.
D. Advise the registrar to ignore the comments to protect their career, and avoid formal reporting because it may escalate conflict.

E. Once the patient's risk is controlled, invite a senior nurse witness to a brief debrief with the registrar, document an objective account, and notify the clinical director/Director of Training per policy, while offering the registrar choices about involvement.
F. Call out the behaviour in front of the patient and ED staff, demanding an apology immediately to demonstrate a zero-tolerance stance.

question: On an older persons' mental health inpatient unit, an international medical graduate registrar inadvertently entered an order for clozapine for an 82-year-old with recent myocarditis. A nurse queried the order and the dose was not administered. The supervising consultant suggests not lodging an incident report 'to protect the trainee from AHPRA' and asks you as unit lead to 'handle it quietly.' The registrar appears distressed and is reluctant to contribute on ward round. What is the most appropriate next step to promote a healthy workplace culture and psychological safety?
options: A. Arrange a just-culture debrief focusing on system contributors (e.g., e-prescribing interface, supervision), lodge a routine incident report, provide supportive supervision and education, and reassure the registrar about the non-punitive intent.
B. Avoid any discussion to prevent retraumatising the registrar; do not report the near-miss so as not to damage team morale.
C. Immediately remove the registrar from prescribing duties for one month and inform the multidisciplinary team to 'learn from the error.'
D. Submit an incident report without telling the registrar to avoid further stress; defer any feedback until their end-of-term assessment.
E. Provide one-on-one teaching but avoid formal reporting so the registrar's record remains clean.

question: You are the on-call consultant psychiatrist in a metropolitan ED. A 16-year-old Māori boy presents with acute suicidal ideation in the context of methamphetamine use. Several other patients await assessment, including one older adult with psychotic agitation. Your sole registrar has already worked 14 hours and is nearing fatigue limits. Management has frozen recruitment and declines to call in additional on-call support due to budget constraints. Which actions best uphold your ethical duty to advocate for a well-resourced and safe mental health system, including safe overtime and valuing trainees? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Submit a formal safety/incident report and escalate to the Clinical Director and ED leadership identifying unsafe staffing and fatigue risks, request immediate backup or service diversion, and prioritise assessment of those at imminent risk.
B. Direct the registrar to skip breaks and continue unpaid overtime, framing it as valuable experience that will prevent complaints against the service.
C. Implement and document a transparent risk-based triage process, cap the registrar’s overtime per fatigue policy, notify ED of service limits and expected delays, and document the rationale.
D. Personally extend your shift indefinitely to clear the queue and avoid reputational harm, deferring any systemic advocacy until a quieter time.

E. Seek advice from the College/industrial bodies on safe overtime limits and contribute de-identified data to support a business case for additional FTE, including protected supervision time for trainees.
F. Expedite flow by prioritising non-intoxicated adults over intoxicated adolescents, as substance-affected youth are harder to assess reliably.

question: On an inpatient unit serving a culturally diverse population, including recently arrived refugees, management proposes replacing overnight on-site psychiatric cover with a single telepsychiatry consultant covering four hospitals. Registrars would handle admissions after-hours with phone advice only and no paid overtime. A 32-year-old Afghan woman with trauma-related dissociation and limited English has been repeatedly admitted overnight due to safety concerns. You also have a private telepsychiatry venture that might benefit from the new model. Which ONE is the most ethically appropriate immediate response?
options: A. Support the proposal because telepsychiatry can be effective, and offer to train registrars to manage crises after-hours without additional pay to help the service transition smoothly.

B. Write to the executive and clinical governance outlining patient safety risks of removing on-site cover, the overtime and supervision implications for registrars, and the need to recognise and resource their contribution; request formal consultation with staff, consumers and carers, and declare your private telepsychiatry interest.
C. Remain neutral publicly but privately assure registrars you will informally supervise by phone after hours to mitigate risks while management trials the new model.
D. Volunteer to take the telepsychiatry contract yourself to ensure quality oversight and do not disclose your private interest because it is an internal arrangement.

question: You supervise a second-year psychiatry registrar, Dr K (a Sri Lankan Muslim woman), after a night shift in the emergency department where an Aboriginal man with acute psychosis required restraint and IM sedation. Dr K reports moral distress about the coercive care and perceived racial bias, with insomnia and intrusive images. She fears that raising concerns could harm her term assessment. There is no immediate patient safety issue. Which single action plan best aligns with your ethical obligation to address trainee wellbeing and support effective organisational, evidence-based responses?
options: A. Offer confidential support and schedule additional supervision; facilitate access to an independent doctors’ health service/GP; arrange temporary rostering adjustments; with her consent, escalate systemic concerns (e.g., potential bias, coercion) via clinical governance; organise externally facilitated reflective practice (e.g., Balint/Schwartz Rounds); ensure no adverse assessment consequences; and avoid providing personal therapy yourself.
B. Require her to attend mandatory single-session critical incident stress debriefing and provide management her detailed account regardless of consent so the service can learn from the event.
C. Reframe her experience as an expected part of psychiatry, encourage resilience, and advise against raising concerns to avoid reputational harm to the service; return to full duties next shift.
D. Refer Dr K to your private rooms for psychotherapy at a reduced fee to expedite access while continuing as her supervisor.
E. Focus on individual coping by enrolling her in a mindfulness app and lead a one-off team meeting yourself to clarify restraint protocols, without altering rosters or notifying governance.

question: You are the sole consultant on a regional Mother–Baby Unit caring for a 29-year-old Māori woman detained with severe postpartum psychosis, scheduled for ECT. Due to vacancies, you have been first on-call for 12 of the last 14 nights and are experiencing burnout and near-miss charting errors. Your registrar also reports fatigue and fear of making mistakes. You worry that stepping back could destabilise care, yet continuing feels unsafe. Which actions best reflect your ethical responsibilities to address clinician wellbeing and support effective organisational strategies? Select THREE.
options: A. Notify the service director and Work Health and Safety of an immediate fatigue-related safety risk; request temporary redistribution of on-call/caseload, activate a fatigue risk management plan, and submit an incident report regarding near misses.
B. Maintain full workload to preserve continuity, avoid raising issues with management to prevent alarm, and rely on brief mindfulness exercises between cases until the staffing crisis passes.

C. Arrange safe handover of on-call and ECT duties to a rested colleague, provide a warm handover to the perinatal team with clear documentation, and promptly access confidential medical care/EAP for yourself and support for the registrar.
D. Implement compulsory single-session psychological debriefs after every seclusion event for all doctors and make attendance part of performance appraisal.

E. Advocate for evidence-based team supports (e.g., Schwartz Rounds or Balint groups), structured peer support, regular protected supervision for registrars, and use validated tools to monitor burnout, informing staffing/rostering changes through governance.

question: On a busy evening in a tertiary hospital acute psychiatric unit, a PGY3 registrar (an international medical graduate who wears a hijab) has just completed a highly stressful seclusion episode for a young man with acute methamphetamine intoxication who directed religious slurs at staff. The registrar is visibly distressed and has not had a break in 10 hours. Multiple new referrals are waiting. You are the consultant and clinical director on call. Which actions best model professional behaviour, support wellbeing, and foster a positive team culture while maintaining patient safety? Select all that apply.
options: A. Acknowledge the registrar’s immediate distress, reallocate workload to facilitate a protected break and a brief structured debrief, notify the bed manager to pace admissions safely, and plan a later check-in.
B. Emphasise resilience and encourage the registrar to complete the shift before discussing support, noting that extended hours are expected in crises.
C. Convene a brief team huddle to address the earlier slurs, reinforce zero tolerance for microaggression, and liaise with the cultural liaison service to support both patient care and staff.
D. Send a group email praising the team’s ‘toughness’ and advising staff to avoid taking sick leave to maintain throughput.

E. Ensure senior supervision is readily available for the rest of the shift (e.g., you remain on the unit, adjust your clinic commitments), and schedule reflective practice/supervision for trainees within the week.

question: At the morning clinical governance meeting following a near-miss, it emerges that a detained patient with mania briefly left the ward after a documentation error on the involuntary treatment order by a first-year psychiatry trainee on provisional registration, who is anxious about visa status. Hospital executives are pressing to ‘hold someone to account.’ As the service director chairing the meeting, what is the most ethically appropriate immediate action to model professional behaviour, prioritise wellbeing, and address safety?
options: A. Publicly name the trainee, dissect the error step-by-step to demonstrate accountability, and invite open critique of the trainee’s performance.

B. Frame the discussion within a just culture, focus on system contributors without naming individuals, commit to a transparent root-cause review, and offer to provide the trainee with private supervision and support after the meeting.
C. Offer to correct the paperwork yourself and declare that the trainee will be excluded from all high-risk cases until competencies are ‘proven’ again.
D. Initiate a mandatory report to the regulator during the meeting on the basis of unsafe practice to reassure the executive.
E. Defer discussion to avoid upsetting staff and instruct the team to move on since no harm ultimately occurred.

question: You supervise a first-year psychiatry registrar of Indian background on a busy inpatient unit. Over the past month they have repeatedly stayed late to complete assessments and now report worsening anxiety and insomnia. They disclose occasionally taking their partner’s zopiclone without a prescription to get some sleep. Today, after three consecutive 14-hour days, they are due to review a patient with depression who has passive suicidal ideation but no current plan or intent; nursing observations and collateral indicate no imminent risk. What is the most ethically appropriate next step that best supports the trainee’s wellbeing and models positive work-life balance while maintaining patient safety?
options: A. Normalize long hours as part of early training and encourage the registrar to complete the review before taking a brief break; schedule a debrief next month when the roster eases.

B. Arrange clinical cover so the registrar can end their shift now; advise prompt, confidential assessment by an independent GP/doctor (not you), avoid prescribing or supervising self-medication, discuss fatigue management and available wellbeing supports (e.g., EAP), and work with the training program to adjust workload while ensuring the patient is reviewed by another clinician today.

C. Immediately notify the professional regulator of an impaired practitioner based solely on the disclosure of occasional non-prescribed hypnotic use, prior to discussing a support plan with the registrar.
D. Ask the registrar to complete a focused mental state exam on the patient now to avoid any delay in care, then take the rest of the day off without changing the roster.
E. Encourage the registrar to share their sleep and anxiety difficulties in the next multidisciplinary team meeting to model openness and reduce stigma.

question: A consultant psychiatrist in a community team has been covering a vacant position for six months. They have a newborn at home and are routinely working 60-hour weeks. A high-profile forensic risk assessment for a patient with psychosis and recent domestic violence charges is due next week. The service manager asks the consultant to cancel all supervision for the registrar (who has protected teaching time) and to add extra on-call weekends to meet deadlines. A colleague also requests the consultant provide informal psychiatric care to the colleague’s close friend, citing urgency and convenience. Which actions best uphold the ethical principle of supporting psychiatrists and trainees in maintaining personal wellbeing and a positive work–life balance while safeguarding patient care? Select all that apply.
options: A. Decline to take on informal care of a colleague’s friend and provide alternative referral pathways, to avoid dual relationships and boundary violations.

B. Negotiate with the service manager to redistribute workload, preserve protected supervision/teaching, request temporary locum or triage measures, and escalate through clinical governance if workload remains unsafe; document concerns.
C. Accept all additional duties and compensate by skipping breaks and completing documentation after hours to ensure deadlines are met in the short term.
D. Retain supervision but shift substantive clinical work to late nights at home (after the family is asleep) so that training time is protected without changing the overall workload.

E. Use team-based care and triage: delegate tasks appropriate to scope within the MDT, prioritize imminent-risk cases, schedule planned leave with handover, and seek peer consultation on fatigue and boundary management.
F. Self-prescribe a low-dose stimulant to mitigate fatigue temporarily while the vacancy remains unfilled.

question: You are the on-call consultant supervising Dr H, a Sudanese–Australian PGY-4 registrar, during an ED psychiatric assessment. An Arabic-speaking man with acute mania and disinhibition requires urgent assessment, but no professional interpreter is immediately available. Staff ask Dr H to interpret because they speak Arabic and are "good with these patients." During the interaction, the patient directs a racist slur at Dr H, who becomes visibly distressed and later reports feeling overburdened by being routinely asked to see all Arabic-speaking patients and to deliver extra cultural outreach talks for the hospital. What is the most ethically appropriate action?
options: A. Arrange a professional interpreter and reassign interpreter duties away from Dr H; redistribute Arabic-speaking caseloads; provide immediate debrief and ongoing supervision; document and address the racist incident; and advocate with management for a clear policy to avoid cultural taxation and to provide protected time and cultural safety supports (with Dr H’s consent to share relevant information).
B. Ask Dr H to proceed with this patient due to rapport and clinical urgency, promising time-in-lieu and ensuring interpreters are used for similar cases in future.
C. Remove Dr H from all care of Arabic-speaking patients indefinitely to prevent further distress, even if they express a wish to continue working with this population for training purposes.
D. Encourage Dr H to submit an incident report about the racism but maintain them as the primary clinician for Arabic-speaking clients because of service demand, while monitoring their wellbeing.
E. Offer to discuss coping strategies and resilience with Dr H, and advise against escalating concerns to management given current workforce shortages and pressures.

question: You are the clinical lead in a community mental health service. Dr R, a Māori PGY-5 registrar, is frequently asked to act as an informal cultural liaison and to advise on tikanga in addition to their clinical roster. They also carry significant iwi and whānau obligations outside work and report fatigue and anxiety. A court has requested a short-notice forensic assessment of a detained Māori man from a neighbouring iwi with whom Dr R has occasional community interactions; there may be mutual acquaintances. Under pressure to meet the deadline, your team proposes assigning the case to Dr R due to cultural concordance. Which actions are ethically appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: A. Acknowledge the additional cultural load and advocate immediately for a formal cultural advisor/consultant; redistribute ad hoc cultural liaison tasks away from Dr R; document the plan and escalate systemic issues to service leadership and the Director of Training.

B. Insist that Dr R conducts the forensic assessment because cultural concordance is likely to improve validity and the court deadline is paramount, with a promise of an extra supervision session afterward.

C. Explore potential dual relationships and perceived bias; if there is any prior relationship or reasonable perception of conflict, reassign the case and support Dr R to communicate this boundary to the court.
D. Offer flexible rostering and protected time to accommodate wellbeing and cultural obligations; facilitate access to confidential supports, including culturally safe supervision or mentorship.
E. Advise Dr R to keep their community roles private at work to prevent such conflicts in the future, and handle the matter informally without involving management.
F. Ask Dr R to provide informal, off-the-record cultural guidance to the assessor since formal cultural advisors are busy; this avoids a conflict of interest while still using Dr R’s expertise.

question: Dr L is the only consultant psychiatrist covering a remote Aboriginal community clinic and supervises an overseas-trained registrar after hours. A 16-year-old Aboriginal boy presents with escalating suicidal ideation following a recent conflict during a cultural ceremony. The registrar requests immediate guidance. There is no other on-site psychiatrist available, and Dr L is fatigued after a long on-call shift. Which is the best action to uphold the ethical principle of promoting and improving supervision, mentorship, and peer review to support clinician wellbeing and patient safety?
options: A. Provide immediate case supervision via a hospital-approved secure telehealth platform; agree on a written supervision contract with scheduled weekly sessions; invite the registrar to the regional peer review/Balint group; and seek cultural input from the Aboriginal Mental Health Worker before finalising the plan.
B. Advise the registrar to manage independently using the local suicide risk protocol and plan to review the case at month’s end during performance appraisal to preserve consultant rest time.
C. Post de-identified case details (no names) to a closed, invitation-only professional social media group of psychiatrists to crowdsource urgent advice for the registrar.
D. Inform the registrar that discussing uncertainties or errors in supervision may create medico-legal exposure, so they should bring only completed cases to supervision to minimise risk.
E. Ask the registrar to obtain cultural mentorship first and defer psychiatric supervision until after the acute risk is settled, to avoid overwhelming the limited service.

question: Dr S, a mid-career forensic psychiatrist, supervises Dr T, a registrar who is also her long-time friend and current research co-author. Following the team’s low-risk assessment, an Aboriginal man dies by suicide in custody. Dr S feels distressed, has insomnia, and has intermittently self-initiated zopiclone. She has missed recent peer-review meetings due to workload and worries that presenting the case could harm reputations. Which actions best align with promoting and improving the role of supervision, mentorship, and peer review in maintaining wellbeing across a psychiatrist’s career? Select all that apply.
options: A. Disclose the dual relationship to the trainee and service; transfer formal supervision to an independent consultant while continuing as an informal mentor, documenting the plan and boundaries.

B. Attend the next structured peer review/M&M and present a de-identified, reflective case analysis within organisational policies and privacy laws, focusing on systems learning and clinician wellbeing supports.
C. Avoid any peer discussion of the case to minimise reputational harm; process distress privately and wait for external reviews to conclude before engaging colleagues.
D. Lean primarily on the supervisee for late-night emotional debriefs because they understand the context best, thus avoiding burdening other colleagues.

E. Seek confidential health assessment and occupational support; if capacity may be affected, inform the clinical director and adjust workload while engaging in regular supervision/mentorship for self-care.
F. Resume peer review attendance only after the coronial investigation is complete to avoid prejudicing the process, even if this delays access to collegial support.

question: An international medical graduate (IMG) psychiatry registrar under your supervision discloses that over the past month, during a high-intensity acute inpatient rotation with overnight on-calls, they have been taking their partner’s diazepam "to get some sleep." They also report a recent near-miss medication error on the ward. They fear that disclosure could jeopardise their visa and future fellowship prospects, and ask you to keep the conversation strictly confidential. Which actions best align with the Code of Ethics principle of evaluating and supporting the wellbeing of psychiatrists and trainees?
options: A. Promptly explain confidentiality limits, assess immediate impairment and risk to patients, document the discussion, and temporarily modify duties (e.g., remove on-calls/medication charting) pending an independent assessment.
B. Prescribe a small, controlled supply of benzodiazepines yourself to prevent withdrawal and avoid external referrals, keeping the matter confidential to preserve trust.
C. File a mandatory notification to the regulator before discussing anything further with the registrar, to prioritise patient safety and avoid conflicts.

D. With the registrar’s consent (or if the risk threshold is met, without), inform the Director of Training and arrange referral to an independent doctors’ health program/occupational health for assessment and treatment, emphasising a non-punitive, supportive plan.
E. Validate the registrar’s concerns about visa and stigma, clarify confidentiality boundaries, and provide clear information about confidential supports such as the Doctors’ Health Advisory Service.

question: You are the clinical director in a rural mental health service. A 58-year-old consultant psychiatrist, Dr K, has returned from recent illness and has made two prescribing errors caught by pharmacy. He confides that he is on high-dose amitriptyline for neuropathic pain and is "not sleeping well," and asks you to keep this confidential because he fears ageism. That afternoon he is scheduled to conduct complex assessments, including Community Treatment Order (CTO) renewals. What is the single best next step, consistent with supporting the wellbeing of psychiatrists while ensuring patient safety?
options: A. Respect his request for confidentiality and say nothing, but assign a junior doctor to shadow him today to catch any errors.

B. Immediately remove Dr K from clinical duties today, explain patient safety concerns, discuss confidentiality limits, and urgently arrange independent assessment via occupational health/doctors’ health services within a non-punitive, supportive framework.
C. Submit a mandatory notification to the regulator without discussing the matter further to avoid any appearance of favouritism.
D. Ask pharmacy to double-check all of Dr K’s charts for the next month while he continues full duties to maintain dignity and safety.
E. Advise Dr K to halve his amitriptyline and swap to shorter clinics for a few weeks, avoiding formal processes if he improves.

question: A 19-year-old Aboriginal man from a remote community presents to the ED with acute psychosis and suicidal ideation following heavy cannabis use. He is detained and admitted to an urban inpatient unit. The hospital has an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health worker (ATSI MHW) who is from a different nation/language group. During the initial ward round and risk assessment, the patient asks to speak with someone from his community or an Elder, and prefers a male worker. The registrar worries about confidentiality and role boundaries and proposes to exclude the ATSI MHW from case conferences, using them only if interpreting is needed. Which actions best uphold the Code of Ethics regarding the role of ATSI MHWs? Select TWO.
options: A. Exclude the ATSI MHW from case conferences and ward rounds to protect the patient's confidentiality, allowing involvement only with explicit written consent for each contact.

B. Include the ATSI MHW as an integral member of the multidisciplinary team with the same privileges as others; explain confidentiality limits to the patient, obtain consent where appropriate, and support the ATSI MHW to engage with relevant local Elders/community given they are from a different group.
C. Limit the ATSI MHW role to interpreting during the risk assessment and avoid involving them in care planning to reduce potential dual roles and boundary issues.
D. Where feasible and lawful, accommodate the patient's request for a male worker by rostering a male ATSI MHW or a male clinician to co-lead the assessment, documenting the rationale and plan.
E. Given the acuity, proceed without involving the ATSI MHW during the initial admission and revisit cultural input after the patient is stabilized to avoid delaying urgent care.

question: You are a non-Indigenous clinical director establishing a new Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health worker (ATSI MHW) position in a youth alcohol and other drug (AOD) psychiatry service with frequent co-occurring trauma and juvenile justice involvement. The service needs culturally safe assessments, liaison with families/Elders, and staff education on cultural competency. Which approach BEST aligns with the Code of Ethics when finalising the position description and recruitment plan? Select ONE.
options: A. Co-design the position description with local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, including Elders and existing ATSI MHWs where possible, to reflect local needs (e.g., youth justice, substance use), incorporate sensitivity to gender preferences, explicitly recognise additional cultural expertise and peer-education responsibilities, ensure equal team privileges, embed liaison with relevant Elders/communities when the worker is unfamiliar with that group (with organisational support), and involve ATSI MHWs in service/policy development and recruitment.
B. Use a standardised, generic PD focused on clinical competencies and avoid specifying cultural responsibilities to ensure equal opportunity and to prevent accusations of reverse discrimination.

C. Restrict the ATSI MHW role to direct clinical case management and exclude responsibilities in policy, recruitment, or cultural competency education to prevent role confusion and perceived conflicts of interest.

D. Allocate cultural competency training to non-Indigenous staff with prior cultural liaison experience to avoid overburdening the ATSI MHW, and limit the ATSI MHW's role to individual consumer consultation.

E. Prefer candidates who have worked in any Aboriginal community; if they lack familiarity with the local area, limit engagement with local Elders for the first year to reduce the risk of missteps in cultural protocols.

question: You are the clinical lead psychiatrist for a rural community mental health team supporting a 23-year-old Aboriginal man with first-episode psychosis and methamphetamine use who disengages unless care is provided through on-Country visits and yarning circles after hours. You plan to recruit an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health worker to provide culturally informed outreach across a wide catchment. HR suggests appointing the role at a lower-paid ‘cultural liaison’ grade because the preferred candidate does not hold a tertiary mental health qualification, even though the role will involve frequent weekend/community travel and out-of-hours engagement. Which of the following is the most ethical action in line with the principle on the value of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health workers’ work?
options: A. Appoint at a lower ‘cultural liaison’ grade due to lack of formal qualifications, and specify that after-hours and extended travel are expected as part of the role without additional remuneration, offset by regular case discussion with the team.

B. Appoint at a level commensurate with the role’s responsibilities and the worker’s cultural expertise, with appropriate remuneration (including loadings/TOIL for after-hours and travel) and access to clinical and cultural supervision.
C. Engage a respected Elder as an unpaid cultural advisor instead, to attend sessions when available, thereby avoiding salary parity issues while preserving cultural input.
D. Advertise a casual position with flexible hours and clarify that weekend and travel work are expected but cannot be included in productivity/KPI reports due to funding rules.
E. Offer a short-term, lower-paid probationary contract and defer salary parity until there is measurable improvement in engagement and risk reduction outcomes.

question: You are a psychiatrist directing a regional perinatal mental health service undergoing redesign and accreditation. Mia, an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health worker who completed a traineeship in your service, has strong local knowledge and supports pregnant women with severe depression and trauma. She often attends community gatherings and travels after hours to outstations to maintain engagement and safety plans. The team is also considering involving Uncle Joe, a respected Elder with no formal qualifications, who has been instrumental in de-escalating crises. Which actions best align with the ethical principle on the value of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health workers’ work? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Establish a formal career pathway for Mia that includes eligibility for promotion and paid professional development, reflecting her skills, cultural competency and contribution.
B. Ensure accreditation metrics and service KPIs properly capture Mia’s after-hours, community-based and geographically extended work, and that rostering/remuneration reflect these demands.

C. Rotate Mia out of the role after 12 months to maintain neutrality and prevent over-identification, recruiting a new trainee each year to ‘refresh’ the service despite community preferences for continuity.

D. Employ Uncle Joe as a part-time Aboriginal mental health worker with structured orientation, cultural safety support for the team, supervision and appropriate remuneration, notwithstanding his lack of formal qualifications.

E. To manage budget constraints, cap Mia’s salary below that of non-Indigenous clinicians at the same grade because her cultural work is ‘non-clinical,’ offering public recognition and flexible hours instead.

question: A 24-year-old Aboriginal man presents with severe agitation and persecutory delusions after methamphetamine use and is threatening self-harm. The unit has just appointed an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health worker, Ms W, who has completed a government-accredited diploma and is in her first fortnight. The on-call psychiatrist is considering asking Ms W to attend the seclusion area alone after hours to conduct an urgent risk assessment due to cultural concordance, and to require her to lead monthly cultural awareness sessions for all staff as a condition of employment. What is the most ethical immediate course of action?
options: A. Send Ms W alone to conduct the risk assessment given cultural concordance may improve engagement; offer debriefing afterwards if she appears distressed.

B. Pair Ms W with a senior clinician for the high-risk assessment, ensure formal clinical supervision is available, clarify her duties to match her level of training, and invite (but do not require) her to contribute to cultural sessions with appropriate remuneration if she wishes.
C. Require Ms W to complete a mandatory vicarious trauma module containing detailed accounts of racial trauma before allowing her to attend such crises so she is adequately prepared.
D. Keep Ms W in an observer-only role for six months without adjusting pay despite her diploma-level training to avoid liability while the unit assesses her readiness.
E. Ask Ms W to draft the unit’s cultural safety policy and lead monthly cultural awareness sessions as a condition of probation, but provide protected time and mentorship to support her.

question: A metropolitan service is preparing for accreditation and planning a cultural awareness program. The service employs an experienced Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health worker, Ms T, who holds a university-accredited certificate. Ms T is also the aunt of a current patient with severe postnatal depression. Which actions best align with the code of ethics regarding training and support for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health workers? Select all that apply.
options: A. Credit attendance at the cultural awareness course toward all staff members’ continuing professional development, including Ms T, and do not require Ms T to take an organisational teaching role when an external educational unit is available unless she volunteers; remunerate any contribution appropriately.
B. Require Ms T to co-facilitate the course to ensure authenticity due to her lived experience, providing time-in-lieu rather than pay for the additional responsibilities.

C. Establish at the time of Ms T’s formal appointment ongoing clinical supervision with a senior clinician and access to cultural supervision with an appropriate Elder or cultural supervisor, including regular debriefing.
D. Make the cultural competency course mandatory for all staff, including Ms T, regardless of potentially re-traumatising content, given the urgency of accreditation timelines.

E. Recognise Ms T’s completed training by aligning her role description and remuneration with her competencies, while ensuring responsibilities remain within scope and that high-risk assessments are supported rather than allocated to her alone.
F. Because Ms T is related to a current patient, exclude her from all discussions or roles involving Aboriginal patients to pre-empt any conflicts of interest.
G. Offer Ms T the option to opt out of specific course modules likely to be re-traumatising and provide alternative CPD activities after discussing her preferences.

question: A 17-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander male with methamphetamine-related psychosis is brought to the ED under the Mental Health Act after threatening self-harm. He is settling with de-escalation but remains guarded. His family request that a male Aboriginal mental health worker (AMHW) and an Elder be present, and prefer the assessment occur in the designated culturally secure engagement room rather than the seclusion room. The only on-site AMHW is a woman who has just completed a 12-hour shift and is rostered again early tomorrow. As the on-call psychiatrist, which actions best align with the ethical principle of resource allocation for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health workers?
options: A. Contact the after-hours manager to source additional Indigenous mental health support (e.g., on-call or neighbouring service) rather than compelling the current AMHW to extend her shift; document the gender request and plan for gender-concordant involvement where feasible to reduce overwork and consider cultural preferences.
B. For efficiency and safety, conduct all current and subsequent assessments in the seclusion room and decline any use of the cultural engagement room due to bed pressures.

C. Once immediate risk is contained, move the assessment to the designated culturally secure room and arrange practical supports (e.g., transport/communication resources) to enable Elder and family involvement; ensure the AMHW has appropriate workspace and equipment.
D. Ask the female AMHW to extend her shift for this case given the urgency, reassuring it will be a rare exception despite her current workload and the family’s preference for a male worker.
E. Advocate with management for paid cultural supervision time, including regular opportunities for the AMHW to return to Country and meet with Elders, given the intensity of the caseload.
F. To protect confidentiality, restrict the AMHW from reviewing the budget for their role and from discussing resource needs with Elders or community members.
