options: A. Focus only on immediate risk and mood assessment, avoiding discussion of gender identity to prevent "reinforcing" distress; defer pronoun choices until family therapy has commenced.

B. Complete a thorough risk assessment using Isla’s affirmed name and pronouns; clarify and document confidentiality limits with her; link her to an accredited LGBTIQ+ youth service and peer supports; and escalate to the service lead a plan to review forms, staff training, and pursue LGBTIQ+-inclusive accreditation (e.g., Rainbow Tick).
C. Provide Isla’s parents with full clinical details because she is a minor, prioritising parental involvement over her expressed confidentiality preferences.
D. Refer Isla solely to a gender clinic and close CAMHS follow-up to avoid duplication of care.
E. Initiate pharmacotherapy today and defer any inclusivity or service-level changes until the next annual quality cycle.

question: A 32-year-old bisexual man, Jacob, presents with moderate depressive symptoms and problematic methamphetamine use associated with chemsex. He has no current suicidal ideation. You practice in a regional private clinic whose website and intake processes are not explicitly LGBTIQ+-inclusive, and you have been asked to lead a quality improvement initiative. Which actions best align with the ethical principle of considering health promotion strategies and service accreditation standards for culturally appropriate care for LGBTIQ+ communities? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Integrate health promotion into Jacob’s care: brief methamphetamine harm-reduction counseling; discuss referral for PrEP/PEP with his GP or a sexual health clinic; screen for intimate partner violence; and provide information on LGBTIQ+-inclusive peer supports.
B. To protect confidentiality, create a separate appointment stream coded “Rainbow” so LGBTIQ+ clients are only booked on Friday afternoons.
C. Maintain a neutral stance by confining discussion strictly to depression and avoiding sexual health unless Jacob raises it explicitly.
D. Use gender-neutral language in notes but delay all staff training and environmental changes until next year when funding is likely.

E. Establish formal referral pathways and MOUs with accredited LGBTIQ+-inclusive services; implement SOGIESC data collection consistent with inclusive practice standards; and update visible inclusion statements and feedback mechanisms tailored for LGBTIQ+ clients.
F. Conduct a gap analysis against recognised LGBTIQ+-inclusive accreditation standards and co-design a quality improvement plan with local LGBTIQ+ community representatives.

question: You are assessing Ari, a 16-year-old Māori trans boy presenting with moderate depressive symptoms and intermittent self-harm urges (no current plan or intent). Ari requests that you use his chosen name and he/him pronouns and not disclose details of his gender dysphoria to his parents. His parents/whānau oppose gender transition and ask to be informed about all discussions to ensure Ari’s safety. You have limited recent CPD in trans youth mental health. Which actions best uphold the ethical principle of staying up-to-date on LGBTIQ+ issues and balancing divergent views of the individual and their whānau?
options: A. Clarify confidentiality and its limits with Ari and his parents at the outset; use Ari’s chosen name/pronouns; co-create a safety plan; negotiate whānau involvement focused on general wellbeing without disclosing Ari’s specific gender-related disclosures without his consent (unless safety thresholds are met); seek supervision/CPD and refer to a local youth gender service and culturally appropriate LGBTIQ+ supports.
B. Delay any gender-related referral until parental agreement is achieved to prevent family conflict and maintain treatment alliance with the parents.
C. Focus strictly on depressive symptoms and avoid discussion of gender concerns until mood improves to minimise complexity and potential disagreement.

D. Provide psychoeducation to Ari’s parents on adolescent mental health and general LGBTIQ+ issues; offer a whānau meeting with a cultural advisor; explore values and concerns while maintaining Ari’s confidentiality about specific disclosures unless imminent risk emerges; continue active monitoring of risk.
E. Ask the school counsellor to notify Ari’s parents if Ari uses a male name at school to ensure consistent messaging across settings.

question: Teuila is a 30-year-old Samoan trans woman with well-controlled bipolar I disorder (euthymic for 18 months) presenting for an assessment letter to support gender-affirming vaginoplasty. She occasionally uses cannabis socially but reports no functional impairment. Her parents strongly oppose surgery and request to be copied into all correspondence. Teuila consents to general family involvement but does not want specific clinical details shared. You have limited prior experience writing surgical readiness letters. Which actions are ethically appropriate and align with up-to-date LGBTIQ+ practice and balancing individual and family/whānau perspectives?
options: A. Disclose Teuila’s gender history and surgical plans to her parents so whānau support can be fully mobilised, as their views should be weighed equally with Teuila’s preferences.

B. Acknowledge your limited experience; review current standards of care for gender-affirming surgery assessments; seek supervision or mentorship; and, if not competent to proceed, refer to an experienced clinician while providing interim supportive care.

C. With Teuila’s consent, facilitate a whānau meeting focused on communication and support without debating her identity; set clear boundaries on what will be shared; and provide general psychoeducation about LGBTIQ+ issues.
D. Decline to provide any letter or referral because of her cannabis use, advising a fixed 12-month abstinence requirement regardless of current functioning or evidence-based criteria.

E. Evaluate decision-making capacity specific to the surgery; ensure mood stability and informed consent; document the assessment; and if criteria are met, proceed with referral in line with contemporary guidelines.

question: A 16-year-old trans girl, Mia, presents after self-harm with ongoing suicidal ideation. One parent is supportive of her gender identity; the other is opposed. Mia asks you to use her chosen name and she is worried you will disclose her gender identity to the unsupportive parent. You have limited experience with gender-affirming care. Which actions best uphold the Code of Ethics principle regarding the unique mental health needs of LGBTIQ+ people and provision of appropriate care? Select TWO.
options: A. Conduct a comprehensive suicide risk assessment immediately using Mia’s chosen name and pronouns; explain confidentiality and its limits; collaboratively develop a safety plan, involve the supportive parent as appropriate, and negotiate what sensitive information is disclosed.
B. Insist on discussing Mia’s gender identity with both parents before proceeding, as they are legal guardians and must be fully informed.
C. Defer risk assessment until the hospital’s gender service can review Mia so you do not practice outside your competence.
D. Encourage the parents to delay any social transition and limit Mia’s engagement with online transgender forums until specialist review to reduce potential iatrogenic influence.

E. Arrange an urgent referral to a gender-affirming clinician and seek supervision; continue interim supportive care yourself, including psychoeducation for family about minority stress and the protective effects of acceptance, while monitoring risk.
F. Use Mia’s legal name only in the consultation and documentation to avoid appearing biased and to maintain record accuracy.

question: You are preparing a court-ordered pre-sentence psychiatric report for a 32-year-old bisexual Aboriginal man charged with assault after an incident in a bar where he reports being subjected to homophobic slurs. He has a history of methamphetamine use. The prosecutor asks you to opine on the role of his sexual orientation in the offence and to include full sexual history details. Which approach best upholds the Code of Ethics principle regarding awareness of LGBTIQ+ needs and provision of appropriate care and support in a forensic context? Select ONE.
options: A. Explain that bisexual orientation is associated with elevated impulsivity and violence risk and likely contributed to the offence.

B. Formulate the offence in terms of relevant factors (e.g., acute intoxication, minority stress from provocation) without pathologising sexual orientation; include only sexual history details relevant to formulation and risk; recommend evidence-based interventions (e.g., substance use treatment, anger management) and culturally safe, LGBTIQ+-affirming supports where appropriate.
C. Provide the full sexual history, including partners’ names and identifiable details, to demonstrate a comprehensive assessment to the court.
D. Recommend parole conditions requiring avoidance of all LGBTIQ+ venues to prevent recurrence of similar incidents.
E. State that sexual orientation is irrelevant in all forensic assessments and should be omitted entirely to prevent bias.
F. Decline the assessment due to discomfort with LGBTIQ+ issues and do not proceed further.

question: You are assessing a 16-year-old who presents to the ED after self-harm. They identify as non-binary (they/them) and have recently broken up with a boyfriend. Their parent, who holds strong religious beliefs, insists staff use the patient’s birth name and refers to them as “my daughter.” The parent wishes to stay for the entire assessment. You must complete an acute risk assessment and safety plan. Which actions best align with the ethical principle of avoiding heteronormative/gender-binary assumptions while meeting clinical needs? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Begin by asking the young person privately how they would like to be addressed and whether it is safe to use that name and pronouns when their parent is present; document their chosen name/pronouns and privacy preferences in the chart.

B. Because there is imminent self-harm risk, proceed using the legal name and sex assigned at birth to avoid confusion, and discuss gender identity details with the parent without the young person’s assent, as this supports collateral gathering.
C. Use neutral, open questions about relationships and sexual health (e.g., asking about “partners” rather than “boyfriend/girlfriend”) and avoid assuming heterosexuality when exploring precipitants.

D. Explain to the parent that while their input is valued, aspects of identity will be discussed with their child’s consent unless there is a clear risk-related need; offer resources on supporting gender-diverse youth.
E. Defer asking about gender identity or pronouns because focusing on identity may distract from the acute risk assessment; such details can be clarified at follow-up.

question: You are preparing a pre-sentence forensic psychiatric report for a 34-year-old trans woman with alcohol use disorder and depression, currently on remand. She asks that you use her affirmed name and pronouns, but the court file lists a different legal name. She has not had gender-affirming surgery. Corrections ask for an opinion on treatment needs and risk. Which ONE approach is MOST ethically appropriate and consistent with avoiding heteronormative/gender-binary assumptions?
options: A. Use legal name and pronouns throughout to match court records; note her preferred name in quotation marks only if she provides documentation of legal change; when discussing intimate relationships, refer to “women he dates” unless otherwise specified, to prevent ambiguity.

B. Use the affirmed name and pronouns throughout, with a parenthetical first mention linking to the legal name for identification (e.g., “Ms X [legal name: Y]”); ask neutral, non-assumptive questions about partners and sexual health; include gender identity details only when relevant to mental state, risk, or treatment planning; and obtain consent before including sensitive identity information unrelated to the referral questions.

C. Decline to discuss gender identity in the report because doing so could be seen as advocacy; restrict the assessment to substance use and risk, and avoid asking about intimate relationships to keep the interview focused.
D. Require verification of hormone therapy or surgical status before agreeing to use affirmed pronouns in the report; if unverified, default to sex assigned at birth in pronouns and categories.
E. To avoid bias, interview a family member about her “real” name and sex and include their account verbatim in the report without seeking her consent, as collateral is standard in forensic work.

question: Alex is a 14-year-old gender diverse young person (assigned female at birth, identifies as a trans boy) presenting with low mood, social withdrawal, and passive self-harm thoughts without plan or intent. He reports recent onset of menses, marked chest dysphoria, and escalating bullying at school. He has not told his mother (in the waiting room) about his gender identity and asks you not to disclose it. Which actions are ethically appropriate at this visit and align with the principle of maintaining awareness of LGBTIQ+ stressors? Select all that apply.
options: A. Clarify confidentiality limits with Alex, explicitly explore coming out stressors, bullying, and pubertal distress, perform a safety assessment, and discuss timely referral to a multidisciplinary gender-affirming service given distress around puberty.
B. Defer all discussion of gender identity until his parent is present to avoid creating secrecy, focusing solely on general adolescent issues for now.
C. Inform his mother of Alex’s gender identity immediately to secure family support, as parental involvement overrides confidentiality in early adolescence.
D. Initiate an antidepressant and provide a standard safety plan while postponing any exploration of gender identity, bullying, or pubertal concerns until his mood improves.
E. With Alex’s consent, liaise with the school to address bullying and implement privacy-protective measures (e.g., chosen name/pronouns use, staff awareness) without outing him.
F. Offer information about local peer support groups for trans/LGBTIQ+ youth, and update clinic records to reflect Alex’s chosen name and pronouns, with staff briefed to use them.

question: Maya is a 15-year-old bisexual student at a religious school, presenting with panic attacks, insomnia, and weekend alcohol use to cope. She reports homophobic bullying at school and is not ready to come out to her parents. Her father asks you not to discuss “identity topics” and to “just treat the anxiety.” The school counselor emails you seeking details about her panic and attendance. There is no current suicidal intent or plan. Which single action best aligns with the ethical principle and your duties as a child and adolescent psychiatrist?
options: A. Focus exclusively on treating panic (e.g., SSRIs/CBT) and defer discussion of sexuality and bullying to minimize family conflict and avoid reinforcing labels.

B. Conduct a comprehensive risk and psychosocial assessment that explicitly explores coming out stressors, bullying, and minority stress; clarify confidentiality with Maya; and, with her consent, plan supportive engagement with her parents and school while protecting her privacy.
C. Encourage immediate disclosure of her sexuality to her parents because family engagement is always the priority in adolescent care.
D. Reply to the school counselor with general information about panic disorder and request details about bullying without Maya’s consent, ensuring you do not disclose her sexuality.
E. Prioritize complete alcohol abstinence as the main target and avoid discussing sexuality or bullying so as not to worsen anxiety through overfocus on identity issues.

question: A 19-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander trans woman, Kai, presents to the emergency department after superficial self-harm and escalating suicidal ideation. She reports increased alcohol use, rejection from some family members who emphasise traditional gender expectations, and fear of being outed at her small community clinic. You are conducting a psychiatric assessment and planning immediate management. Which actions best uphold the Code of Ethics principle about recognising the intersections of LGBTIQ+ identity, traditional roles, community acceptance, and multiple layers of discrimination?
options: A. With Kai’s informed consent, involve an Aboriginal health worker and, if she wishes, a trusted Elder or community advocate to help co-develop a culturally safe, gender-affirming risk management and follow-up plan.
B. Defer discussions of gender-affirming care until there is clear family/elder acceptance to avoid cultural conflict and reduce the risk of community backlash.

C. Use Kai’s affirmed name and pronouns in all clinical interactions; discuss documentation constraints and agree a plan that minimises risk of inadvertent outing while ensuring safe clinical communication.

D. Focus solely on the immediate suicide risk and alcohol use; postpone any exploration of cultural identity, kinship obligations, or community dynamics until a later appointment to avoid “complicating” the assessment.
E. Offer referral (with consent) to an Indigenous LGBTIQ+ peer support service, and consider legal advocacy for discrimination alongside mental health and alcohol treatment plans.

question: A 32-year-old Māori person who identifies as takatāpui and non-binary is seen for a court-ordered psychiatric assessment related to methamphetamine use, to inform potential diversion. There is no current acute risk. A probation officer emails asking you to record the client as “male or female” for program placement and requests that you disclose the client’s gender identity to the whānau at a planned hui to ‘ensure support’. You also realise you know the client’s cousin from your rugby club. What is the single best course of action that most closely aligns with the Code of Ethics principle on intersectionality and discrimination?
options: A. Record gender as sex assigned at birth to meet justice paperwork requirements, and share the client’s non-binary identity with whānau by default to enable cultural support; proceed without mentioning your acquaintance with the cousin to avoid delays.

B. Respect the client’s takatāpui identity in assessment and planning; with the client’s consent, involve a Māori health worker and whānau; advocate to probation for a placement that accommodates non-binary identity; and disclose your prior acquaintance to manage any potential conflict of interest as per policy.

C. Prioritise the substance use disorder only; defer discussion of gender identity and cultural context until sustained abstinence; complete the form as either male or female based on your clinical judgement to avoid delaying access to treatment.
D. Decline advocacy and immediately transfer care solely because the forms cannot be changed, noting that engaging with systems issues may be perceived as partiality.

question: Dr K is a consultant psychiatrist at a public hospital and sits on the mental health budget committee. Last week, Dr K assessed a 19-year-old transgender woman in the emergency department after severe family violence and suicidality; the patient engaged well with the hospital’s LGBTIQ+-specific family-violence service, which reports high demand and a waiting list. The committee is considering consolidating several “niche” programs into a single mainstream intimate partner violence clinic to reduce duplication. Local audit data show LGBTIQ+ clients underuse mainstream services and report misgendering and lack of safety. Dr K occasionally receives honoraria for educational sessions from the community LGBTIQ+ NGO that partners with the hospital service. What is the most ethical course of action for Dr K?
options: A. Disclose the honoraria, but recommend reallocating funds away from the LGBTIQ+-specific service to a single mainstream clinic for equity and efficiency, with a plan to offer optional LGBTIQ+ training later.

B. Disclose the honoraria and any perceived conflict, present the local data on unmet need and safety concerns, and advocate to maintain or increase dedicated, ongoing funding for the LGBTIQ+-specific family-violence service; propose formal evaluation and cross-service liaison, and recuse from the final vote if governance requires.
C. Withhold disclosure of the honoraria to avoid distracting the committee, and strongly lobby to protect the LGBTIQ+-specific service based on clinical experience.
D. Support closing the LGBTIQ+-specific program if the mainstream clinic commits to a one-off inclusivity workshop and displays LGBTIQ+ affirming signage to signal safety.
E. Abstain from any discussion or provision of relevant data due to conflict, allowing others to decide, even if that means the LGBTIQ+-specific program is defunded.

question: An emergency department psychiatrist assesses Alex, a 32-year-old non-binary person with alcohol use disorder, presenting after an assault by a same-sex partner. Alex fears being outed; the partner works in administration at the local mainstream sexual assault service. Alex requests LGBTIQ+-specific supports. The hospital social worker notes constrained discharge resources and suggests referring only to the mainstream service. Which actions best align with ethical obligations, including support for LGBTIQ+-specific services for those experiencing sexual/family violence?
options: A. Coordinate an immediate referral and warm handover to an LGBTIQ+-specific sexual assault/family-violence service and crisis accommodation if needed; if capacity is limited, escalate to the duty manager to secure urgent access or flexible funding; ensure confidentiality is protected given the partner’s employment at the mainstream service.
B. Refer exclusively to the mainstream service, emphasizing that all clinicians are expected to be culturally safe, and avoid discussing the partner’s employment to prevent ethical complications.
C. Place Alex on a waitlist for the LGBTIQ+-specific service due to funding limits, offer general hotline numbers, and discharge with instructions to return if risk escalates.

D. With Alex’s informed consent, provide a de-identified account to hospital leadership to advocate for sustained funding of LGBTIQ+-specific family-violence services, while arranging interim contact with LGBTIQ+ helplines and peer support.
E. Avoid documenting gender identity or sexuality to reduce bias and maintain neutrality in the record, as these details are not central to risk management.

question: An aged-care facility psychiatrist is asked to assess decision-making capacity for antipsychotic treatment and to advise on end-of-life preferences for Ms T, a 76-year-old trans woman with moderate Alzheimer’s disease admitted for agitation and pneumonia. Staff inconsistently use her affirmed name and pronouns. Her adult son insists she be referred to by her male birth name and claims next-of-kin status. An existing Advance Care Directive (ACD) names her long-term female partner as substitute decision-maker and specifies her affirmed name/pronouns. What is the most ethically appropriate course of action?
options: A. For therapeutic neutrality, avoid engaging in discussions about gender identity and focus solely on antipsychotic capacity; standardize documentation to legal sex to reduce confusion among staff.

B. Review and honour the ACD, including the named substitute decision-maker and affirmed name/pronouns; perform a decision-specific capacity assessment; document and communicate the affirmed identity to staff; and engage inclusive aged-care resources to support care.
C. As dementia implies global incapacity, rely on a next-of-kin hierarchy; seek the son’s consent for antipsychotic and end-of-life decisions and update records to reflect his preference.
D. If capacity is lacking, default to the public guardian due to family conflict, setting aside the ACD to ensure impartiality.
E. Provide the son with full details of the ACD and clinical plan without Ms T’s consent because family inclusion is essential for continuity of care.

question: Mr Y, an 84-year-old gay man with mild vascular neurocognitive disorder, is admitted to the oncology ward with metastatic cancer. He has a 30-year male partner, Mr K, with whom he lives; they are not married. Mr Y presents with low mood and is referred to you for depressive symptoms and assistance completing an Advance Care Plan (ACP) addressing goals of care and resuscitation. His estranged daughter (with strong religious views) opposes involving Mr K, calling him “just a friend.” Mr Y’s attention sometimes fluctuates, but he is presently conversant and engaged. Which actions best align with ethical care that considers the intersection of LGBTIQ+ identity, dementia, and end-of-life decision-making? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Seek Mr Y’s consent to include Mr K; clarify and document whether Mr Y has nominated or wishes to nominate Mr K as substitute decision-maker; explicitly record chosen family and relationship status to guide clinical care.

B. Conduct a decision- and time-specific capacity assessment for ACP and end-of-life choices; if capacity is sufficient now, complete and document the ACP using supportive strategies (e.g., plain language, breaks) and plan to revisit if cognition fluctuates.

C. Screen for minority stress and potential discrimination in the ward; brief staff on inclusive, respectful care for the couple, as this may affect depressive symptoms, trust, and engagement with end-of-life planning.
D. Defer ACP discussions until cognitive decline progresses further to minimize distress and focus solely on treating depression first.
E. Involve the daughter as the primary decision-maker due to blood relation and exclude Mr K from care meetings unless the daughter consents.
F. Avoid documenting sexual orientation or partner details in psychiatric notes to protect confidentiality; rely on verbal handovers instead.

question: You are a child and adolescent psychiatrist on an inpatient unit. Ari, a 15-year-old with an intersex variation, was admitted after a suicide attempt and meets criteria for a major depressive episode. Ari's parents, from a culturally conservative background, ask the team to arrange a 'corrective' gonadectomy and genital surgery during this admission to minimise future distress. Ari says they are unsure about their gender identity, do not want surgery now, and request that details of their intersex status not be shared with extended family. The surgical team notes there is no acute medical indication and the procedures would be elective. Which actions are most ethically appropriate for you to take now?
options: A. Support the parents’ request and recommend proceeding with surgery during the admission to alleviate distress, with capacity assessment after recovery.

B. Prioritise safety and depressive symptom management; validate Ari’s identity and uncertainty; assess decision-making capacity/Gillick competence; defer any irreversible, non-urgent procedures; convene an intersex-competent multidisciplinary meeting (endocrinology, surgery, ethics, cultural liaison) and involve parents with Ari’s consent; share information in line with confidentiality obligations.
C. Avoid involving an ethics consultation to prevent delay and maintain parental authority; provide psychiatric clearance for surgery given the severity of depression.
D. Disclose Ari’s intersex details to grandparents to enhance family support, as cultural considerations supersede confidentiality for minors.

E. Provide evidence-based psychoeducation to the family about outcomes and human rights concerns regarding non-essential surgery in children/adolescents; facilitate access to intersex peer/lived-experience resources; plan for shared decision-making over time rather than in crisis.

F. Document Ari’s preferred name and pronouns; ensure discharge planning includes trauma-informed therapy, family work, and—with Ari’s consent—liaison with school to reduce discrimination and promote dignity.

question: You are asked to complete an independent fitness-for-duty assessment for Sam, a 29-year-old intersex, nonbinary software engineer referred by their employer after extended leave for panic attacks and anxiety linked to workplace harassment. Sam consents to the assessment but explicitly requests that their intersex variation not be disclosed to the employer. There is no imminent risk. The employer asks for diagnosis, treatment recommendations, and an opinion on readiness to return to work. Which single approach best aligns with ethical obligations and the principle of recognising and validating intersex identities?
options: A. Provide a comprehensive report including details of Sam’s intersex variation because it contextualises anxiety and may guide workplace adjustments.
B. Decline the assessment unless the employer agrees that Sam can preview and remove any reference to intersex status from the report.

C. Conduct the assessment using Sam’s affirmed name and pronouns; obtain informed consent about the scope and limits of the report; limit disclosure to functional capacity and recommended supports without identifying intersex status unless essential for the referral question; note the need for anti-discrimination protections; offer a separate clinical letter to Sam and their GP.
D. Use sex assigned at birth and avoid they/them pronouns in the medico-legal report to match HR records and prevent confusion.
E. Recommend hormonal or surgical normalisation as a strategy to improve workplace acceptance, postponing psychological treatment until after any procedures.

question: Mr J is a 45-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander man with chronic schizophrenia, living independently. He attends with his sister, who reports increased thought disorder. Mr J refuses a switch to a long-acting injectable antipsychotic and declines to sign consent for any medication changes. He is calm, denies suicidal or homicidal ideation, and there is no evidence of immediate risk to self or others. He states he understands there is a risk of relapse but prefers to “take his chances.” His sister asks you to proceed and says she will consent on his behalf. English is his second language. Which is the most appropriate next step in relation to capacity and consent?
options: A. Accept the sister’s consent as next-of-kin and proceed, because schizophrenia commonly impairs capacity to refuse medication.

B. Conduct a culturally safe, decision-specific capacity assessment, using a qualified interpreter or cultural liaison if needed; if capacity is present, respect his refusal, documenting the assessment and discussion.
C. Use the Mental Health Act to authorise treatment for relapse prevention even without immediate risk, because preventing deterioration is a sufficient legal basis.
D. Proceed after providing standard information and recording his nod as implied consent, given he attended voluntarily.
E. Ask a community Elder to co-sign a consent form in lieu of formal assessment to avoid straining family relationships.

question: Ms Q is a 32-year-old recent migrant with limited English, admitted with a first-episode psychosis. She is grandiose and guarded and refuses antipsychotic medication. There is no immediate risk requiring emergency treatment. Her spouse insists he can “consent for her” and requests you start a depot antipsychotic today. The team seeks your advice on consent. Which of the following actions are consistent with the RANZCP Code of Ethics and relevant laws about assessing capacity and obtaining consent in this situation? Select all that apply.
options: A. Arrange an accredited interpreter and conduct a task- and time-specific capacity assessment regarding antipsychotic treatment, ensuring information is provided in a way she can understand.
B. If she demonstrates decision-making capacity, respect her refusal of medication despite family pressure, and continue to engage therapeutically.
C. If she lacks decision-making capacity and statutory criteria are met, use the appropriate Mental Health Act pathway for involuntary assessment/treatment rather than relying on spousal consent.
D. Accept the spouse’s consent as sufficient under implied agency, because spouses are default substitute decision-makers in most clinical settings.
E. Proceed under emergency treatment provisions to administer depot medication today, because untreated psychosis poses long-term risks even without immediate danger.
F. Withhold discussion of material risks to avoid exacerbating her paranoia, as therapeutic privilege allows clinicians to omit distressing information when capacity is impaired.

question: You are the on-call psychiatrist in a metropolitan ED that has seen a sharp rise in self-harm presentations among transgender and nonbinary adolescents. Hospital executives request you lead a rapid project to collect detailed gender identity data to inform service planning and support a forthcoming funding proposal. Some young people express fear of being outed to parents, and numbers are small enough that detailed cross-tabs might risk re-identification. Which of the following approaches best align with the ethical principle that enhanced LGBTIQ+ mental health research should be undertaken with sensitivity and with individual and community consultation and participation? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Convene a local LGBTIQ+ youth advisory group (including trans/nonbinary peers) to co-design data elements, consent language, distress protocols, and safeguards before any data collection.
B. Proceed under a hospital quality-improvement exemption without HREC review to avoid delays, given the imminent risk of self-harm in this group.
C. Require mandatory recording of legal sex and assigned sex at birth for all adolescents to ensure complete data, and remove any 'prefer not to say' options that would reduce statistical utility.

D. Use an opt-in consent process with clear explanations of purpose, voluntary participation, and the option to skip identity questions; implement cell-size suppression and aggregate reporting to reduce re-identification risk.
E. Share a de-identified line-list (names and MRNs removed) with a national research collaborator immediately to boost sample size, without formal agreements, since data are not identifiable.
F. Provide targeted training to ED staff on gender-affirming, non-stigmatizing language and confidentiality practices so that research participation does not affect care or perceived safety.

question: A private psychiatrist in a small regional town plans a case series on methamphetamine-associated psychosis among bisexual men in his practice. The clinic serves a tight-knit community where participants could be readily identifiable. Several patients report previous negative experiences with research. The psychiatrist intends to submit findings to a national journal. Which ONE action best aligns with the ethical principle that enhanced LGBTIQ+ mental health research should be conducted sensitively with individual and community consultation and participation?
options: A. Draft the protocol and submit to the HREC; after approval, recruit only during clinical appointments with clear statements that participation is voluntary and with modest compensation.

B. Partner with a local LGBTIQ+ health organisation to co-develop the research questions and consent materials, include peer researchers on the team, and plan to present preliminary findings back to the community for feedback before publication.
C. Reduce stigma by removing explicit references to bisexuality from the paper and using the term 'atypical sexual histories,' while retaining detailed demographic and location descriptors.
D. Launch an anonymous national online survey advertised via the clinic website to avoid coercion, and proceed without HREC review because data will be anonymous.

E. Request de-identified meth-related presentation data from the local ED and police about 'men who have sex with men' to triangulate findings, without community consultation, as long as identifiers are stripped.

question: In an emergency department, a 27-year-old Rohingya asylum seeker presents with escalating suicidal ideation following a recent visa interview. She speaks little English, appears hypervigilant, and discloses prior sexual violence in an offshore detention setting. Her partner and 6-year-old child accompany her. She expresses fear that anything she says could be used to deport her. Which single option best reflects an ethically appropriate, trauma-informed and culturally sensitive response aligned with RANZCP guidance on refugees and asylum seekers?
options: A. Proceed with the risk assessment using her partner as an interpreter to build rapport and expedite care, given the clinical urgency and lack of interpreter availability.

B. Arrange an accredited female interpreter, conduct a trauma-informed assessment in private, explicitly explain confidentiality (including that clinical information is not routinely shared with immigration without consent unless legally required), and prioritise referral to a specialist refugee mental health service and community supports while safety planning.
C. Minimise discussion of trauma to avoid re-traumatisation, provide a short course of benzodiazepines for sleep, and discharge with GP follow-up once immediate distress settles.
D. Contact the detention case officer to corroborate her account and to inform them of her presentation, ensuring continuity and efficient coordination with immigration services.

E. Provide psychoeducation and delay using a professional interpreter because of cost and time constraints; use a translation app for key questions and arrange a formal interpreter at a later follow-up.

question: You lead a community psychiatry service that has seen rising referrals of asylum seekers and refugees with PTSD, depression, and detention-related trauma. Interpreter use is inconsistent, and some patients miss appointments due to fear of immigration repercussions. Funding is tight, but a local PHN/Te Whatu Ora network invites you to propose a redesign. Which strategies are most ethically aligned with the RANZCP’s recommendations regarding refugees and asylum seekers? (Select all that apply.)
options: A. Establish formal partnerships with refugee support organisations to co-locate clinics and outreach, integrate bicultural workers, and streamline warm handovers to facilitate access to holistic support.
B. Defer all research activities involving refugees until service capacity improves, to avoid adding burden; avoid research participation entirely so as not to risk re-traumatisation.

C. Advocate with funders and policymakers for Medicare/NHI-equivalent access to interpreters, confidentiality safeguards from immigration authorities, and transport subsidies to reduce practical and perceived barriers to care.

D. Require all clinicians to complete training in cultural competence, trauma-informed care, and the mental health impacts of detention; ringfence protected time and seek targeted funding to support this.
E. Limit service eligibility to refugees with permanent protection visas to improve continuity and reduce non-attendance, reserving scarce resources for those most likely to remain long-term.

question: During an inpatient risk assessment, Dr. K is treating a 23-year-old transgender woman admitted after a serious suicide attempt. The patient expresses distrust of clinicians and says, "You can't possibly understand what this is like." Dr. K has a personal history of major depression, now in sustained remission. Which approaches best align with the ethical principle that psychiatrists’ lived experience can add value while acknowledging that the best ways to use it require further exploration and research?
options: A. Seek supervision to consider a brief, purpose-driven self-disclosure only if it is likely to support engagement and safety for this patient at this time; keep details minimal, avoid shifting focus from the patient, and document the rationale, risks, and benefits.
B. Refrain from any self-disclosure in all circumstances because sharing personal mental health history is always unprofessional and undermines objectivity.
C. Share a detailed narrative of her own episode and hospitalisation to normalise the patient’s experience and expedite alliance, as current evidence consistently supports this approach.

D. Consider a general, non-specific acknowledgement of lived experience only if the patient raises it and there is a clear therapeutic aim; avoid using disclosure to influence specific clinical choices (e.g., medication acceptance), and plan debriefing/supervision to reflect on impact.

E. Inform the multidisciplinary team of her lived experience so they can align messaging and strategically incorporate it into the patient’s care, relying on team confidentiality to protect her privacy.

question: Dr. R is instructed to conduct an independent forensic psychiatric evaluation (child custody determination) of a 32-year-old father of Māori descent with recurrent depression and opioid use disorder. Dr. R has a personal history of opioid dependence in sustained remission. How should Dr. R best manage this in line with the principle that lived experience may add value, while recognising the need for careful boundaries and that optimal approaches require further research?
options: A. Disclose the lived experience to the evaluee at the outset to improve openness and include a section in the court report detailing this background to enhance transparency.

B. Avoid self-disclosure to the evaluee; seek peer consultation to monitor for bias related to lived experience; disclose any potential conflict-of-interest concerns to the instructing party if relevant to impartiality; base opinions strictly on evidence and do not include personal health history in the report.
C. Decline the case because psychiatrists with similar lived experience cannot be sufficiently objective in substance use evaluations.
D. Proceed without any adjustments or reflection because lived experience has no bearing on forensic work and need not be considered.
E. Use lived experience to emphasise recovery potential and recommend against supervised visitation to avoid unnecessary restriction.

question: You are the inpatient unit consultant in a busy public hospital. A 32-year-old Indian-Australian psychiatry registrar you supervise asks for a confidential discussion after a restrictive intervention debrief. He discloses a past diagnosis of major depressive disorder with prior suicidal ideation, now well and under the care of an external psychiatrist, and current SSRI use. He is concerned about stigma and career impact if colleagues find out, and asks you to keep this private unless there is a safety concern. There is no indication of imminent risk or impaired performance. Which action best aligns with the Code of Ethics principle regarding psychiatrists’ lived experience of mental illness? Choose ONE best answer.
options: A. Immediately remove him from on-call and acute admissions work and notify credentialing and HR to arrange mandatory occupational health assessment before return to any clinical duties, to protect patient safety and organisational reputation.

B. Explore his current wellbeing and any risks; offer confidential support pathways (e.g., employee assistance, occupational health if he chooses, time to see his treating psychiatrist); affirm privacy and discuss his preferences around any disclosure; consider non-punitive workload adjustments only if he requests or if risks are identified.
C. Encourage him to share his lived experience at the next departmental meeting to reduce stigma; as his supervisor, advise you will announce this in advance to normalise disclosure.

D. Advise him not to disclose to anyone at work because prejudice is inevitable; suggest he keep treatment entirely separate from work and avoid taking medication at work to prevent negative career consequences.

E. Offer him the role of a 'lived-experience champion' for the unit and invite him to co-lead a project on clinicians’ mental health during his current term to demonstrate the service’s commitment to inclusion; explain that declining may be seen as a missed opportunity.

question: Dr Lee, a consultant psychiatrist, supervises Dr Harris, a transgender psychiatry trainee who has publicly spoken at a hospital panel about her lived experience of bipolar disorder and past alcohol use disorder (both in sustained remission). The emergency department is developing a brief intervention pathway for co-occurring mood and substance use disorders, and Dr Lee is asked to convene a working group. Dr Harris is on the same rotation and is being directly assessed by Dr Lee. Which actions most appropriately uphold the Code of Ethics principle on psychiatrists’ lived experience? Choose ALL that apply.
options: A. Invite Dr Harris to join because her lived experience could enrich the work, but clearly state participation is voluntary; establish a psychological safety charter and clarify boundaries (e.g., her decision will not influence assessments); offer alternative ways to contribute (e.g., anonymous consultation) and document that non-participation will not affect training progression.

B. Exclude Dr Harris to avoid any appearance of favouritism or bias, and explain that staff with lived experience should not be involved in clinical program design to prevent personal perspectives from influencing service models.

C. If Dr Harris participates, ensure the minutes do not document her lived experience without explicit consent; agree on what, if anything, is shared beyond the group; remind members to maintain confidentiality; offer access to peer supervision or staff wellbeing resources.
D. Encourage Dr Harris to share detailed relapse narratives at the first meeting to inspire others; transparency about her history is essential for credibility in the role.

E. Seek institutional ethics advice about whether aspects of the pathway work constitute research; if so, consider including clinicians with lived experience as co-researchers and implement safeguards against coercion (e.g., independent recruitment, separate from supervision).

F. Note Dr Harris’s lived experience in her end-of-term assessment as a strength and as context for past sick leave, even without explicit consent, because she has already discussed it in a public forum.

question: You are the on-call psychiatrist in an acute inpatient unit. Tama, a 24-year-old Māori man, has been admitted involuntarily with methamphetamine-associated psychosis. He assaulted a peer in the ED earlier but is now calmer. He asks for rongoā Māori (traditional healing) input and wants his whānau involved, but the team is pressed for time and prioritising rapid symptom control. Which actions are most consistent with a recovery-oriented approach, as required by the Code of Ethics, across all settings including acute involuntary care?
options: A. Arrange an early hui with Tama and his whānau (with his consent), engage Māori health workers/kaumātua, co-create short-term personally meaningful goals (e.g., reconnecting with whānau, sleep, safety), and integrate harm-reduction planning for methamphetamine use alongside antipsychotic treatment.
B. Defer all recovery planning until he is symptom-free and discharged; during admission focus exclusively on medication, observation, and behavioural containment to minimise immediate risk.

C. Review and apply relevant NZ and Australian recovery-oriented competency frameworks (e.g., Let’s get real; National framework for recovery-oriented mental health services), update the team’s co-existing disorders skills, and document how care plans reflect these standards.
D. Decline any whānau engagement until Tama is fully well and can provide written consent; discussing whānau involvement now risks coercion and should be avoided on busy acute units.
E. Treat the methamphetamine use only after psychosis resolves, since discussing substance issues during acute admission may compromise engagement and is not core to immediate care.

F. Offer choices where possible (e.g., medication formulation), invite a peer support worker, and co-produce a brief crisis plan that includes early warning signs and preferred de-escalation strategies.

question: You are preparing a court-ordered pre-sentence psychiatric report for Jack, a 32-year-old Aboriginal man with schizophrenia and recent violent offending in the context of alcohol use and homelessness. During interview he asks for advice on services that could help him with housing and cultural supports after sentencing. Which single option best reflects a recovery-oriented approach while maintaining your forensic role and ethical obligations?
options: A. Explain your assessor role and decline to discuss his goals or any services, as recovery principles do not apply to forensic assessments and could compromise objectivity.

B. Clarify your independent role and limits of confidentiality; invite Jack’s values, strengths, and goals to inform a formulation and recommendations (e.g., housing pathways, AOD treatment, cultural and community Elder engagement), reference relevant AU/NZ recovery-oriented standards, and signpost services without establishing a treatment relationship.
C. Restrict the report to diagnosis and risk to avoid any perception of advocacy; recovery content is inappropriate in pre-sentence contexts.
D. Contact family and community Elders without consent to demonstrate cultural responsiveness and gather information, as cultural recovery needs outweigh confidentiality in court reports.
E. State that because Jack is in custody he lacks capacity for goal-setting; defer all recovery considerations until after sentencing.

question: You are a private psychiatrist seeing Amir, a 25-year-old Afghan refugee with PTSD and hazardous alcohol use. He reports intermittent suicidal ideation without plan or intent, and is focused on improving sleep, returning to study, and reconnecting with his cultural community. His sister phones asking for updates and offers to attend sessions. Your clinic has not previously used recovery-oriented resources. The local Mental Health Commission invites you to trial a co-produced recovery planning tool with training led by people with lived experience, tailored for private psychiatrists. Which actions best align with the RANZCP’s commitments to recovery-oriented practice?
options: A. Prioritise symptom checklists and risk management only; defer discussion of education/employment or cultural reconnection until PTSD symptoms are markedly reduced; decline external programs to avoid role confusion.

B. With Amir’s informed consent, invite his sister to one session to understand supports and recovery goals; co-create a plan that includes education/employment and cultural reconnection; integrate a peer worker’s input via the Commission’s training.

C. Decline the Commission’s program, explaining that private psychiatrists should avoid tools developed with lived experience until confirmed by randomised controlled trials; maintain a strictly biomedical focus to ensure evidence-based practice.

D. Optimise evidence-based PTSD and alcohol interventions and refer to a culturally specific community program; schedule a review focused on Amir’s self-defined goals; participate in the Commission’s co-designed training to update your clinic’s resources.
E. Provide general progress updates to his sister to enhance family support even if Amir is uncertain about involving her, as this is often beneficial in collectivist cultures.

question: Dr Li, a senior psychiatrist with lived experience of major depressive disorder now in remission, is asked to deliver a registrar teaching session on recovery-oriented care. She also supervises a registrar who has recently disclosed personal stress and low mood. Which approach best aligns with the RANZCP’s stance on valuing psychiatrists with lived experience and promoting recovery-oriented education?
options: A. Avoid any mention of personal lived experience in professional settings, as it risks undermining credibility and should never be discussed with trainees.
B. Share detailed personal clinical records and intimate experiences, including medication dosages and family conflicts, to model openness and reduce stigma.

C. Offer a planned, limited self-disclosure framed around recovery principles (hope, self-determination, supports, relapse prevention), with clear boundaries; discuss partnering with people with lived experience to co-produce training resources; liaise with the Mental Health Commission to incorporate co-designed materials into local education.
D. Advise the struggling registrar to disclose their mental health history to all patients to normalise clinicians’ lived experience and reduce stigma.
E. Focus solely on regulatory clinical standards and omit recovery concepts and lived experience, as these are outside the scope of medical training.

question: Perinatal psychiatry and conflict of interest: A community perinatal psychiatrist is asked to advise a regional health service responding to high rates of alcohol-related harm and suspected FASD among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families. Simultaneously, a beverage company offers a consultancy to help shape a ‘responsible drinking’ advertising campaign targeting pregnant women. Which options align with the RANZCP’s evidence-based ethical commitments in this situation? Select THREE.
options: A. Decline the beverage company consultancy due to conflict of interest and advocate for independent regulation of alcohol marketing with clear health-warning labelling, particularly regarding pregnancy.

B. Support minimum unit pricing and reduced outlet density/hours to lower availability, while proposing the legal purchasing age be lowered to integrate youth into regulated venues that can ‘model responsibility’.

C. Recommend investment in culturally led services that improve access to care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, including training local health professionals, early identification of children with FASD, and supports for family/whānau.
D. Advise against universal alcohol screening in antenatal clinics to avoid stigmatising mothers, instead relying on clinical ‘red flags’ to trigger assessment.

E. Promote cross‑agency integration (primary care, antenatal, child protection, schools) with universal screening and brief interventions, and incorporate community recovery narratives to encourage help‑seeking.
F. Accept beverage industry funding for research on youth drinking, allowing the sponsor to review and veto findings to ensure messaging remains ‘balanced’ and not ‘anti‑industry’.

question: During an overnight assessment in the ED, you see Hana, a 16-year-old Māori high-school student brought in after binge drinking at a party. She is drowsy but improving, denies self-harm intent, and will likely be discharged to family later that morning. Your hospital is recruiting to a trial of a co-designed smartphone app to reduce binge drinking among adolescents. The principal investigator (a colleague) texts you asking that you approach Hana now to enroll her, noting the importance of Māori representation. Which TWO actions are ethically appropriate and align with the RANZCP’s support for research into innovative tools for young people and engagement with Māori communities? Select TWO answers.
options: A. Approach Hana immediately while she remains sedated to obtain her assent; obtain guardian consent by phone later, documenting that the need to include Māori participants justifies recruitment in the ED.

B. Defer any research approach until Hana has decision-making capacity and her immediate clinical care and safety needs are addressed; if she later expresses interest, obtain informed assent/consent (and guardian consent as required) and ensure participation is clearly voluntary and unrelated to her care.

C. Before approaching Hana about the trial, consult the hospital Māori health unit and the study’s Māori community advisory group to confirm culturally safe processes, appropriate whānau involvement, and safeguards against inadvertent coercion.
D. Exclude Māori youth from this phase of the trial to avoid potential stigma; plan to include them only once the app has been proven effective in non-Indigenous adolescents.

E. Screen Hana and all adolescents in the ED with an adult-focused alcohol screening tool (e.g., AUDIT) as a research endpoint without prior ethics approval, given the practical constraints of emergency care.

question: You are assessing Kye, a 7-year-old Aboriginal boy with learning and behavioral difficulties. Prenatal alcohol exposure is suspected but unconfirmed. A multisite research team invites your service to join a study developing and validating a diagnostic tool for FASD to enable consistent and universal screening. Kye’s parents are concerned about stigma and confidentiality. Which ONE approach best aligns with the RANZCP’s ethical support for further research into FASD diagnostic tools and culturally appropriate engagement with Aboriginal communities, while meeting Kye’s clinical needs?
options: A. Use the investigational FASD tool clinically now to assign a diagnosis so Kye can access services more quickly, noting in the file that the tool is still under validation.

B. Provide a comprehensive clinical assessment using current best-practice methods to guide care now; offer optional participation in the validation study with transparent informed consent, culturally appropriate community governance input, and clear assurances that declining will not affect Kye’s care.
C. Defer all assessments until the new FASD diagnostic tool is validated, to avoid any risk of mislabeling or stigma.
D. Enroll Kye in the research study without parental consent because community Elders have expressed general support for research participation to improve services.
E. Implement universal screening of all Aboriginal children in your service with the investigational tool to improve representation and accelerate validation.

question: You are seeing a 28-year-old trans woman with generalized anxiety disorder who presents after seeing multiple Instagram ads for a new brand-name anxiolytic. She insists the product is “non-addictive and life-changing” and requests that specific brand, declining to discuss SSRIs or psychotherapy. She has limited health literacy and is between jobs. Which ONE action best aligns with the RANZCP’s position on direct‑to‑consumer advertising, health literacy, and fostering dialogue free from commercial influence?
options: A. Explore her goals and concerns, explain that direct‑to‑consumer ads can be misleading, provide unbiased written resources (e.g., TGA/Medsafe consumer information, NPS MedicineWise) about evidence‑based options including non‑pharmacological treatments, discuss risks/benefits in plain language without endorsing a brand, and invite questions.
B. Prescribe the requested brand briefly to maintain the therapeutic alliance, with a plan to switch to an evidence‑based alternative at the next review once rapport is stronger.
C. Direct her to the manufacturer’s patient-support website for detailed information and financial assistance programs, noting that you have no financial relationship with the company.

D. Inform her that, because of College policy against pharmaceutical advertising, you cannot discuss any medication she learned about from an advertisement and advise her to ask her GP about it instead.
E. Offer to arrange a short Q&A with the company’s representative during clinic hours so she can ask product-specific questions directly before you formalize a treatment plan.

question: A rural New Zealand psychiatrist provides maintenance care to a 62-year-old Māori man with schizophrenia who is stable on an oral antipsychotic. His daughter pressures for a switch to a brand‑name long‑acting injectable she saw advertised on television. The community clinic has received an unrestricted educational grant from that same manufacturer for general mental health education. Which TWO actions best align with the RANZCP’s recommendations regarding prohibition of direct‑to‑consumer advertising, improving health literacy, and ensuring dialogue free from commercial influence? Select TWO.
options: A. Acknowledge and disclose the clinic’s funding relationship, avoid brand-specific recommendations, provide culturally appropriate, unbiased consumer resources (e.g., Medsafe/TGA consumer information) comparing LAIs and oral options, and use shared decision-making to explore pros/cons and preferences.
B. Decline to discuss the advertised medicine altogether and refer the family to the company’s nurse educator to address their questions about the product.
C. Offer to host an educational lunchtime session at the local marae with sponsorship from the manufacturer so the company’s representative can answer community questions in your presence.

D. Explain the evidence for LAIs in a brand‑neutral manner, discuss risks, benefits, side‑effects, costs, and monitoring compared with his current regimen, correct misleading claims from the ad, and lodge a concern about the advertisement with Medsafe/ASA, noting RANZCP’s advocacy against direct‑to‑consumer advertising.
E. Switch him immediately to the advertised LAI to reduce caregiver anxiety and potential non‑adherence, documenting that the change was requested by family after seeing the TV ad.

question: A 17-year-old Māori student in New Zealand is on weekly psychotherapy and sertraline for anxiety, with comorbid cannabis use disorder. He is charged after a school fight. The Youth Court issues a subpoena for his entire psychiatric file, including psychotherapy notes. He refuses consent for disclosure. There is no current risk to self or others. Which actions are most consistent with the RANZCP’s commitment to confidentiality while meeting legal obligations? Select THREE.
options: A. Immediately send the full, unredacted file because a subpoena overrides confidentiality and, in criminal matters, the therapeutic value of confidentiality is secondary.

B. Through counsel, challenge scope and relevance, and request that any necessary evidence be heard in closed court (in camera) or subject to suppression orders, citing protections under the New Zealand Evidence Act and the need to balance open justice with privacy.
C. Provide a brief letter confirming diagnosis and attendance only, ignoring the subpoena’s request for the entire file, because minimal disclosure is always sufficient.

D. Engage the young person and their lawyer to explain limits of confidentiality, explore informed consent, and advocate for the least intrusive alternative (e.g., an agreed clinician report limited to relevant issues) rather than wholesale file disclosure.
E. Refuse to participate in the legal process altogether to protect the therapeutic alliance, documenting your ethical objection.

F. Seek judicial directions that any material produced be sealed, accessible only to the court and counsel, with permission to redact sensitive, non-relevant psychotherapy content—invoking judicial discretion to protect confidential professional relationships.

question: A 45-year-old Aboriginal man is admitted for alcohol withdrawal management after a relapse. Police investigating an alleged minor assault call you (his treating psychiatrist) requesting his recent records, including any blood alcohol results noted in your file. He refuses consent. There is no imminent risk to self or others. What is the most appropriate next step, consistent with the RANZCP’s confidentiality commitments? Select ONE.
options: A. Provide the minimum necessary facts (e.g., dates of attendance and objective test results), as these are unlikely to harm the therapeutic relationship.

B. Decline to disclose without the patient’s consent or a valid legal compulsion (e.g., subpoena/court order); advise police to pursue lawful channels, and prepare—if an order issues—to advocate for judicial discretion and the narrowest, least harmful disclosure.
C. Supply a de-identified extract of the notes so police can still use the information without breaching privacy.
D. Discuss with police the patient’s likely diagnosis and specific risks related to alcohol withdrawal without naming him, since they already know his identity.
E. Delay responding and revisit once the investigation is complete to avoid interfering with justice.

question: You are the consultant psychiatrist on a secure forensic unit. Mr K, a 28-year-old man on remand for armed robbery, originally from South Sudan with limited English proficiency, is admitted for a fitness-to-plead assessment. He reports intermittent chest pain and requests to speak privately with his lawyer about an upcoming bail hearing. A custody officer insists on remaining in the room for all clinical and legal discussions "for security" and suggests the chest pain is likely anxiety, advising you to "stick to the psych". An in-person interpreter is next available in 5 days. Which action best upholds the ethical principle of equity of access to health care and legal representation?
options: A. Conduct the clinical interview with the custody officer present and defer the interpreter until next week; focus on mental state and risk only, as legal matters fall outside your clinical remit.

B. Arrange timely access to legal counsel in as much privacy as safely possible (e.g., custody observation without audio), document the request, organise an accredited interpreter (phone/video if needed), initiate an equivalent medical workup for chest pain as would occur in the community, and involve a cultural liaison worker.
C. Decline the patient’s legal access until the fitness-to-plead assessment is completed, to avoid influencing your report; refer physical health concerns to custodial primary care for later review.
D. To expedite proceedings, provide the lawyer with a detailed verbal clinical summary without the patient’s consent, given the forensic context.
E. Address only psychiatric symptoms; defer both legal and physical health needs to corrective services unless a court order directs otherwise.

question: You are treating Ms T, a 34-year-old transgender woman on a forensic community treatment order after an assault while psychotic. She has schizoaffective disorder and moderate intellectual disability. She is now stable and requests: (1) help applying for disability supports for supported accommodation and allied health; (2) referral for gender-affirming hormone therapy; and (3) assistance to obtain legal representation to review blanket restrictions on her internet access. The service faces long waitlists, and a colleague suggests prioritising non-offender clients to maintain public trust. There is no current imminent risk to others. Which actions are ethically required to uphold equity of access to health care and legal representation? Select all that apply.
options: A. Actively support and facilitate applications for disability supports (e.g., NDIS), including providing necessary clinical documentation, to ensure access equivalent to non-forensic clients.
B. Defer gender-affirming hormone therapy for all patients with violent index offences until they have been offence-free for 12 months, to promote public confidence.
C. Ensure she has access to competent legal representation to review her conditions, and provide impartial clinical reports and decision-making capacity assessments as needed.
D. Provide trauma-informed, gender-affirming care, including endocrine referral if clinically indicated, and do not withhold solely because of her forensic status.
E. Allocate scarce psychotherapy slots preferentially to non-offender clients when demand exceeds supply, as they are more likely to benefit and it reassures the public.
F. Review and update her care plan collaboratively to reflect her preferences and cultural/spiritual needs, and arrange interpreter/advocate support if communication barriers are present.

question: A 24-year-old man on remand with a history of methamphetamine use presents with florid psychosis and active suicidal ideation. The magistrate has just classified him as a forensic patient under mental health legislation. The prison medical director advises there is no forensic bed for 10 days and proposes holding him in the prison health wing, staffed by correctional nurses with telepsychiatry input. His family requests he remain close to home. Which action is most consistent with the ethical principle that forensic patients must be managed by mental health services, not correctional services?
options: A. Accept temporary placement in the prison health wing with daily telepsychiatry input until a forensic bed becomes available, to minimise disruption and maintain family contact.

B. Arrange immediate transfer to a secure forensic inpatient unit owned, funded and staffed by the jurisdictional health directorate, beyond the prison boundary, with clinical and security staff employed by the health service.
C. Transfer him to the public hospital’s medical ward under an MOU, with correctional officers providing bedside security, and review for forensic unit transfer after 72 hours.
D. Defer transfer due to high absconding risk; commence depot antipsychotic in the prison clinic and plan transfer once stabilised.

question: A 36-year-old transgender woman has been classified as a forensic patient following court proceedings. She is acutely manic with psychotic features and has assaulted another inmate. The correctional service offers a new therapeutic secure unit inside the prison perimeter, run by corrections, and asks you to lead her ongoing management there. What actions align with the ethical principle that forensic patients must be managed by mental health services, not correctional services?
options: A. Decline ongoing clinical care within a correctional-run unit and advocate for immediate transfer to a secure forensic inpatient facility owned and staffed by the health service, outside the prison boundary.

B. Accept leadership of the prison-based unit if all clinicians are re-badged as health employees, while keeping correctional officers as security and retaining the unit within the prison for efficiency.

C. Provide interim stabilisation advice solely to enable safe transfer out of custody to a health-run forensic service (e.g., a one-time loading dose and sedation protocol), while documenting that ongoing correctional management is inappropriate.

D. Agree to a joint model where corrections retains funding and staffing (including clinical and security roles) but you hold clinical governance to ensure humane treatment within the prison perimeter.

E. Escalate to the jurisdictional health directorate and forensic mental health leadership to establish or use a health-owned, health-staffed secure inpatient service, preferably co-located with other health services, for her immediate care.

question: You are the treating psychiatrist for a 29-year-old man found not guilty due to mental impairment after a violent offense during a psychotic episode. He has responded well to clozapine, and recent structured risk assessments suggest low imminent risk if conditionally released to supervised accommodation. A month before an election, the Health Minister’s office phones you, citing community concern and the victim’s family’s wishes, and requests that you "sign off" a conditional release immediately to demonstrate responsiveness. The media is requesting comment. What is the most ethically appropriate next step under the Code of Ethics principle regarding detention, release and transfer?
options: A. Agree to the Minister’s request and sign a conditional release order under hospital authority, noting that clinical stability and public sentiment support this course.

B. Prepare a balanced, evidence-based report addressing the statutory legal tests for release, submit it to the independent court/tribunal, ensure families, carers and victim support services can access the transparent hearing process, and maintain confidentiality of clinical records except as required by the tribunal. Inform parties of appeal rights.
C. Hold a public forum to explain the clinical rationale for conditional release and share excerpts of the clinical file to promote transparency and reduce backlash.
D. Ask the hospital legal team to seek an executive (Governor/Administrator in Council) release to avoid delays, given the political urgency.
E. Decline to provide any report due to political pressure and ask a junior registrar to handle communications while you disengage from the process.

question: A 35-year-old Aboriginal man subject to a forensic order for arson associated with methamphetamine use and schizophrenia is currently in a secure inpatient unit. He is clinically stable and expresses a strong wish to transfer to a medium-secure unit in a neighboring state to be near extended family and Country. Police request an immediate cross-border transfer for logistical reasons. A victims’ advocacy group demands the full clinical file prior to any tribunal, asserting a right to transparency. The patient’s family lives remotely and cannot easily attend hearings in person. Which actions are ethically required or appropriate under the Code of Ethics principle? Select all that apply.
options: A. Apply to the relevant independent court/tribunal for transfer approval, basing the submission solely on the applicable legal tests and evidence from suitably qualified mental health practitioners.
B. Proceed with the transfer under a joint email agreement between police and hospital executives, then seek retrospective endorsement from the tribunal to reduce administrative burden.

C. Arrange for accessible participation by family, carers and victim support services in the hearing (e.g., telephone or video link, interpreters as needed) and ensure all parties are advised of appeal rights.
D. Provide the victim group with the patient’s full clinical file in advance of the hearing to maximize transparency and community trust.
E. Provide a focused clinical summary and risk opinion to the court/tribunal with usual protections of confidentiality, releasing broader clinical notes only if lawfully ordered.
F. Accept a direction from the Minister’s office to fast-track the transfer in the “public interest,” substituting an executive memo for detailed clinical evidence.
G. Liaise with the health department and the neighboring jurisdiction to utilize or establish a consistent cross-border agreement to enable a planned transfer, subject to tribunal approval.

question: A 27-year-old Aboriginal man with schizoaffective disorder and prior methamphetamine use is a forensic inpatient after a serious assault during florid psychosis. He has been stable for 4 months on long-acting antipsychotic medication, engaging with an Aboriginal health worker and family. Current structured risk assessment suggests risk can be managed through supervised accommodation, a community treatment order (CTO), and close follow-up. A victims' advocacy group has called for an indefinite inpatient stay. A local court has indicated it is inclined to order a specific long-term anger management program and restrict any community leave. Which course of action best aligns with the code of ethics regarding least restrictive care and the role of courts/tribunals?
options: A. Maintain indefinite inpatient detention and accept the court’s order for a specific program, deferring treatment decisions to the court to ensure public confidence.

B. Recommend conditional leave with step-down to a supervised community placement under a CTO, present a documented risk management plan to the tribunal, involve the Aboriginal health worker and victim liaison in discharge planning without granting them veto power, and seek a time-limited order with clear review points.
C. Keep him inpatient until he completes 12 months of verified abstinence and a full anger management course before considering any leave, regardless of current risk assessment.
D. Offer graded leave only if the victims’ group provides written consent, to ensure accountability to the community.
E. Continue admission principally because of his forensic status, even though a civil patient with the same clinical profile would be discharged to supported community care.

question: A 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder committed arson while manic and was found not guilty by reason of mental impairment. She has been stable for 18 months under a community treatment order (CTO) with regular mood monitoring. She recently missed two appointments and has early insomnia but denies intent to harm self or others; collateral suggests no imminent risk. Neighbours petition for her immediate recall to hospital and demand a blanket prohibition on her living within 10 km of the incident site. A victims’ representative asks the tribunal to order a mandatory "fire-setting offender program" and a curfew. What actions are most consistent with the ethical requirement for the least restrictive environment, the responsibilities of the treating team, and the attributes of aftercare systems?
options: A. Recall her to inpatient care immediately to reassure the public, even though current risk appears manageable in the community with intensified supports.

B. Intensify community management (e.g., prompt medication review, increased case management contacts, practical safety measures, and daily check-ins), liaise with a victims’ liaison service to incorporate concerns into the plan, document the rationale and set a review date, and seek tribunal oversight that includes clear avenues for appeal.
C. Support the tribunal mandating a specific intervention program and a blanket curfew, as externally imposed structure will ensure accountability regardless of the treating team’s plan.

D. Convene a case conference including the patient, family, and a victims’ advocate to incorporate their perspectives, while making clear that clinical decisions remain the treating team’s responsibility; provide written reasons for any restrictions.
E. Recommend extending restrictions beyond those applied to clinically similar non-forensic patients solely due to her forensic status, given the public concern.
F. If any restriction is imposed, ensure it is proportionate to current risk, time-limited, subject to regular review, and includes a mechanism for appeal.

question: Ms K, a 35-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder, PTSD, and recent alcohol use, has become highly agitated, threatened staff, and thrown a chair. She has a history of restraint-related trauma. The registrar must decide immediate measures to manage risk. According to the code, which actions are ethically appropriate? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Undertake an immediate, documented professional risk assessment to guide an individually tailored level of observation and security, while prioritising de-escalation strategies (verbal engagement, space, offering oral medication) and culturally safe support.
B. Place Ms K in seclusion immediately for a fixed 8-hour period to prevent modelling of aggression to other patients, and record it as a behavioural management intervention.
