C. If imminent harm persists after de-escalation and least-restrictive options are exhausted or inappropriate, use brief, closely monitored physical restraint solely for safety, with rapid medical review, continuous observation, and a time-limited order.
D. Institute a blanket ward lockdown and restrict all patient privileges until the following day to stabilise the overall ward milieu.
E. Maintain seclusion until Ms K agrees to accept a depot antipsychotic and apologises to staff, to reinforce boundaries and prevent future incidents.

F. Once the situation is safe, debrief with Ms K and staff; review precipitants and triggers; update her treatment plan; and document the rationale, alternatives considered, and why any seclusion/restraint was used as a last resort.

question: Mr T, a 29-year-old man with mild intellectual disability and major depressive disorder, is a forensic patient following conviction for online sexual offences. He is engaging in therapy and showing clinical improvement. The Child Protection Unit emails requesting that he be immediately placed on the Child Protection Register, and a senior nurse suggests keeping him on maximum security status until he's listed. Which ONE response best aligns with the code?
options: A. Agree to automatically place Mr T on the Child Protection Register because of the nature of the index offence to reassure the community.

B. Decline automatic registration and prepare a formal application to the appropriate court or authority for determination regarding registry status, providing an up-to-date professional risk assessment, treatment progress, and safety planning.
C. Defer any consideration of registration to probation after discharge, as the mental health service should focus solely on recovery rather than public protection.
D. Place Mr T on a Sex Offender Register temporarily via internal policy, pending later judicial review, given community concern.
E. Provide the Child Protection Unit with all of Mr T’s clinical records without consent because public safety overrides confidentiality in all forensic cases.
F. Maintain maximum security status irrespective of his current risk assessment until registry issues are resolved, to model consistency across the service.

question: You are the treating forensic psychiatrist for a 34-year-old Māori man in a medium-secure unit. He has a schizoaffective disorder and a methamphetamine use disorder. His index offence was a violent assault during psychosis. He is 3 months from a parole hearing. The parole board requests a risk assessment. The service is under resource pressure, but he has expressed willingness to engage with a Māori health worker and an in-reach AOD program. Which is the most ethically appropriate approach to reduce recidivism?
options: A. Provide a structured risk assessment focused on institutional behaviour and advise that parole should be contingent solely on incident-free custody; defer alcohol and drug treatment until after release under probation supervision, and avoid proposing culturally specific supports to maintain neutrality.

B. Develop an integrated, culturally competent rehabilitation plan including antipsychotic optimisation (considering LAI), in-custody AOD treatment, offence-focused work on criminogenic needs, and engagement with a Māori health worker; complete pre-release planning with warm handover to community mental health, AOD services, and stable housing; include these concrete supports in the report to the parole board.

C. Emphasise security classification and behavioural management in your report; recommend uniform programming without cultural tailoring to ensure fairness, and leave accommodation arrangements to probation to prevent scope creep.
D. Offer telepsychiatry follow-up into the community but decline a formal care handover to community teams citing confidentiality; advise the patient to self-refer to AOD services after release.

E. Prioritise commencing a long-acting antipsychotic and recommend delaying access to substance programs to minimise drug-seeking behaviours in-custody; advise no parole until 12 months of incident-free behaviour is demonstrated.

question: A 17-year-old Aboriginal girl in a youth justice centre has an intellectual disability (IQ 62), harmful alcohol use, and recent self-harm episodes. She has a history of trauma and is due to transition to adult services within 6 months. The centre asks you, the visiting psychiatrist, to advise on a treatment and release plan. Which options best align with ethical obligations to reduce recidivism?
options: A. Advocate for placement in a dedicated adolescent forensic mental health unit or, if not feasible, implement an equivalent wraparound package within the centre that includes ID-informed interventions, AOD treatment, trauma-focused care, and early pre-release planning; avoid unnecessary delays to release and document any barriers to access.

B. With the young person’s consent, engage Aboriginal health workers and involve family/elders; plan for on-country supports and ensure a warm handover to community-controlled health services and youth AOD programs pre-release.
C. Focus on short-term stabilisation only and defer substance use and criminogenic interventions until she transitions to adult corrections to avoid duplication of services.

D. Provide a risk management plan for self-harm/aggression and, given limited resources, restrict care to psychotropic medication and brief supportive sessions until transfer, noting attempts to obtain specialist ID input but without pursuing broader rehabilitation components.

E. Recommend parole conditions emphasising abstinence monitoring and curfew at a mixed adult hostel; schedule monthly psychiatric reviews post-release and leave housing and case management to corrective services to maintain professional boundaries.

F. Create a written shared-care plan addressing criminogenic needs (e.g., impulsivity, peer affiliation), adapted CBT for mild ID, and coordination with in-centre education/vocational programs; schedule a warm handover to adult community mental health and youth AOD services prior to release.

question: You are the court liaison psychiatrist asked to urgently assess a 19-year-old Aboriginal man on remand for an alleged assault. He has a known diagnosis of schizophrenia and heavy cannabis use. Nursing notes indicate ongoing thought disorder and auditory hallucinations. The prosecutor emails you suggesting that a quick report confirming he is fit will enable a plea and a community sentence with treatment conditions. The duty lawyer asks whether you will also consider an insanity (mental impairment) defence. What is the most ethically appropriate course of action in line with the RANZCP principle regarding insanity defence, fitness to stand trial, and diversion from punishment?
options: A. Provide a concise letter endorsing a plea deal to ensure prompt access to treatment in prison, noting that public safety and expediency outweigh delays caused by a full forensic assessment.
B. Recommend that the court determine guilt before you address insanity or fitness, to avoid appearing partisan and to preserve your neutrality.

C. Seek an adjournment to complete a comprehensive assessment of fitness to stand trial and mental state at the time of the alleged offence; advise that if he is found unfit or not guilty by reason of mental impairment, he should be diverted to secure hospital treatment rather than punished.
D. Limit your report to current risk and substance use, leaving questions of fitness and criminal responsibility to legal submissions by counsel.
E. Certify fitness to proceed based on current improvement on antipsychotic medication so the matter can move to sentencing and a community order with treatment conditions.

question: You are asked to provide a court report on Mr K, a 62-year-old Māori man charged with grievous bodily harm after an unprovoked assault on a care worker in his residential facility. You saw him 6 months ago in a memory clinic and documented probable frontotemporal dementia with behavioural disinhibition. He is currently in remand, intermittently agitated, and there is concern for further violence. The prosecutor requests you keep the report narrow and avoid raising the insanity defence. The victim’s family is calling for a custodial sentence to denounce the harm. Which of the following actions best align with the RANZCP ethical position supporting the insanity defence, fitness determinations, and ensuring those found not guilty by reason of mental impairment or unfit are not punished?
options: A. Disclose the prior treating relationship to the court and consider declining the instruction unless the court and parties accept your dual role and you are confident you can remain objective; if proceeding, obtain consent where possible and maintain clear boundaries.

B. Structure the report around current and past mental state, explicitly analysing fitness to stand trial and the relationship between the neurocognitive disorder and the alleged offence, and state that if found unfit or NGRMI he should receive treatment in a secure hospital rather than imprisonment.
C. Recommend a short, proportional custodial sentence with mandatory behavioural programs to balance treatment needs with appropriate punishment given the seriousness of harm.
D. Avoid discussing insanity or fitness, as raising these issues could appear to advocate for the defendant; confine the report to diagnosis and a general risk formulation.
E. Agree to omit consideration of the insanity defence because charging decisions and defences are the prosecutor's remit, not the psychiatrist's.
F. Share full historical cognitive assessment results with the victim’s family to support restorative justice, as transparency promotes community trust.
G. Recommend interim transfer to a forensic mental health unit for assessment and management of behavioural dyscontrol while fitness is determined, given current risk.

question: In a regional Australian emergency department, Dr Patel assesses K., a 19-year-old Aboriginal man with first-episode psychosis and daily cannabis use. He is distressed but not imminently dangerous; with support, he can be managed in the community. The ED director notes recent tightening of Mental Health Act (MHA) compliance audits and asks clinicians to 'err on the safe side' by using more Community Treatment Orders (CTOs). There has been no increase in community staffing or early psychosis capacity, and waiting lists are long. K.'s family request culturally safe, non-coercive supports through their local Aboriginal community-controlled health service. Which actions best align with the RANZCP’s ethical recommendations to governments regarding MHAs?
options: A. Proceed with a CTO now to meet regulatory expectations, and plan to advocate for expanded early psychosis services once budget cycles allow

B. Engage the Aboriginal health liaison and local community-controlled services to offer culturally-informed alternatives to involuntary treatment, and advocate through service leadership to state health authorities for resources matched to regulatory changes, including workforce analysis
C. Decline to consider any CTOs until MHA provisions are nationally harmonised and clearer; inform the family that care must wait for legislative consistency

D. Develop a voluntary, assertive early-intervention plan with close follow-up, while formally recommending (in writing) investment in early identification/treatment capacity to safely reduce reliance on compulsion in line with the MHA’s aspirations
E. Write to the mental health tribunal requesting it direct clinicians to increase CTO use until community resources improve, to ensure audit compliance

F. Support and contribute to a service submission urging inclusion/activation of provisions for regular MHA review to identify and correct unintended outcomes (e.g., rising compulsory care among youth) in a timely manner

question: In New Zealand, under the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992, a judicial hearing has been scheduled for M., a 45-year-old Māori woman with severe psychotic depression who has not responded to several antidepressant and antipsychotic trials. ECT is being considered. The judge’s clerk requests the weekly ECT stimulus dosing parameters and exact session numbers for approval. M. and her whānau express a preference for kaupapa Māori supports and worry about cultural safety. What is the most ethically appropriate response consistent with RANZCP recommendations to governments?
options: A. Provide the granular ECT dosing protocol so the judge can approve the clinical plan; detailed judicial control ensures accountability

B. Provide a clinical summary justifying ECT if indicated while resisting judicial micromanagement of dosing parameters; advocate (via Te Whatu Ora/DHB and RANZCP) for evaluation of outcomes comparing judicial hearings with multidisciplinary tribunals, and ensure investment and access to culturally-informed alternatives for Māori that may avert compulsory ECT
C. Request adjournment until New Zealand adopts the Australian-style tribunal model, stating the current judicial process is unethical
D. Explain that the MHA is complex and varies so it cannot be clearly explained; proceed with the hearing and note that cultural interventions are optional and should not delay compulsory treatment
E. Comply with the hearing but omit mention of culturally-informed alternatives to avoid complicating the process

question: You are the visiting psychiatrist to a metropolitan remand prison. A 29-year-old man with known schizophrenia has been loudly responding to voices, refusing oral medication, and intermittently threatening staff. He is distressed but not imminently life-threateningly unwell; he is contained in a safe cell. The correctional manager requests you authorise a forced long-acting injectable antipsychotic to be given on the unit "to restore order," noting a designated forensic mental health unit 30 minutes away can take transfers under the mental health act, but transfer would be logistically difficult today. The manager also asks to sit in during your assessment. Which is the most appropriate action aligned with the ethical principle?
options: A. Arrange urgent transfer to the designated mental health facility and, if statutory criteria are met, commence involuntary treatment there; decline to authorise involuntary treatment within the prison.
B. Authorise a one-off involuntary long-acting antipsychotic in the prison to stabilise behaviour, then reassess for transfer later if he remains unwell.
C. Defer any treatment until after a court-ordered fitness-to-stand-trial assessment is completed, to avoid contaminating the forensic evaluation.
D. Proceed with forced medication on the unit citing joint clinical–security decision-making, provided the use of force is documented and witnessed by custodial staff.
E. Conduct the clinical assessment with the manager present to expedite a decision and share full clinical details with custody staff to aid behaviour management.

question: You are the treating psychiatrist for a 27-year-old Māori transgender woman (software engineer) with PTSD related to workplace bullying. She is 8 months into EMDR and an SNRI with good progress. Her employer’s insurer has: (1) scheduled monthly psychiatric IMEs, (2) asked you to pause EMDR until IMEs are complete, (3) suggested switching to a cheaper SSRI, and (4) referenced surveillance of her socialising to question the diagnosis. Which actions best align with the RANZCP view that compensation processes should support, not undermine, recovery, including less adversarial pathways, non-discriminatory practice, limiting unnecessary IMEs, adherence to guidelines on IMEs/surveillance, and minimising interference with treatment? Select all that apply.
options: A. Decline all IMEs categorically and advise the patient to suspend the claim until the insurer ceases all interference, to protect the therapeutic alliance.

B. Propose a non-adversarial case conference with the insurer, patient (if willing), and treating team to set a collaborative plan; request that IMEs be limited to clinically justified frequency with clear questions, and that any use of surveillance adhere to governance guidelines.
C. Provide the entire clinical file, including historical and gender-affirming care notes unrelated to the claim, to demonstrate transparency and avoid further IMEs.

D. Escalate concerns about repeated IMEs and interference with prescribed treatment to the scheme’s clinical panel/ombudsman or equivalent, citing RANZCP guidance on limiting IMEs and minimising treatment disruption.
E. Accept the insurer’s suggestion to switch to a cheaper SSRI despite current response to an SNRI, to facilitate claim approval and reduce conflict.

F. With the patient’s informed consent, provide a concise, clinically focused report addressing diagnosis, functional impact, risk, and treatment progress to reduce duplication and the need for repeated IMEs.

question: You are approached to conduct a second psychiatric IME within 3 weeks of a prior IME for a 58-year-old Aboriginal man with major depression and chronic pain after a workplace injury. The insurer instructs you to comment on the claimant’s credibility using surveillance footage and to recommend capping psychotherapy at six sessions to control costs. They indicate that if your opinion is ‘not satisfactory’ they will obtain further psychiatric IMEs. What is the most ethically appropriate first response?
options: A. Accept the referral as-is, review the surveillance footage, provide an opinion on credibility, and recommend a cap on psychotherapy to harmonise with scheme expectations and promote efficiency.

B. Before accepting, communicate that you will only proceed if the referral scope is clarified, repeated IMEs are clinically and procedurally justified (with a commitment to avoid ‘doctor shopping’), and a non-adversarial process is pursued (e.g., pre-IME case conference); state you will not recommend treatment caps that interfere with the treating plan without clinical justification.
C. Proceed immediately to avoid delays and advise the insurer to book an additional neuropsychiatric IME after yours to triangulate opinions and ensure objectivity.
D. Contact the treating psychiatrist to direct treatment changes aimed at faster return to work, emphasising cost-effectiveness and scheme norms.
E. Conduct the IME but decline to consider surveillance evidence under any circumstances and do not inform the claimant that the assessment is for compensation to avoid bias.

question: You are the treating forensic psychiatrist for a 28-year-old Aboriginal man with schizoaffective disorder and methamphetamine use disorder who is preparing for conditional release from a secure unit following a violent offence. The multidisciplinary team has developed an individualised risk management plan (depot antipsychotic, assertive community treatment, cultural supports, and family involvement). Community Corrections asks you to endorse an ankle electronic monitoring device to reassure the public and because it is now being recommended for all high-risk releases. The patient has clearly refused electronic monitoring, stating it is humiliating and will disrupt his engagement with treatment. Which ONE action best aligns with the RANZCP’s ethical guidance on electronic monitoring in forensic patients? (Select ONE)
options: A. Decline to support electronic monitoring because the patient does not provide valid consent, and communicate to Community Corrections that risk will be managed through the agreed, individualised plan developed by the treating team, offering to review and strengthen that plan if needed.
B. Apply to the guardianship tribunal for substitute consent to electronic monitoring on the basis of impaired insight, given its perceived public safety benefit.
C. Agree to a time-limited three-month period of electronic monitoring despite the patient’s refusal, to bolster community confidence while maintaining conditional release.
D. Propose installation of a smartphone-based geolocation app as a less intrusive alternative and proceed if the patient provides verbal assent during a brief discussion on the ward round.
E. Convene a case conference primarily to persuade the patient that refusal of monitoring could jeopardise their release, and recommend monitoring on that basis.

question: A 45-year-old Samoan man with mild intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder is being assessed for transition from a forensic inpatient unit to supervised community living after a sexual offence. The parole board asks for your advice on adding GPS electronic monitoring as a condition. In a brief session, the patient says he is "okay" with the idea but appears highly suggestible. Your service has not yet finalised the individualised community risk management plan. A commercial vendor has also emailed you offering paid consultancy about monitoring devices. Which actions are ethically appropriate according to RANZCP guidance on electronic monitoring in forensic patients? (Select TWO)
options: A. Formally assess the patient’s decision-making capacity and voluntariness specific to electronic monitoring; if valid consent is established, consider electronic monitoring only as a voluntary measure embedded within a documented, individualised risk management plan developed by the treating clinical team.
B. Recommend the parole board mandate electronic monitoring immediately to protect the community while the treating team completes the risk plan, with a view to integrating it later.

C. Disclose the approach from the vendor as a potential conflict of interest to your service and the parole board, decline any financial relationship, and refrain from advocating for electronic monitoring until the conflict is transparently managed.
D. Proceed with electronic monitoring on the basis of the patient’s verbal agreement, forgoing a capacity assessment to avoid undermining autonomy.
E. Suggest family-monitored geofencing via a consumer smartphone app to minimise intrusiveness, without involving the treating team to avoid delays.

F. Offer a time-limited, voluntary trial of electronic monitoring immediately, documenting the rationale and planning to retrospectively incorporate it into the risk plan at the next multidisciplinary meeting.

question: A 22-year-old Māori man with a history of methamphetamine use and a prior psychotic episode is on a forensic treatment order after a serious assault. He is now adherent to antipsychotic treatment, has sustained remission of psychosis for 9 months, and is assessed as low acute risk with modifiable dynamic factors (unstable housing, limited pro-social supports). The parole board seeks your recommendation on conditions for a possible step-down to supervised community living. Corrections proposes mandatory GPS ankle monitoring to ensure compliance, noting current resource constraints in the community. Which actions best align with the RANZCP’s recommended approach to supporting forensic patients’ recovery?
options: A. Advocate for enhanced investment in the community forensic mental health team to provide assertive outreach, culturally responsive, evidence-based treatment and risk management, and recommend a release pathway individualized to his goals and risk formulation rather than defaulting to GPS monitoring.
B. Recommend mandatory GPS ankle monitoring for all forensic patients upon release as a uniform risk management tool until stronger evidence emerges.

C. Support a conditional release focusing on person-centred factors (stable housing, employment training, cultural supports), with graduated leave and regular multidisciplinary risk review, and decline to endorse GPS monitoring outside an approved research protocol.
D. Support continued detention due to limited community forensic capacity, and suggest that general adult services manage any future community care with standard outpatient follow-up.

E. If residual concerns persist, propose participation in an independent, ethics-approved research study of location tracking with fully informed, voluntary consent, clear withdrawal rights, and independent oversight, ensuring equivalent non-electronic supports are offered if he declines.
F. To reassure the victim’s family, proactively provide detailed clinical updates without explicit patient consent, since the offense is a matter of public record and under court supervision.

question: A 45-year-old woman from a culturally and linguistically diverse background is a forensic inpatient following arson during a manic episode of bipolar I disorder. She is now euthymic for 6 months with good insight and engagement in psychological therapies. Your service is piloting smartphone-based geofencing as part of a research study to support graded community leave, but evidence of effectiveness is preliminary. You sit on the hospital’s steering committee for this pilot. The tribunal asks you to advise whether to recommend geofencing as a condition of leave. What is the most ethically appropriate response?
options: A. Recommend compulsory smartphone geofencing as a condition of leave based on promising early internal experience, even though robust evidence is lacking and outside a formal research protocol.
B. Offer geofencing as a voluntary option within the pilot, emphasizing recovery goals and consent, but do not address your involvement in the study unless asked.
C. Decline to consider any technology-enabled monitoring in all forensic cases because it is inherently coercive and incompatible with recovery-focused care.

D. Disclose your conflict of interest and recuse yourself from advising on the geofencing device, while recommending person-focused, evidence-based supports and a structured leave plan; suggest the tribunal consider technology only within independent, ethics-approved research with voluntary consent and alternatives.
E. Avoid proactively disclosing your role in the pilot to prevent perceived bias, and recommend geofencing as an emerging standard of care.

question: A 19-year-old Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander man is brought to the ED under an involuntary hold for acute psychosis with command hallucinations to self-harm. He wears a cross necklace. His parents are in the waiting room. Nursing staff ask whether to contact the on-call hospital chaplain or a local community Elder now. Which is the MOST ethical next step consistent with the RANZCP’s guidance on religious/spiritual matters?
options: A) Based on his necklace and background, proactively contact the hospital chaplain and a local Elder without discussing it with him, as this will enhance cultural safety and reduce imminent risk.
B) Focus exclusively on medical stabilisation and defer any spiritual or cultural exploration until after discharge, as discussing such matters may reinforce psychotic content.

C) Prioritise immediate safety and clinical containment; once he can engage briefly, ask how his spiritual/cultural beliefs relate to his distress and care preferences; offer, and only with his explicit consent, referral to a chaplain or Aboriginal health worker; document preferences and revisit as capacity fluctuates.
D) Ask his parents to consent on his behalf for the chaplain/Elder to attend, as detention implies a lack of capacity for such decisions.
E) Provide psychoeducation that religious ideas are part of his psychosis and advise abstaining from all spiritual practices during admission to minimise risk.

question: A 38-year-old Muslim woman with generalised anxiety disorder is taking sertraline 100 mg daily and lorazepam 0.5 mg PRN. She plans to fast during Ramadan and worries about medication timing and daytime drowsiness as an ICU nurse. You know her husband socially (he coaches your child’s soccer team) and he is also a local imam. She asks for guidance and possible links to community supports. Which actions best align with the RANZCP’s guidance on religious/spiritual issues? Select ALL that apply.
options: A) Explore how her observance and values intersect with her treatment; discuss risks/benefits and consider adjusting medication timing (e.g., suhoor/iftar) if clinically appropriate; seek her explicit consent before contacting any religious advisor.
B) Because her husband is both spouse and an imam, call him to coordinate medication advice and spiritual support, as his role implies consent.

C) Acknowledge limits to your expertise in Islamic practices; offer to review reputable resources together and, with her permission, liaise with a Muslim chaplain or culturally informed health worker; avoid assumptions based on her name or attire.
D) Encourage her to replace prayer with secular mindfulness because it is more evidence-based, and recommend limiting or ceasing fasting to prevent relapse.
E) Decline to discuss religious issues as outside the scope of psychiatric care; focus the session on pharmacology and symptom scales.

F) Disclose your social connection to her husband; reassure her you will not contact him without her permission; offer the option to continue or transfer care depending on her preference, and document her choice.

question: A 35-year-old Māori man with bipolar I disorder (recent mania now resolving) smokes 25 cigarettes/day and has mild COPD. He wants to cut down while on the inpatient unit, stating that varenicline caused adverse effects in the past and nicotine patches alone were unhelpful. A local vape retailer has dropped off several free sample kits to the ward. He has a 6-year-old child at home. Which of the following actions are ethically appropriate and consistent with RANZCP guidance on nicotine vaping products (NVPs)? Select all that apply.
options: A. Offer an NVP as a harm-minimisation option, ensuring any product used is compliant with TGA/VRA standards, and incorporate it into a documented quit/harm-reduction plan with follow-up.
B. Provide the patient one of the retailer-donated sample kits so he can trial vaping before discharge, as this reduces costs and improves engagement.
C. Avoid discussing NVPs given uncertain long-term effects and rely solely on nicotine replacement therapy.
D. If he chooses to vape, counsel him to avoid use around children and to store devices/fluids safely, making clear they are not to be made available to minors.
E. Suggest he source a higher-concentration device from any online vendor to maximise nicotine delivery, without needing to check safety standards or regulatory compliance.

question: A 17-year-old student with generalised anxiety disorder denies any tobacco use. He asks you to prescribe a vape to help with stress and concentration because “everyone at school vapes.” His parent phones later to request a prescription to “keep him away from cigarettes,” and a local school invites you to give a talk promoting vaping as a safe alternative for students. What is the single most ethically appropriate next step consistent with RANZCP guidance on NVPs?
options: A. Prescribe a low-dose NVP pre-emptively to reduce the chance of future cigarette smoking, as a harm-minimisation strategy.

B. Decline to prescribe an NVP; instead, provide smoking-prevention and evidence-based anxiety management advice, avoid endorsing vaping to minors (decline the promotional talk), and, with the young person’s consent, discuss general health information with the parent.
C. Provide the parent with a prescription for an NVP to keep at home as a deterrent, but advise not to inform the adolescent to preserve the therapeutic alliance.
D. Accept the school’s invitation and present NVPs as a safe coping aid for student anxiety, highlighting availability of regulated products.
E. Recommend a nicotine-free vape for situational anxiety because this avoids prescribing an NVP to a non–nicotine-dependent youth.

question: You work in a rural community service in Aotearoa New Zealand. Mere, a 72-year-old Māori woman with recurrent major depression and type 2 diabetes, has limited income, a basic smartphone with a prepaid plan, and lives 2 hours from the clinic. Your service is considering introducing a mood-monitoring and CBT skills app for follow-up between telepsychiatry reviews. Mere’s husband worries about data privacy; Mere worries about data costs and her confidence with technology. Which actions best align with RANZCP recommendations on e‑mental health? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Offer the app as part of a stepped-care plan with clear opt-in consent; discuss benefits, risks (including privacy, data costs, and limitations), and available non-digital alternatives; ensure clinicians are trained to support targeted use and agree on outcome monitoring.
B. Make the app mandatory for all outpatients to standardise metrics and reduce travel burden, with discharge for non-adherence unless there is acute risk.

C. Verify the app’s evidence base, data security, and local regulatory/endorsement status in Australia/New Zealand; prefer tools with independent oversight and report any misleading claims to relevant bodies.
D. Ask Mere’s adult grandson to manage her login and view her mood entries to facilitate whānau support, without seeking explicit permission to minimise anxiety about technology.
E. Advocate for clinic-level or government-funded support (e.g., devices, data vouchers, public Wi‑Fi access) to improve equitable access for consenting patients in remote communities.

question: In an Early Psychosis Intervention Service in Australia, a startup offers a free 6‑month pilot of an AI-enabled smartphone tool that predicts relapse and self-harm risk. The company invites you to join its advisory board with honoraria. Published evidence is limited to a small feasibility study; the app stores data on overseas servers and claims 90% accuracy in suicide prediction. The team wants to roll it out quickly due to several high-risk cases and frequent cannabis use in the cohort. What is the MOST appropriate next step according to RANZCP recommendations? Select ONE.
options: A. Implement the tool across the caseload immediately because potential benefits outweigh uncertainties, and plan to audit outcomes later.
B. Decline the pilot and avoid any e‑mental health tools in early psychosis until multiple large RCTs with long-term outcomes are available.

C. Disclose and manage the conflict of interest (recuse from procurement decisions), seek independent ethics/privacy and cybersecurity review including data jurisdiction, verify evidence and marketing claims, and if approved pilot within a formal research framework with informed consent and integration into usual care pathways.
D. Proceed with the trial using deidentified data only, which obviates the need for specific patient consent or external oversight.
E. Ask the company to tone down its marketing claims and begin the pilot, as marketing is the primary ethical concern rather than data governance or research design.

question: An ADF base hospital psychiatrist is treating L., a 28-year-old infantry veteran, 6 weeks postpartum, with PTSD and hazardous alcohol use. She is scheduled to separate from service in 2 months. Attendance is erratic; she declines involvement of her Māori partner and wider whānau "for now." There is no imminent risk. She has no identified community GP. In line with RANZCP recommendations to support current service members, veterans and their families, which is the most appropriate next action?
options: A. Seek L.’s consent to liaise with the Defence Transition Unit and Veterans’ Affairs to arrange a standardised wellbeing and health assessment as part of discharge; with consent, coordinate proactive outreach follow-up with a community GP, and offer an optional family/whānau session plus carer support referrals for her partner.

B. Defer interagency coordination until after discharge to avoid overwhelming her; focus only on symptom management within Defence clinic appointments and do not contact family/whānau unless she initiates it.

C. Rely on implied consent for continuity of care to share clinically relevant details with the Defence Transition Unit and her partner despite her preference to exclude family, given the complexity of transition and absence of acute risk.

D. Draft a policy letter advocating for future embedding of psychiatric expertise within transition services and postpone any discussions about family engagement or sharing information with other services until after separation.
E. Enrol L. into a service-evaluation research dataset without explicit consent so her information can inform long-term improvements to veterans’ services.

question: You are seconded for 12 months to a joint Australian–New Zealand veterans agency to help design a mental health support program for current service members and those transitioning to civilian life. Which proposals are ethically aligned with the RANZCP recommendations for governments regarding support, specialist embedding, coordination across the service lifecycle, research, lifetime wellbeing assessment at discharge, and the role of family/whānau and carers?
options: A. Introduce a routine, standardised lifetime wellbeing and health assessment offered to all personnel at discharge with proactive outreach and scheduled follow-ups; conduct it only with informed consent and, with consent, share relevant information with primary care and veterans’ services; offer family/whānau sessions and carer support options.
B. Embed consultant psychiatrists within Defence Transition Units and Veterans’ Affairs case management teams to provide clinical leadership, consultation-liaison, and workforce training.
C. Limit program eligibility to those with formal DSM-5 psychiatric diagnoses to preserve resources and avoid medicalising transition; exclude families/whānau to prioritise individual privacy.

D. Establish a longitudinal research registry with robust governance that collects de-identified outcomes (e.g., mental health, employment, housing, family wellbeing) using informed, opt-in consent, and commit to regular evaluation cycles that adapt services to identified gaps.

E. Channel all counselling through community charities and keep government services at arm’s length to avoid perceived state interference; avoid coordination with primary care to minimise privacy risks.
F. Implement a high-risk-only outreach model that initiates contact after sentinel events (e.g., suicide attempts, police reports) to respect autonomy by avoiding proactive engagement.

question: A 23-year-old trans woman, an international student from a refugee background, presents with panic, nightmares, heavy episodic alcohol use, and passive suicidal thoughts. She discloses she was sexually assaulted but says she does not want to discuss details today. Her mother, who is unaware of the assault, is in the waiting room asking for information. There is no plan or intent and she agrees to stay with a friend tonight. What is the most ethically appropriate next step consistent with trauma-informed practice? Select ONE best answer.
options: A. Acknowledge her disclosure and feelings, use her preferred name and pronouns, seek consent for a brief, proportionate safety assessment and collaborative plan; defer detailed trauma exploration; offer choices about involving supports and referrals (including LGBTIQ+-affirming and alcohol services), and instill hope about recovery.
B. Proceed with a detailed trauma interview including sensory details to promote desensitisation, as avoidance risks worsening PTSD; inform her mother afterward to ensure social support.
C. Avoid all questions about trauma or suicide to prevent re-traumatisation; prescribe a benzodiazepine for immediate relief; discharge and call her mother for collateral without her consent.

D. Explain that trauma reactions are maladaptive learned behaviours that should be extinguished; require abstinence from alcohol as a prerequisite for any care; book prolonged exposure starting tomorrow and encourage confronting the memory now.
E. Focus exclusively on panic symptoms and start an SSRI; advise that trauma can be revisited in a month; document “no trauma history” since details were not discussed.

question: A 45-year-old Aboriginal man with schizoaffective disorder and a history of childhood institutionalisation is stable on a long-acting antipsychotic. After a landlord inspection, he had an angry outburst; the housing service requests a report about tenancy risk. He denies current intent to harm self or others. His adult daughter expresses concern for the grandchildren, noting family and community trauma. Which actions best reflect trauma-informed practice in this context? Select THREE answers.
options: A. Engage collaboratively to understand triggers and environmental stressors; frame anger as an adaptive survival response in context; co-develop a plan that emphasises strengths and choices; offer linkage to an Aboriginal health worker and family-inclusive practice; obtain consent before contacting family or services.
B. For a thorough report, require detailed written accounts of all traumatic events from both the patient and his daughter, noting it may be distressing but is necessary for accurate documentation.

C. With the patient’s informed consent, liaise with the housing service, GP, and an Aboriginal community-controlled health service to build integrated supports for tenancy stressors and ensure continuity of care.
D. Advise the daughter that the effects of trauma are largely genetic and there is little services can do to mitigate transgenerational transmission; avoid raising unrealistic hopes.

E. Offer psychoeducation (with the patient’s consent) about how trauma affects affect regulation and brain physiology; use hopeful language about recovery and post-traumatic growth; screen proportionately for suicidality and family safety as indicated.

F. To remain neutral for the housing report, avoid discussing trauma at all and provide only diagnosis and risk ratings without contextual context; do not consult culturally specific supports to avoid bias.

question: A 24-year-old Aboriginal man presents to the emergency department highly agitated after methamphetamine use, with shouting and pacing but no weapon. His aunt reports he has a history of being restrained by police and becomes panicked when confined. Security is nearby. The Aboriginal liaison officer is on-call and can attend in 10–15 minutes. Which ONE approach best aligns with trauma-informed practice (TIP) while addressing safety?
options: A. Prioritise control by immediate intramuscular sedation and seclusion with 1:1 observations; defer any family involvement or cultural liaison until he is sober to avoid confusion; afterwards consider arranging TIP training for staff.

B. Attempt de-escalation and offer clear choices; involve the Aboriginal liaison and the aunt if the patient agrees; avoid seclusion unless all less-restrictive measures fail; if medication is needed, explain the rationale and options; plan a brief post-incident debrief for staff and family to minimise retraumatisation.

C. Given likely impaired capacity due to intoxication, obtain collateral from the aunt and proceed without seeking the patient’s permission for her involvement; cultural liaison is unnecessary in acute agitation; use firm limit-setting with visible security to establish control.
D. Follow the standard behavioural emergency pathway without modifications for trauma history to ensure consistency and equity; document that TIP adjustments could introduce bias.
E. Ask security to restrain him briefly so a detailed trauma history can be documented immediately, allowing the ED team to avoid triggers later in the shift.

question: You are clinical director of a community mental health service that includes a general adult team and a small forensic outreach stream. About 35% of service users identify as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander. The manager proposes a minimal, low-cost rollout of “trauma-informed care.” Which options best align with RANZCP recommendations for trauma-informed practice at a service level? (Select ALL that apply.)
options: A. Establish a co-design group that includes people with lived experience of trauma, carers, Indigenous representatives, psychiatrists and other clinicians to guide service redesign, staff recruitment criteria, funding priorities, and physical environment changes (e.g., calming spaces, sensory modulation options) to reduce retraumatisation.
B. Provide a single, brief workshop for psychiatrists only this year; defer training for nursing, allied health and peer workers to future years, relying on psychiatrists to model TIP until then.
C. Choose one proprietary TIP framework and mandate exclusive use of that model across the service to ensure uniformity; discourage blending principles from multiple sources.

D. Embed routine, sensitive, consent-based trauma inquiry and response protocols across all disciplines, with privacy safeguards, options for declining questions, and staff supervision to mitigate vicarious trauma.

E. Provide ongoing TIP education and reflective practice for all team members, with specific modules on historical trauma and cultural safety for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and Māori service users; track outcomes such as reduced restraint/seclusion and complaint rates.
F. Outsource trauma-specific issues to external therapists so general service staff can avoid engaging with trauma content and thereby minimise harm.

question: You are the on-call psychiatrist for a regional hospital. At 2:00 a.m., a 17-year-old Māori rangatahi presents to the emergency department after an episode of self-harm with stated intent to die. He is mildly intoxicated with alcohol, distressed about recent school exclusion and homelessness, and requests that his aunt (whānau) be involved. There is no on-site mental health clinician after midnight, but a telepsychiatry service is available. Which ONE of the following responses best aligns with the RANZCP ethical recommendations for suicide prevention? Select ONE answer.
options: A. Admit the patient to the general ward under security observation and defer any psychiatric assessment until morning, given the limited overnight resources and his improving agitation.

B. Activate an immediate telepsychiatry consultation; with consent, involve a Māori health navigator and whānau; complete a culturally responsive, trauma-informed risk assessment and co-produced safety plan; arrange an active warm handover to 24/7 crisis supports; and organise assertive post-attempt aftercare with trained peer support.

C. Notify police and child protection services due to the patient’s age and intoxication, restrict family involvement because of confidentiality concerns, and plan for an outpatient psychiatry referral in several days.
D. Focus ED care on medical stabilisation only and postpone all mental health involvement until the patient is fully sober the next day, when an outpatient appointment can be scheduled.

E. Provide a brief trauma-informed conversation and involve whānau with consent, but discharge the patient with written information and next-day GP follow-up, as telepsychiatry is not routinely used overnight.

question: You are the clinical director of a community mental health service asked to co-design a district suicide prevention plan after several recent deaths among young men working in construction, LGBTQ+ youth, and people recently discharged from inpatient units. Partners include primary care, EDs, drug and alcohol services, peer-led organisations, and Māori and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community-controlled health services. Data privacy concerns and budget constraints have been raised. Which of the following actions are MOST consistent with the RANZCP ethical recommendations? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Standardise ED discharge after suicidal presentation to a generic leaflet and GP advice, avoiding active aftercare contacts to minimise privacy risks and staff workload.

B. Implement individualised, assertive post-attempt aftercare with rapid follow-up, caring contacts, and warm handovers; integrate trained peer support and alcohol and other drug services; use opt-out consent with clear information and robust privacy safeguards.
C. Exclude lived-experience workers from training design and delivery to prevent potential re-traumatisation, limiting curriculum development to psychiatrists and senior clinicians.

D. Provide system-wide training for ED, primary care, and community staff in suicide prevention competencies and Trauma Informed Practice, with specific modules addressing culturally responsive care for high-risk groups.
E. Reallocate resources from 24/7 crisis lines to expand business-hours clinics, reducing duplication with emergency departments.

F. Participate in a governed, privacy-protected real-time suicide and self-harm surveillance initiative that includes Indigenous data sovereignty, collects demographic and social determinants (e.g., unemployment, homelessness), and uses findings to iteratively adjust targeted interventions.

question: You are assessing a 38-year-old recently arrived refugee woman in a public community clinic for major depressive symptoms and chronic pain. She has multiple bruises of varying ages. Her husband, who speaks more English, insists on staying as her interpreter due to religious and cultural norms about modesty and privacy. The woman avoids eye contact and gives brief answers. There are two young children at home. Which of the following actions best align with ethical obligations regarding family violence in psychiatric assessment and care?
options: A. Accept the husband as interpreter to respect cultural practices and build rapport; defer any inquiry into family violence until she volunteers information at a later appointment.

B. Arrange a professional female interpreter; ensure private time with the patient; explain limits of confidentiality; conduct a sensitive, evidence-based inquiry about current and past family violence, assess immediate risk (including for children), and initiate safety planning with referral to specialist family violence services.
C. Document your concerns but avoid referral or direct questioning until she explicitly discloses abuse, as proactive screening risks cultural insensitivity and may undermine therapeutic alliance.

D. Use a validated family violence screening tool; provide psychoeducation about the link between family violence and mental health; with her consent, refer to local culturally competent family violence support and schedule prompt follow-up to monitor risk.

E. Because there is no clear imminent risk, focus on treating depression first and advise her to discuss relationship matters with her primary care doctor, avoiding direct questions that may be re-traumatising.

question: A 45-year-old man is referred by a court-mandated program following an assault charge related to an incident with his pregnant partner. He reports binge drinking but minimises risk, asking you for a letter stating he poses no danger to expedite return home. You recognise his partner as someone you treated two years ago for anxiety; she is not currently your patient. Which actions best uphold ethical responsibilities regarding family violence in psychiatric practice?
options: A. Provide a factual letter that outlines attendance and current clinical engagement without offering assurances about risk; conduct a structured risk assessment, and with his consent liaise with a specialist perpetrator intervention program and substance use services.
B. Write a supportive letter emphasising his motivation for treatment and defer risk assessment until therapy is well-established, because risk opinions are for the court, not clinicians.

C. Since you previously treated his partner, include details from her prior clinical records in your court report without seeking her consent, as disclosure is in the public interest to protect her safety.

D. Clarify limits of confidentiality, assess imminent and ongoing risk to the partner and unborn child, and if risk is high, follow legal and service protocols (e.g., contacting appropriate protection services), documenting rationale and actions taken.

E. Refer him to a culturally responsive perpetrator intervention and integrated alcohol treatment while continuing psychiatric care that avoids colluding with minimisation; seek supervision regarding the prior therapeutic relationship with his partner and consider transferring care to avoid conflict of interest.

question: You assess a 16-year-old trans boy presenting to the ED with worsening depression and recent superficial self-harm, but no current imminent risk. His mother is supportive; his father is opposed to any gender-affirming care and demands all information be shared with him. The young person requests confidentiality, asks for accurate information about care pathways, and a referral to a multidisciplinary gender service. As the on-call child and adolescent psychiatrist, which ONE action best aligns with the RANZCP’s recommendations for TGD care?
options: A. Focus solely on treating depression and self-harm, deferring any gender-related discussions until psychiatric symptoms fully remit to avoid diagnostic overshadowing.

B. Undertake a developmentally appropriate, person-centred assessment including gender history, capacity and risk; provide high-quality information about care pathways (e.g., psychosocial support, puberty suppression if indicated); clarify confidentiality limits with the young person and parents; engage the supportive parent; and facilitate timely referral to a multidisciplinary gender service alongside a safety plan.
C. Inform both parents that no referrals will be made until an independent forensic evaluation determines the authenticity of gender dysphoria, given medico-legal risk.
D. Because of the recent self-harm, recommend at least 12 months without any self-harm and complete abstinence from substances before considering any gender-affirming interventions or referral.
E. Initiate testosterone in the ED under implied consent given the patient’s age, to demonstrate support and reduce distress, and arrange endocrine review after discharge.

question: A 28-year-old Māori trans woman with schizophrenia is admitted involuntarily for acute psychosis. She has been taking estradiol and an anti-androgen as part of established gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT). Some staff are unsure whether to continue GAHT; misgendering has occurred on the ward. You also sit on the hospital’s formulary committee. Which actions best align with the RANZCP’s recommendations for TGD care? Select THREE.
options: A. Continue her established GAHT during admission unless there are clear contraindications or interactions, reviewing risks and monitoring appropriately.
B. Use her legal sex marker and avoid pronouns during admission to minimise staff confusion, returning to affirmed name/pronouns at discharge.
C. Arrange cultural support (e.g., Māori health worker), ensure correct name/pronouns are used, and address staff training needs to promote cultural safety.
D. Delay restarting GAHT until an outpatient endocrinology review post-discharge to avoid taking responsibility for gender-related treatment decisions during psychosis.

E. Provide high-quality information and psychoeducation about TGD health; discuss informed consent principles before changing any medications; document consent and involve her nominated support person if she wishes.
F. Refrain from advocating for TGD-inclusive policies or access on the ward due to your membership on the formulary committee, to avoid any perception of conflict of interest.
G. Invite her to a TGD mental health research study as a condition of continuing GAHT in hospital, to help address evidence gaps.

question: A 22-year-old Māori man, Tane, is brought in by police following methamphetamine intoxication and agitation. He is now calmer but intermittently disoriented. He asks that his uncle speak with you and be involved in decisions. There is no on-site Māori health worker overnight, but an on-call cultural advisory line is available via telehealth. Bed pressures are high, and you need to make a risk and admission decision. Which ONE option best upholds the RANZCP cultural safety guidance while meeting clinical obligations?
options: A. Proceed immediately with a full assessment excluding whānau due to confidentiality, as Tane is intoxicated and cannot consent to their involvement.

B. Seek and document Tane’s consent to involve his uncle, use the on-call Māori cultural advisory telehealth service to support the assessment, and incorporate cultural considerations into risk formulation and the immediate management plan.
C. Defer assessment until a Māori health worker is on shift the next day to ensure cultural safety, even if this delays decisions about imminent risk.
D. Ask the non-Indigenous social worker to provide cultural advice for Māori consumers given their local experience, and proceed without cultural supervision.
E. Use a standard risk assessment template only and avoid considering cultural factors to ensure equitable, uniform care.

question: You are clinical director of a metropolitan inpatient psychiatry unit serving large Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Māori, Pasifika, and refugee communities. Interpreter use is inconsistent, a small group of bilingual staff are frequently asked to interpret and report burnout, family/whānau involvement is restricted to standard visiting hours, and cultural safety is not mentioned in the service code of conduct. After a complaint about culturally unsafe care, you are asked to propose changes. Which of the following service-level actions are ethically required or strongly consistent with the RANZCP recommendations on cultural safety? Select ALL that apply.
options: A. Mandate annual CPD for all psychiatrists and trainees on cultural safety and health equity, including reflective practice with accredited cultural supervisors, and embed expectations into performance review.
B. Recruit and appropriately remunerate bilingual peer workers and cultural liaison officers from key communities served, and include them in leadership and co-design committees.
C. To avoid burdening diverse staff, discourage them from any culture-related roles and remove cultural considerations from care plans to promote uniformity.

D. Establish a system to routinely collect, monitor, and publicly report cultural safety outcomes (e.g., experiences of care by ethnicity, interpreter uptake, recruitment and retention of diverse staff) with community governance input.
E. Use bilingual clinical staff as interpreters instead of professional interpreters, as their clinical knowledge ensures accuracy and reduces costs.
F. Update the service code of conduct to explicitly endorse culturally safe practice and require training, supervision, appropriate interpreter use, and whānau-inclusive care where appropriate.
G. Permit family/whānau involvement only after discharge to avoid confidentiality issues during inpatient treatment.

question: You are treating a 23-year-old Somali refugee with PTSD and major depression in an outpatient trauma clinic. After a record-breaking heatwave worsened his insomnia and distress, you posted on your professional social media a photo of your waiting room with the caption: "My 23-year-old Somali patient’s symptoms worsened this week—climate crisis is a health emergency." No name is used and the patient’s face is not visible. A colleague raises concerns about confidentiality and ethics. Which single next step best aligns with ethical climate action for psychiatrists while respecting professional obligations?
options: A. Keep the post up because it serves the public interest; every voice counts and clinicians should use their platforms prominently in health emergencies.

B. Remove the post immediately, acknowledge and remediate the confidentiality risk (including apologizing to the patient if identifiable), and channel advocacy into evidence-based, non-identifiable avenues (e.g., de-identified data, peer-reviewed work) while undertaking CPD on climate–mental health.
C. Leave the post up but disable comments and add a disclaimer that no patient-identifying information was disclosed.
D. Seek ethics committee approval to continue posting similar case anecdotes provided you avoid names and directly identifying details.

question: You are conducting a court-ordered risk assessment of a 58-year-old male farmer who allegedly threatened a neighbour during an extreme heat event. He has major depressive disorder and hazardous alcohol use. He dismisses climate change and becomes defensive if the topic is raised. You also serve on your hospital’s sustainability committee and are invited to sign a departmental statement recognising climate change as a health emergency. Which of the following actions are ethically appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
options: A. Use the forensic interview to challenge the patient’s beliefs about climate change and emphasise your committee role to persuade him, as this educative approach benefits public health.

B. In the report, incorporate peer-reviewed evidence on extreme heat, sleep disturbance, and aggression/suicide risk as relevant to this individual’s formulation, avoiding moralising and remaining within the forensic brief.
C. Decline all climate-related professional activities to preserve the appearance of neutrality in forensic work, even outside the assessment context.

D. Undertake CPD on climate–mental health impacts in rural settings and integrate an environmental stressor screen (e.g., heat, bushfire exposure, drought) into your assessment where clinically relevant.
E. Collaborate on a de-identified audit of heat-related behavioural disturbances in forensic referrals and submit findings to a peer-reviewed venue to inform services.

question: You are the on-call psychiatrist for a regional service. A 23-year-old Māori man with major depressive disorder has escalating suicidal ideation with intent. He lives 250 km away in a flood-affected town where internet and phone coverage are unreliable. The local ED is staffed by nurses but has no on-site psychiatry. The service has committed to reducing its carbon emissions, including encouraging telepsychiatry and minimizing travel where clinically appropriate. Which is the most ethical next step?
options: A) Conduct a telepsychiatry assessment from your office despite poor connectivity and a lack of a private room at the rural site, relying on an ED nurse to remain with the patient for safety.

B) Arrange an urgent in-person psychiatric assessment by the nearest available psychiatrist (yourself or a regional colleague), coordinate with the crisis team to minimize duplicate trips, and plan travel efficiently; use telehealth only if it can be conducted safely and confidentially.
C) Delay assessment for 48 hours to consolidate multiple outreach visits into one trip, thereby reducing emissions while the ED nurse provides observational support.
D) Complete a risk assessment by phone with the patient’s family and GP only, and write a management plan without direct patient assessment to avoid travel given the climate impact.
E) Decline assessment and recommend a police welfare check and compulsory admission without psychiatric review, citing the service’s commitment to reducing travel-related emissions.

question: Dr L runs a metropolitan youth anxiety clinic and performs monthly outreach to a rural Aboriginal community 300 km away. Many patients have intermittent internet access; one 19-year-old with PTSD has recent self-harm. After a severe heatwave, the local council invites Dr L to speak about mental health impacts of extreme heat. Dr L’s personal superannuation is in an index fund with significant fossil fuel exposure. Which actions best align with ethical responsibilities regarding climate and mental health? Select all that apply.
options: A) Accept the invitation and present an evidence-based summary of climate-related mental health impacts, avoid any patient-identifying material, disclose relevant conflicts of interest, and advocate for practical measures (e.g., cooling centers, shaded spaces).
B) Decline the invitation because advocacy on climate is political and outside the remit of psychiatric practice; restrict activities to individual clinical care.

C) Review and adjust clinic travel by preferring telehealth only where clinically appropriate, confidential, and safe; bundle rural appointments to reduce trips; retain in-person reviews for high-risk patients and those with digital or cultural access barriers.
D) Maintain current personal and practice investments in fossil-fuel–focused funds because financial choices are private and unrelated to professional ethics.

E) Seek a research grant from a gas company to study eco-anxiety, proceed without institutional ethics review because it is low-risk survey work, and agree to keep the funding source confidential to reduce perceived bias.
F) Integrate routine screening for climate-related stressors (e.g., heat exposure, smoke, displacement) into assessments and undertake CPD to update knowledge on climate–mental health links.

question: During an inpatient admission on a rural mental health unit, you are treating J, a 22-year-old Aboriginal man with moderate intellectual disability (ID), schizoaffective disorder, and hazardous alcohol use. He has been excluded from group programs due to behavioural escalation, and his NDIS-funded group home requests discharge within 48 hours after a recent police caution for an altercation. There is ongoing moderate risk to others if discharged without supports. The hospital has no specialist ID mental health team. You also sit on the hospital’s mental health advisory committee. Which action best aligns with the ethical principle for systems addressing the mental health needs of people with ID?
options: A. Expedite discharge via the standard psychosis pathway and refer to generic alcohol counselling; avoid raising systemic gaps at committee level to prevent tokenistic policy changes.

B. Convene an immediate cross-sector case conference (disability provider/NDIS planner, Aboriginal health worker, justice liaison, AOD service, group home), obtain consent to share information, request specialist ID mental health outreach/telehealth input, document his needs in the service dataset, and escalate to the advisory committee the need for dedicated ID funding and inclusion of ID clinical and lived-experience representation.
C. Prioritise short-term risk reduction by adjusting medication; defer data collection and inter-agency collaboration until outpatient follow-up to avoid delaying discharge.
D. Provide a one-off de-escalation workshop for ward staff, but decline to involve the Primary Health Network or disability sector as this extends beyond your clinical remit.
E. Place J on a Community Treatment Order and instruct the group home to enforce adherence; withhold clinical information from the disability provider citing confidentiality even if J consents.

question: You are a consultant psychiatrist in a forensic alcohol and other drug (AOD) diversion service. S is a 35-year-old woman with mild ID, PTSD, and methamphetamine use disorder on a drug court order. The service is revising policies to improve completion rates. The working group has no ID specialist clinicians or peer/lived-experience representatives. Preliminary audit suggests poorer outcomes for participants with ID, but ID status and related needs are inconsistently recorded. Funding discussions propose internal redistribution only, with no additional budget. Which recommendations are ethically indicated under the principle?
options: A. Advocate for inclusion of an ID mental health specialist psychiatrist and people with lived experience (including peer workforce roles) on the advisory/working group.

B. Establish systematic collection of data on ID status, mental health needs, and outcomes for service users with ID, with appropriate consent and privacy safeguards, to inform planning and evaluation.
C. Recommend training for all justice, AOD, and mental health staff to adapt care for people with ID, and commission specialist ID mental health clinics to support complex cases.
D. Support covering ID-focused initiatives purely by reallocating existing general mental health funds and explicitly avoid dedicated budget lines to prevent overall budget growth.
E. Prefer universal policy language without naming ID explicitly to avoid stigmatization, relying on standard clinical pathways to be inclusive by default.

question: You are the on-call consultant psychiatrist in a metropolitan hospital. Alex, a 28-year-old Autistic woman who is gender diverse (she/they), presents to ED with severe anxiety, depressive symptoms, and intermittent passive suicidal ideation after losing her job. She occasionally uses cannabis. The ED is crowded and brightly lit; security has been called twice due to escalating distress. Alex declines family involvement but nominates a peer support worker as a support person. The ward has no formal autism pathway. Which actions best align with the ethical principle that systems addressing the mental health needs of Autistic people should be cohesive, cross-sector, inclusive of Autistic voices, and supported by training and appropriate resourcing? Select THREE options.
options: A. With Alex’s consent, involve the ward occupational therapist and a local Autistic peer advisor to co-design a sensory-adapted care plan for ED and the ward (e.g., low-stimulation environment, communication preferences), and incorporate Alex’s stated priorities into a shared safety and discharge plan.
B. Describe Alex as “high functioning” and proceed with standard ward routines to maintain equity between patients, deferring any autism-specific adjustments unless incidents recur.

C. Escalate to hospital leadership to implement autism-specific training for ED, inpatient, and security staff; develop a protocol for reasonable adjustments; and seek funding for a small specialist autism liaison function to support complex presentations.

D. Discharge Alex to a standard group CBT for depression without modification, as the evidence base is strong regardless of neurodevelopmental status, and avoid coordination with disability or social services to keep care within mental health.

E. Convene a multidisciplinary cross-sector case conference prior to discharge (with Alex’s consent) including primary care, NDIS/support coordination, housing services, addiction services, and LGBTQ+ community supports to ensure integrated follow-up and role clarity.

question: You are commissioned by Youth Justice to assess K., a 16-year-old Autistic Aboriginal boy in a regional youth detention centre following several aggressive outbursts toward staff. There is ongoing risk to others. The centre has limited allied health availability and no autism-specific training. K.’s mother lives remotely and wants to be involved; K. agrees to her involvement. Which approach BEST aligns with the ethical principle that systems for Autistic people’s mental health should be cohesive, cross-sector, include Autistic voices, fund training and research, and operate within health/mental health/disability frameworks?
options: A. Restrict recommendations to pharmacotherapy and incident-management strategies inside the detention unit, noting that broader service or policy reforms are outside the scope of a clinical assessment.

B. Recommend an integrated, multidisciplinary plan across justice health, education-in-custody, disability supports, and community services; arrange autism-specific training for detention staff; include K.’s preferences and his mother via Aboriginal liaison; and propose a pilot sensory-modulation program with de-identified outcomes contributed to an ethics-approved service evaluation to inform future funding.
C. Seek urgent transfer to the state adolescent acute psychiatric unit to stabilise behaviour first, with a plan to consider cross-sector engagement only after discharge from hospital.
D. Avoid family involvement due to the custodial setting and maintain confidentiality by not contacting K.’s mother despite his consent.
E. Arrange telehealth follow-up with a city autism clinic after release while deferring any environmental modifications or staff training during detention to avoid overburdening the centre.

question: In a regional CAMHS clinic in Aotearoa New Zealand, you assess Tama, a 10-year-old Māori boy with emerging conduct problems (aggression at school and at home following his father’s recent incarceration). There is no current imminent risk to self or others; risk is situational and presently contained. The school is threatening suspension; Oranga Tamariki was previously involved but the case is closed. Hospital administration has asked clinicians to minimise time spent on external meetings due to budget pressures. Which course of action best aligns with RANZCP recommendations about early intervention, cross-agency collaboration, culturally responsive care for children with conduct disorder, and strengthening the specialised workforce?
options: A. With mother’s consent, organise an interagency case conference (school, Oranga Tamariki intake, and primary care) to coordinate supports that minimise school disruption; refer the family to an evidence-based, early parent-management program with Māori health/whānau engagement; and write to service managers advocating for timely access to specialist child and adolescent psychiatry input for Tama and similar cases.

B. Provide clinic-based therapy to Tama alone and defer parent or school involvement for three months to avoid potential stigma and confidentiality issues, reassessing interagency needs later if behaviours persist.
C. Delay early referrals until a formal external diagnostic confirmation of conduct disorder is obtained, as early intervention may mislabel the child; focus on watchful waiting with brief check-ins.

D. Initiate medication monotherapy and discharge follow-up to the GP to conserve specialist resources, advising the school to manage behaviour via its disciplinary policy rather than clinical collaboration.

E. Notify Oranga Tamariki immediately and share full records without discussing with the mother, as interagency collaboration is required for conduct problems even when there are no current safety concerns.

question: You are preparing a court-ordered psychiatric report for Jayden, a 14-year-old Aboriginal boy on a youth justice order with conduct disorder and cannabis use. He has no current imminent self-harm risk but has a history of fighting and school exclusion. The magistrate asks you to recommend a treatment plan and systemic supports. You also sit (unpaid) on the advisory board of a local private residential behaviour program that is seeking referrals. Which recommendations align with RANZCP principles about early intervention/prevention, cross-agency collaboration to minimise disruption, investment in targeted research, and workforce training for specialised child and adolescent services?
options: A. Recommend a coordinated plan spanning youth justice, education, primary care, and the family, with culturally safe, evidence-based parent management training and re-engagement with school to minimise disruption; propose a funded case coordinator to ensure continuity across agencies.

B. Recommend placement in the residential program on whose advisory board you sit, without declaration of your role, emphasising that the program offers specialised services lacking in public settings.
C. Suggest that the court prioritise expanding detention capacity over prevention services, as containment is necessary before any therapeutic gains can be attempted.

D. Propose referral to a university-affiliated trial of targeted prevention/early intervention for conduct problems that includes whānau/family engagement, ensuring informed consent, cultural safety, and clear separation between clinical care and research governance in your role.

E. Advise that cross-agency collaboration (justice, education, health) should be avoided to protect privacy; recommend that youth justice clinicians proceed independently to reduce information overload.

F. Recommend that the youth justice service, local schools, and community health invest in staff upskilling on conduct disorder (e.g., training in de-escalation and parent-focused interventions) and support the creation of additional child and adolescent psychiatry training posts in the region.

question: A 13-year-old Aboriginal boy living in a remote community presents with persistent aggression, school suspensions, and a history of multiple out-of-home placements. He meets criteria for conduct disorder and has a background of significant trauma. The regional health planning authority asks you, as the consulting psychiatrist, to advise on service design. The local hospital frequently sees him in the ED, and the school is pressuring for a “strong medication plan.” Which TWO recommendations are MOST ethically aligned with RANZCP guidance for health planning authorities in this context? Select TWO options.
options: A. Advocate for a trauma-informed pathway across ED/paediatrics and child protection, including staff training on avoiding re-traumatisation of children in care; partner with local Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations to co-design family-inclusive and culturally safe care for youth with conduct problems.

B. Advise planners to prioritise pharmacological management by adopting guidance that most adolescents with conduct disorder commence moderate-dose atypical antipsychotics as first-line, to be continued long term to reduce incidents across schools and EDs.

C. Recommend commissioning and scaling Multisystemic Therapy and Functional Family Therapy with outreach capacity, integration with schools, and facilitated family engagement, while developing a local workforce to deliver these interventions.
D. To minimise distress triggers, recommend limiting contact with carers and teachers during interventions and focus primarily on 1:1 clinician–youth work until symptoms stabilise.
E. Centralise specialised conduct-disorder services in the metropolitan hub and provide infrequent fly-in/fly-out clinics to remote areas, as local programs are unlikely to be sustainable.

question: A 12-year-old Māori girl is referred by her school for escalating fights after bullying incidents. She meets criteria for conduct disorder and has comorbid ADHD. There is no current imminent risk. Her grandmother (primary caregiver) reports past family trauma and requests culturally appropriate care. The school asks you to send her full psychiatric notes to “help with behaviour plans.” Which ONE of the following immediate plans best aligns with the RANZCP’s recommendations to health planning authorities while addressing ethical considerations in clinical practice?
options: A. Start risperidone at a moderate dose with the intention of indefinite continuation to stabilise behaviour, and advise the school to apply a firm zero-tolerance approach to enforce behavioural change.

B.
